import type { MeditationScript } from "./meditation-scripts";

export const childhoodBlueprint: MeditationScript = {
  id: "gen-childhood-blueprint",
  title: "The Childhood Blueprint",
  subtitle: "Tracing patterns back to their origin",
  category: "inner-work",
  durationSec: 720,
  description: "A gentle guided reflection to explore how childhood coping strategies may have evolved into adult patterns. Understanding the origin softens the grip.",
  evidenceSource: "Developmental trauma research; IFS (Schwartz); Beyond Addiction (Foote et al.)",
  tags: ["addiction-recovery", "inner-work", "childhood", "coping", "self-compassion", "root-cause"],
  phase: "all",
  backgroundMusic: "binaural",
  ttsScript: `Welcome to The Childhood Blueprint.

Find a quiet, private space. Settle into a comfortable position where your body feels fully supported. Gently close your eyes.

Take a slow breath in through your nose... and release it softly through your mouth. Again. Inhale... and let go. One more time. Inhale deeply... and exhale everything you've been carrying today.

Allow your breath to find its own natural rhythm now.

Today, you are going to travel gently backward in time. Not to relive anything painful, but to understand something important about yourself. You are here because you are brave enough to look.

Think about a pattern in your life that you want to understand. A habit, a reaction, a way of coping that feels automatic. Hold it lightly in your awareness.

Now... let your mind drift back. Not to a specific memory, but to a feeling. What did it feel like to be you as a child? What was the emotional atmosphere of your home?

Was it safe to express your feelings? Or did you learn to keep them inside?
Was it okay to need things? Or did you learn that needing was a burden?
Were big emotions welcomed? Or were they met with silence, anger, or withdrawal?

Notice what comes up. There are no wrong answers here. Just honest noticing.

As a child, you were extraordinarily intelligent. You figured out what you needed to do to survive, to feel safe, to be loved. Maybe you learned to be very quiet. Maybe you learned to perform. Maybe you learned to disappear. Maybe you learned to numb.

These were not flaws. They were strategies. Brilliant strategies for a child who had no other options.

Now... bring your current pattern back to mind. The one you want to understand.

Can you see how it might be connected to that younger version of you? Can you see the thread?

The child who learned that feeling was dangerous... might have grown into an adult who reaches for anything to avoid feeling.
The child who learned that love was conditional... might have grown into an adult who constantly seeks external validation or comfort.
The child who learned that the world was unpredictable... might have grown into an adult who craves control, or its opposite, total surrender.

You do not need to have a perfect insight right now. Just notice if something resonates. If something feels true in your body. Where do you feel it? Your chest? Your throat? Your stomach?

Place a gentle hand there if it feels right.

Now... imagine that younger version of you. Picture them clearly. Their face. Their eyes.

Silently, say to them:
I see you.
I understand why you did what you did.
You were doing your best with what you had.
You do not have to protect me in that way anymore.
I am here now. I can take care of us.

Let these words settle. Feel whatever comes. Grief, tenderness, relief. It is all welcome here.

You are not broken. You are not your patterns. You are the awareness that can hold it all... the child, the adult, the pattern, and the possibility of something new.

Take one more deep, grounding breath. Inhale compassion for that child. Exhale gratitude for your willingness to look.

When you are ready, gently open your eyes. Carry this understanding with you softly.`,
  steps: [
    { id: "s1", title: "Ground & Settle", body: "Breath work and intention setting.", startTimeSec: 0, endTimeSec: 90 },
    { id: "s2", title: "Recall Childhood", body: "Explore the emotional atmosphere of early life.", startTimeSec: 90, endTimeSec: 240 },
    { id: "s3", title: "Identify Strategies", body: "Recognise childhood coping as intelligence.", startTimeSec: 240, endTimeSec: 380 },
    { id: "s4", title: "Connect the Thread", body: "Link childhood strategies to adult patterns.", startTimeSec: 380, endTimeSec: 500 },
    { id: "s5", title: "Speak to the Child", body: "Offer words of understanding to younger self.", startTimeSec: 500, endTimeSec: 650 },
    { id: "s6", title: "Close", body: "Integrate with compassion.", startTimeSec: 650, endTimeSec: 720 },
  ],
};

export const shameInventory: MeditationScript = {
  id: "gen-shame-inventory",
  title: "The Shame Inventory",
  subtitle: "Gently releasing shame that fuels cycles",
  category: "inner-work",
  durationSec: 600,
  description: "A compassionate guided practice to identify shame that feeds addictive cycles, and begin to separate your identity from your behaviour.",
  evidenceSource: "Brene Brown shame resilience theory; Beyond Addiction (Foote et al.)",
  tags: ["addiction-recovery", "inner-work", "shame", "self-worth", "identity", "self-compassion"],
  phase: "all",
  backgroundMusic: "gentle",
  ttsScript: `Welcome to The Shame Inventory.

Find a comfortable, private place where you will not be disturbed. This practice asks for honesty, and honesty needs safety. So make sure you feel safe right now.

Settle into your body. Close your eyes. Take three slow breaths, each one a little deeper than the last.

Inhale... exhale.
Inhale... exhale.
Inhale... and let everything go.

Shame is one of the most powerful forces in the human experience. It whispers that something is fundamentally wrong with you. Not that you made a mistake, but that you are a mistake. And that whisper... it fuels the very cycles you are trying to break.

Today, you are going to look at shame directly. Not to wallow in it. But to take its power away.

Think of something you feel ashamed about. A behaviour. A moment. A pattern. Something you have hidden from others, or even from yourself.

Notice what happens in your body when you bring it to mind. Does your chest tighten? Does heat rise to your face? Does your stomach drop? Do you want to look away?

That is shame talking. And right now, you are going to do something radical. You are going to stay.

Shame survives in secrecy and silence. It loses its power the moment it is seen with compassion. So let us see it.

The thing you feel ashamed of... is it a behaviour? Good. Behaviours can change. They are things you did. They are not who you are.

Say this silently: I am not my worst moment.

Say it again: I am not defined by my patterns.

One more time: I am a whole person who is learning.

Now consider this... the behaviour that brought shame, what was it trying to do for you? Was it trying to help you cope? To escape pain? To feel something, or to feel nothing?

Even the things we are most ashamed of often started as attempts to survive. They deserve understanding, even as you choose to move beyond them.

Imagine gathering this shame... like a heavy stone you have been carrying. Feel its weight. You have been carrying it for so long.

Now, imagine setting it down. Not throwing it away in anger. Just... gently placing it on the ground beside you. You can look at it. You can acknowledge it. But you no longer need to carry it.

You are not your shame. You are the person who had the courage to look at it.

Take a deep, releasing breath. Feel your shoulders soften. Feel the space where that weight used to be.

You are worthy of compassion. Not because you are perfect. Because you are human.

When you are ready, gently open your eyes.`,
  steps: [
    { id: "s1", title: "Create Safety", body: "Settle and establish a safe inner space.", startTimeSec: 0, endTimeSec: 90 },
    { id: "s2", title: "Name the Shame", body: "Bring a specific shame to awareness.", startTimeSec: 90, endTimeSec: 200 },
    { id: "s3", title: "Stay Present", body: "Notice the body's response without fleeing.", startTimeSec: 200, endTimeSec: 300 },
    { id: "s4", title: "Separate Identity", body: "You are not your behaviour.", startTimeSec: 300, endTimeSec: 420 },
    { id: "s5", title: "Set It Down", body: "Visualise releasing the weight of shame.", startTimeSec: 420, endTimeSec: 540 },
    { id: "s6", title: "Close", body: "Affirm worth and open eyes.", startTimeSec: 540, endTimeSec: 600 },
  ],
};

export const emotionalLandscape: MeditationScript = {
  id: "gen-emotional-landscape",
  title: "Mapping Your Emotional Landscape",
  subtitle: "Discover which feelings you avoid",
  category: "inner-work",
  durationSec: 480,
  description: "Identify the specific emotions you struggle to feel, and how avoidance of those emotions drives habitual or compulsive behaviour.",
  evidenceSource: "Emotional literacy frameworks; ACT (Hayes); Brianna Wiest, The Human Element",
  tags: ["addiction-recovery", "inner-work", "emotions", "avoidance", "awareness", "self-inquiry"],
  phase: "all",
  backgroundMusic: "gentle",
  ttsScript: `Welcome to Mapping Your Emotional Landscape.

Settle into a comfortable position. Let your body soften. Close your eyes.

Breathe slowly. In through your nose... out through your mouth. Let each exhale carry away a little more tension.

Today, you are going to explore your relationship with your own emotions. Not to judge, but to map. To understand which feelings you welcome, and which ones you have learned to run from.

Imagine your emotional world as a landscape. A vast, open terrain.

Some areas are well-trodden. You visit them often. Maybe joy feels accessible. Or maybe anger is familiar. Or perhaps worry is where you spend most of your time.

But there are other areas... places you rarely go. Emotions you avoid, distract from, or numb.

Let us explore those quieter corners.

Sadness. How does your body respond to that word? Do you feel open to it, or does something tighten? When was the last time you let yourself feel truly sad without trying to fix it or move past it?

Loneliness. Not being alone... but feeling alone. Feeling unseen. Unmet. Does this feeling have a place in your landscape, or have you walled it off?

Vulnerability. The feeling of being exposed. Open. Unprotected. Where does this live in you? Do you allow it, or do you armour against it?

Grief. For things lost, for things that never were, for the person you thought you would become. Is there grief you have not fully felt?

Now... here is the key insight. The emotions we avoid... are often the ones that drive our most compulsive behaviours. We reach for food, for screens, for substances, for distraction... not because we are weak, but because we are trying not to feel something specific.

What emotion are you most afraid to feel? Sit with that question. Do not rush to answer. Let your body tell you.

Where do you feel the avoidance? Is it a wall in your chest? A locked door in your belly? A turning away in your mind?

What if you did not have to feel it all at once? What if you could just... acknowledge it exists? Just say: I know you are there. I am not ready to feel you fully yet, and that is okay. But I see you.

That acknowledgment alone begins to change the pattern. Because the pattern was built on pretending the feeling did not exist.

Take a breath. A deep, honest breath. You have just mapped something important.

You do not need to be an expert in your emotions. You just need to be willing to notice them. That willingness is everything.

When you are ready, gently open your eyes.`,
  steps: [
    { id: "s1", title: "Settle", body: "Ground and visualise emotional landscape.", startTimeSec: 0, endTimeSec: 80 },
    { id: "s2", title: "Familiar Territory", body: "Identify emotions you visit often.", startTimeSec: 80, endTimeSec: 150 },
    { id: "s3", title: "The Avoided", body: "Explore sadness, loneliness, vulnerability, grief.", startTimeSec: 150, endTimeSec: 300 },
    { id: "s4", title: "The Connection", body: "Link avoidance to compulsive behaviour.", startTimeSec: 300, endTimeSec: 400 },
    { id: "s5", title: "Acknowledge", body: "See the feeling without forcing it.", startTimeSec: 400, endTimeSec: 480 },
  ],
};

export const letterNeverSent: MeditationScript = {
  id: "gen-letter-never-sent",
  title: "The Letter You Never Sent",
  subtitle: "A meditation-journaling hybrid for release",
  category: "inner-work",
  durationSec: 900,
  description: "Mentally compose a letter to someone connected to your pattern. A parent, a younger self, or anyone whose relationship shaped your coping. Deeply cathartic.",
  evidenceSource: "Narrative therapy (White and Epston); Gestalt empty-chair technique; Brianna Wiest",
  tags: ["addiction-recovery", "inner-work", "catharsis", "relationships", "grief", "forgiveness"],
  phase: "all",
  backgroundMusic: "binaural",
  ttsScript: `Welcome to The Letter You Never Sent.

This is a deeply personal practice. You will need privacy and time. There is no pressure to share what comes up. This is just for you.

Find a comfortable position. Close your eyes. Take a long, slow breath in... and release it fully.

Again. Inhale... and let everything soften on the exhale.

One more. Breathe in courage... and breathe out the need to be perfect.

Today, you are going to write a letter in your mind. Not on paper, not to send. A letter to someone connected to one of your patterns. This might be a parent. A partner. A friend. A younger version of yourself. Or even the pattern itself.

Take a moment to let a person come to mind. Do not overthink it. Trust the first person who appears. They are the right one for today.

See them clearly. Their face. Their presence. The way they made you feel.

Now... begin the letter.

Dear...

What do you want them to know? What have you never said?

Maybe it starts with something simple: I have been carrying this for a long time.

Or maybe it is more direct: You hurt me, and I never told you.

Or tender: I wish things had been different between us.

Or honest: I became this way partly because of you, and I need you to know that.

Let the words come. They do not need to be eloquent. They do not need to be fair. They just need to be true.

Pause here. Let the words form at their own pace. There is no rush.

What do you feel as these words take shape? Where in your body does this letter live? Is there heat? Tears? Tightness? Relief?

Stay with it. You are doing something incredibly brave right now.

Now, if it feels right... is there anything else? Something you have been protecting them from hearing? Something you have been protecting yourself from saying?

Say it now. In the silence of your own mind. No consequences. No judgment. Just truth.

When the letter feels complete, or as complete as it can be today... take a breath.

You might want to end it with forgiveness. Or with a boundary. Or with love. Or with grief. Or simply with: I needed to say this.

There is no correct ending. Only your ending.

Now, imagine folding this letter gently. Holding it in your hands. And then... releasing it. Watching it dissolve into light, or float away on water, or simply fade into the quiet air around you.

You do not have to carry these unsaid words anymore.

Place one hand on your heart. Feel it beating. Feel the aliveness in you that persists through everything.

Say to yourself: I am lighter for having spoken my truth, even if only to myself.

Take a final deep breath. Inhale presence... exhale the past.

When you are ready, gently open your eyes.`,
  steps: [
    { id: "s1", title: "Ground", body: "Settle and set intention for deep honesty.", startTimeSec: 0, endTimeSec: 120 },
    { id: "s2", title: "Choose the Recipient", body: "Let someone connected to your pattern appear.", startTimeSec: 120, endTimeSec: 210 },
    { id: "s3", title: "Begin the Letter", body: "Let the unsaid words form.", startTimeSec: 210, endTimeSec: 450 },
    { id: "s4", title: "Go Deeper", body: "Say what you have been protecting.", startTimeSec: 450, endTimeSec: 650 },
    { id: "s5", title: "Release", body: "Fold and let the letter go.", startTimeSec: 650, endTimeSec: 820 },
    { id: "s6", title: "Close", body: "Hand on heart, affirm lightness.", startTimeSec: 820, endTimeSec: 900 },
  ],
};

export const reclaimingPower: MeditationScript = {
  id: "gen-reclaiming-power",
  title: "Reclaiming Your Power",
  subtitle: "Choosing awareness over autopilot",
  category: "inner-work",
  durationSec: 600,
  description: "A forward-looking empowerment practice to identify what you gain control over when you choose awareness instead of autopilot. Hopeful, practical, grounding.",
  evidenceSource: "Self-Determination Theory (Deci and Ryan); ACT values work; Brianna Wiest, The Mountain Is You",
  tags: ["addiction-recovery", "inner-work", "empowerment", "agency", "values", "forward-looking"],
  phase: "all",
  backgroundMusic: "gentle",
  ttsScript: `Welcome to Reclaiming Your Power.

Find a comfortable, upright position. Something that feels both relaxed and alert. You are not winding down. You are waking up.

Close your eyes. Take a breath that fills your entire chest. And exhale with intention. Like you are choosing to let go.

Again. Inhale choice... exhale old stories.

One more. Inhale possibility... exhale limitation.

You have been doing extraordinary work. Looking at patterns. Exploring roots. Sitting with discomfort. Naming shame. Feeling feelings you have avoided for years.

That takes more courage than most people will ever understand. And today, you are going to turn all of that awareness into something powerful. Into choice.

Here is the truth that changes everything: every time you notice a pattern and choose not to follow it on autopilot... you reclaim a piece of your power.

Not power over others. Power over your own life. Your own story. Your own next moment.

Let us get specific. Think about your pattern. The one you have been working with.

What do you lose when you follow it on autopilot? Be honest.
Maybe you lose time. Maybe you lose self-respect. Maybe you lose presence with people you love. Maybe you lose trust in yourself.

Now... what do you gain when you pause, notice, and choose differently?

You gain a morning without regret. You gain the ability to look at yourself clearly. You gain the quiet pride of doing something hard. You gain one more day of evidence that you can trust yourself.

These are not small things. These are the building blocks of a different life.

Now, look further forward. Imagine yourself six months from now. A version of you who has been practising awareness, choosing differently, not perfectly, but consistently.

What does that person's morning look like? How do they feel in their body? How do they relate to themselves?

Can you feel that version of you? Not as a fantasy, but as a real possibility?

That person is not someone else. That person is you... with six months of choices between here and there.

And every choice starts the same way. With a pause. With a breath. With the question: What do I actually want right now? Not what does the pattern want. What do I want?

You want to feel alive. You want to feel present. You want to feel worthy. You want to feel free.

And you can. Not by being perfect. By being aware.

Your power is not in never struggling. It is in what you do when the struggle arrives. And you are already doing it. Right now. By being here.

Take a deep, triumphant breath. You are choosing yourself. That is the most powerful thing a person can do.

When you are ready, open your eyes. And carry this knowing with you: you are not stuck. You are in motion. And every conscious choice is proof.`,
  steps: [
    { id: "s1", title: "Arrive", body: "Alert, upright, intentional breathing.", startTimeSec: 0, endTimeSec: 90 },

};

    id: "gen-the-obstacle-is-the-way",
    title: "The Obstacle Is the Way",
    subtitle: "A Stoic reflection on transforming adversity into opportunity.",
    category: "meditation",
    durationSec: 420,
    description: "Inspired by Stoic philosophy, this meditation guides you to view challenges not as hindrances, but as opportunities for growth and practice. Learn to choose your response to adversity and cultivate inner strength.",
    evidenceSource: "Ryan Holiday, The Daily Stoic",
    tags: ["stoicism", "resilience", "adversity", "perspective", "growth"],
    phase: "all",
    backgroundMusic: "gentle",
    ttsScript: "Settle into a comfortable posture... allowing your body to relax... and your mind to quiet... ...Close your eyes gently... and bring your awareness to your breath... ...Inhaling deeply... and exhaling fully... ...Allow yourself to be fully present... in this moment... ...Today, we’ll reflect on a profound Stoic principle: 'The obstacle is the way.'... ...This idea invites us to see every challenge... every difficulty... not as something to be avoided... but as a path... an opportunity... ...Consider a current obstacle in your life... something that feels like a barrier... or a source of frustration... ...Hold this challenge lightly in your mind... without judgment... just observing it... ...Now, instead of resisting it... imagine for a moment... that this obstacle is precisely what you need... to learn... to grow... to become stronger... ...The Stoics remind us... that while we cannot control external events... we always possess the freedom... to choose our response... ...This is your true power... your inner fortress... ...Feel this freedom within you... the capacity to decide... how you will interpret... and react to... what happens... ...How might this obstacle... be teaching you patience?... ...Resilience?... ...Creativity?... ...How might it be revealing your own inner strength... that you didn't even know you possessed?... ...Instead of asking 'Why me?'... ask 'What is this teaching me?'... or 'How can I use this?'... ...Transforming something that feels like a hindrance... into a stepping stone... ...Breathe into this new perspective... allowing a sense of calm strength to permeate your being... ...The way forward... is often found... not around the obstacle... but through the wisdom... we gain in engaging with it... ...Take a final deep breath... feeling grounded and resolute... ...When you are ready... gently open your eyes... carrying this resilient mindset into the rest of your day...",
    steps: [
      { id: "intro-grounding", title: "Grounding Breath and Posture", body: "Settle into a comfortable position, close your eyes, and connect with your breath to arrive in the present moment.", startTimeSec: 0, endTimeSec: 30 },
      { id: "introduce-stoic-idea", title: "The Obstacle Is the Way", body: "Reflect on the Stoic principle that every challenge is an opportunity, not something to be avoided.", startTimeSec: 30, endTimeSec: 90 },
      { id: "identify-obstacle", title: "Consider a Current Challenge", body: "Bring a current obstacle to mind, observing it without judgment. See it as something designed to help you learn and grow.", startTimeSec: 90, endTimeSec: 150 },
      { id: "freedom-to-choose", title: "Your Freedom to Respond", body: "Remember your inherent power to choose your response, regardless of external events. Feel this freedom within you.", startTimeSec: 150, endTimeSec: 210 },
      { id: "learn-from-obstacle", title: "What Is It Teaching You?", body: "Explore how this obstacle might be teaching you patience, resilience, or creativity, revealing hidden strengths.", startTimeSec: 210, endTimeSec: 300 },
      { id: "shift-perspective", title: "Transforming the Challenge", body: "Shift from 'Why me?' to 'What is this teaching me?' or 'How can I use this?' Transform hindrance into a stepping stone.", startTimeSec: 300, endTimeSec: 360 },
      { id: "integrate-wisdom", title: "Integrate New Wisdom", body: "Breathe deeply, allowing this calm strength and new perspective to permeate your being. The path forward is through engagement.", startTimeSec: 360, endTimeSec: 390 },
      { id: "return-to-day", title: "Return with Resilience", body: "Take a final deep breath and gently open your eyes, carrying this resilient mindset into your day.", startTimeSec: 390, endTimeSec: 420 }
    ]

    ttsScript: "Find a comfortable position... where you can remain still and at ease... allowing your shoulders to drop... and your spine to lengthen... ...Gently close your eyes... or soften your wisdom can emerge... unburdened by preconceptions... ...'I alone am still and inactive, revealing no sign,' the sage might say... ...This doesn't mean apathy... but a profound engagement with the present moment... through a lens of calm observation... ...Take a deep breath... feeling this stillness... this connection to the natural flow of existence... ...As you exhale, let go of any remaining efforts... simply be... in this moment... ...When you are ready... gently bring your awareness back to your body... back to the sounds around you... and slowly open your eyes... keeping this inner calm with you...",

    description: "This practice invites you to observe your constant inner monologue, not to silence it, but to untether your true self from its endless commentary. Discover the profound freedom that comes from recognizing you are the awareness behind your thoughts, not the thoughts themselves.",

    phase: "all",

    ttsScript: "Close your eyes softly... allowing your body to relax completely... ...Take a few deep, intentional breaths... inviting calm into your being... ...Settle into the quiet space... within you... ...Today, we'll explore the 'untethered soul'... the idea that you are not your inner voice... but the awareness that hears it... ...Begin to simply observe your inner monologue... ...Listen to the constant stream of thoughts... the commentary... the judgments... the planning... the memories... ...Notice how this inner voice... seems to have a mind of its own... speaking without your conscious invitation... ...Don't try to stop it... or change it... just listen... as if you are listening to someone speaking in the next room... ...Recognize that there is a 'you' that is hearing these thoughts... ...This 'you' is the witness... the observer... the pure awareness... ...Feel the distinction... between the voice that speaks... and the consciousness that perceives the voice... ...When you identify with your thoughts... with your inner voice... you become tethered... pulled along by its endless narrative... ...But when you step back... and simply observe... you untether yourself... you create space... ...Experience the lightness... the freedom... that comes with this detachment... ...You are not the thoughts of worry... you are the one aware of worry... ...You are not the thoughts of judgment... you are the one aware of judgment... ...This witnessing consciousness... is your true Self... a quiet, ever-present space... ...Return to this awareness... again and again... whenever you get caught in the mind's chatter... ...You are here... simply watching... simply knowing... ...Breathe into this profound truth... 'I am the awareness, not the thoughts.'... ...Feel a sense of deep peace... of liberation... ...You are important... you are here to enable the divine purpose of the universe to unfold... ...And that purpose begins with your own inner freedom... ...When you are ready... gently open your eyes... carrying this quiet, powerful awareness with you...",

That is how important you are!'... ...This unfolding happens... in the Now... ...Take one final, deep breath... affirming your connection to this eternal present... ...As you exhale, softly open your eyes... carrying this profound 'now-awareness' with you into the rest of your day...",

      { id: "the-power-of-now", title: "Embrace the Power of Now", body: "Reflect on the truth that the present moment is all there is. Recognize how the mind often pulls us away from this reality.", startTimeSec: 45, endTimeSec: 105 },

  {
    id: "gen-witnessing-mind",
    title: "Witnessing the Unstressable Mind",
    subtitle: "Observing thoughts without judgment to find inner calm.",
    category: "meditation",
    durationSec: 540,
    description: "This meditation guides you to become the neutral observer of your thoughts, rather than being swept away by them. By recognizing that feeling stressed is a choice in how you deal with events, you cultivate an 'unstressable' mind, able to find calm amidst life's challenges.",
    evidenceSource: "Mo Gawdat, Unstressable",
    tags: ["stress reduction", "mindfulness", "thought observation", "choice", "inner calm", "resilience"],
    phase: "all",
    backgroundMusic: "gentle",
    ttsScript: "Find a comfortable position... allowing your body to be at ease... and your breath to flow naturally... ...Gently close your eyes... or soften your gaze... bringing your full attention inward... ...Today, we'll explore the path to an 'unstressable' mind... understanding that it's not the events that stress us... but how we deal with them... ...We're going to practice becoming the neutral witness... to our own thoughts... ...Imagine yourself sitting beside a gentle stream... and your thoughts are like leaves... floating by on the water... ...Each leaf is a thought... a memory... a worry... a plan... ...Observe each leaf as it passes... without jumping onto it... without following it down the stream... ...Simply acknowledge its presence... and let it float on by... ...Notice any emotions that arise... perhaps a feeling of stress... or anxiety... ...See these emotions as separate from 'you'... just as the leaves are separate from the stream... ...You are the steady bank of the stream... the observer... the awareness that witnesses... ...Recognize that you have a choice... in how you engage with these thoughts and feelings... ...You can choose to be swept away... or you can choose to remain the tranquil witness... ...This choice... is the core of becoming unstressable... ...It doesn't mean denying challenges... or eliminating all thoughts... ...It means cultivating the inner skill... to observe them... without judgment... and without allowing them to dictate your inner state... ...Feel a sense of calm strength growing within you... as you practice this detachment... ...Even if the 'stream' of your mind is sometimes turbulent... your capacity to witness... remains peaceful... ...Breathe deeply... affirming to yourself: 'I am the observer of my thoughts. I choose my response to life's events.'... ...Internalize this feeling of agency... of inner resilience... ...This is your innate ability... to find a silver lining... to develop skills and resources to de-stress... ...Take one final, deep breath... bringing this 'unstressable' awareness into every cell of your being... ...When you are ready... gently open your eyes... carrying this calm and discerning presence into your day...",
    steps: [
      { id: "intro-settle", title: "Settle and Breathe", body: "Find a comfortable position, close your eyes, and allow your breath to flow naturally, bringing attention inward.", startTimeSec: 0, endTimeSec: 45 },

      { id: "leaves-on-stream", title: "Thoughts as Leaves", body: "Imagine thoughts as leaves floating on a stream. Observe each one without engagement, allowing it to pass by.", startTimeSec: 90, endTimeSec: 210 },
      { id: "observer-awareness", title: "The Observer Within", body: "Notice emotions as separate from 'you.' Recognize yourself as the steady bank of the stream, the awareness that witnesses.", startTimeSec: 210, endTimeSec: 270 },
      { id: "choice-to-engage", title: "Choose Your Engagement", body: "Realize you have a choice: be swept away or remain the tranquil witness. This choice is vital for becoming unstressable.", startTimeSec: 270, endTimeSec: 360 },
      { id: "calm-strength", title: "Cultivate Inner Calm", body: "Feel calm strength grow as you practice detachment. Your capacity to witness remains peaceful, even in turbulence.", startTimeSec: 360, endTimeSec: 420 },
      { id: "affirm-resilience", title: "Affirm Agency and Resilience", body: "Breathe deeply, affirming: 'I am the observer of my thoughts. I choose my response.' Internalize this inner resilience.", startTimeSec: 420, endTimeSec: 480 },

            "title": "Rules of the Speaker-Listener",
            "instruction": "Swipe through these cards to remember the key rules for both the Speaker and the Listener roles.",
            "content": {
              "cards": [
                {
                  "title": "Rule for Speaker",
                  "body": "Speak only for yourself using 'I' statements — 'I feel…' not 'You always…'. Keep statements brief and focused on one issue at a time. After each key point, pause and let the Listener paraphrase back what they heard. Don't move on until they've accurately reflected your message. You hold 'the floor' — only the Speaker talks.",
                  "icon": "lucide-mic"
                },
                {
                  "title": "Rule for Listener",
                  "body": "Your only job is to understand, not to agree, fix, or rebut. Paraphrase what you hear in your own words: 'So what you're saying is…'. Check back: 'Did I get that right?' Don't insert your perspective until it's your turn as Speaker. This feels unnatural at first — but it's transformative when practised consistently.",
                  "icon": "lucide-headphones"
                },
                {
                  "title": "Rule for Both",
                  "body": "The goal is understanding, never agreement or problem-solving during this exchange. Use a physical object (a pen, a cushion) as 'the floor' — whoever holds it speaks. Switch roles frequently. If emotions escalate, either partner can call a 20-minute break. This structure prevents the conversation from spiralling into attack-defend loops.",
                  "icon": "lucide-users"
                }
              ]
            },
            "saveToVault": false
          },
          {
            "id": "m3-l3-a1b",
            "type": "flip_card",
            "title": "Communication Concepts: Key Terms",
            "instruction": "Flip each card to reinforce the core concepts of constructive communication.",
            "content": {
              "cards": [
                { "front": "Gentle Start-Up", "back": "Initiating a difficult conversation with 'I feel… about… and I need…' rather than 'You always/never…'. Research shows the first three minutes of a conflict conversation predict its entire trajectory — a gentle start prevents the cascade toward defensiveness.", "emoji": "🌸", "tag": "Gottman" },
                { "front": "Speaker-Listener Technique", "back": "A structured dialogue tool where only the person holding 'the floor' speaks, and the listener's sole job is to paraphrase accurately before responding. It slows down emotional escalation by separating speaking from defending.", "emoji": "🎤", "tag": "Technique" },
                { "front": "Active Listening", "back": "Listening to understand, not to respond. Involves reflecting feelings ('It sounds like you felt…'), validating ('That makes sense given…'), and asking clarifying questions. The goal is for your partner to feel heard — not agreed with, but genuinely heard.", "emoji": "👂", "tag": "Skill" },
                { "front": "Flooding", "back": "When physiological arousal (heart rate above ~100 bpm) overwhelms the brain's capacity to process information calmly. Flooded partners cannot listen, think clearly, or problem-solve. A deliberate 20-minute break is the only effective intervention.", "emoji": "🌊", "tag": "Gottman" }
              ]
            }
          },
          {
            "id": "m3-l3-a2",
            "type": "decision_point",
            "title": "Speaker-Listener in Action",
            "instruction": "You are the Listener. Your partner says: 'I'm tired of feeling like I have to guess what you want for dinner every night. It makes me feel unappreciated.' How do you respond using the Listener rules?",
            "content": {

                { "front": "Full Apology", "back": "A genuine apology has five components: expressing remorse ('I'm sorry'), taking responsibility ('I was wrong to…'), acknowledging the impact ('I can see that hurt you because…'), showing understanding of their perspective, and making a plan to prevent recurrence.     "icon": "lucide-flame",
    "estimatedMinutes": 75,

        "description": "Understand why anger deserves your respect and attention — and why suppressing it keeps you stuck.",
        "estimatedMinutes": 15,
        "activities": [
          {
            "id": "m11-l1-a0",
            "type": "reaction_slider",
            "title": "Check In",
            "instruction": "Before we explore anger and boundaries, take a moment to reflect.",
            "content": {

                { "emoji": "🙂", "label": "Generally okay — I can usually name and share it" },

          },
          {
            "id": "m11-l1-a1",
            "type": "carousel",
            "title": "The Two Sides of the Coin",
            "instruction": "Swipe through to understand the two common patterns women fall into when dealing with anger.",
            "content": {
              "cards": [
                {
                  "title": "The 'Nice Lady'",
                  "body": "Stays silent to avoid conflict. Puts others' comfort first. Feels guilty for having needs. Accumulates resentment beneath the surface until she either shuts down or explodes.",
                  "icon": "lucide-smile"
                },
                {
                  "title": "The 'Bitchy' Woman",

                  "icon": "lucide-zap"
                },
                {
                  "title": "The Truth",
                  "body": "Both patterns are two sides of the same coin. Neither leads to real change. Both leave you feeling helpless and powerless. The goal is a third way: clarity, calm assertion, and self-definition.",
                  "icon": "lucide-lightbulb"
                }
              ]
            },
            "saveToVault": false
          },
          {
            "id": "m11-l1-a1b",
            "type": "flip_card",
            "title": "Anger & Boundaries: Key Concepts",
            "instruction": "Flip each card to understand Harriet Lerner's core insights on anger and self-definition.",
            "content": {
              "cards": [
                { "front": "Anger as Signal", "back": "Lerner's central insight: anger is not a problem to be managed or eliminated — it is information. The goal is to decode the message anger sends, then act with clarity rather than reactivity.", "emoji": "🚦", "tag": "Lerner" },
                { "front": "De-Selfing", "back": "The gradual loss of self that occurs when you chronically prioritise others' needs, approval, and comfort over your own.                 { "front": "Countermove", "back": "When you change a habitual pattern in a relationship — say no, set a boundary, express a need — the other person will push back to restore the old dynamic.                 { "front": "Self-Definition vs. Reactivity", "back": "The alternative to both silence and explosion is self-definition: clearly stating your position using 'I' language without attacking, defending, or over-explaining.       {
        "id": "module-11-lesson-3",
        "title": "The Art of Saying No with Clarity",
        "description": "Learn to communicate your position without attacking, defending, or over-explaining — using 'I' statements and clear boundaries.",
        "estimatedMinutes": 15,
        "activities": [
          {
            "id": "m11-l3-a1",
            "type": "carousel",
            "title": "From Reactivity to Clarity",
            "instruction": "Learn the key principles of clear communication from The Dance of Anger.",
            "content": {
              "cards": [
                {
                  "title": "Use 'I' Language",
                  "body": "Say 'I think…', 'I feel…', 'I want…' instead of 'You always…' or 'You never…'. The goal is to share your experience, not diagnose the other person's problem.",
                  "icon": "lucide-user"
                },
                {
                  "title": "Don't Prescribe",
                  "body": "State your position without telling the other person what they should feel, think, or do. You can only change your own steps in the dance — not your partner's.",
                  "icon": "lucide-ban"
                },
                {
                  "title": "Expect Countermoves",
                  "body": "When you change your pattern, others will push back. They'll test whether you really mean it. This is normal. The key is to hold your position calmly, without escalating or backing down.",
                  "icon": "lucide-shield"
                },
                {
                  "title": "Short & Clear",
                  "body": "Over-explaining is a form of anxiety. A clear 'no' doesn't need a paragraph of justification. 'I'm not comfortable with that' is a complete sentence.",
                  "icon": "lucide-check"
                }
              ]
            },
            "saveToVault": false
          },
          {
            "id": "m11-l3-a2",
            "type": "comparison",
            "title": "Reactive vs. Clear Communication",
            "instruction": "Compare these two approaches to the same situation. Notice the difference in clarity and emotional tone.",
            "content": {
              "pairs": [
                {
                  "left": { "label": "Reactive", "text": "'You never help around the house! You're so lazy and selfish!'" },
                  "right": { "label": "Clear", "text": "'I feel overwhelmed managing the household alone. I need us to divide chores more evenly. Here's what I'm proposing…'" }
                },
                {
                  "left": { "label": "Reactive", "text": "'Fine, I'll just do it myself like I always do.'" },
                  "right": { "label": "Clear", "text": "'I'm not willing to take this on alone. I need to know if you can commit to handling [specific task] by [specific time].'" }
                },
                {
                  "left": { "label": "Reactive", "text": "'You don't even care about my feelings!'" },
                  "right": { "label": "Clear", "text": "'When I share something important and get a distracted response, I feel dismissed. I need to know you're really listening.'" }
                }
              ]
            },
            "saveToVault": false
          },
          {
            "id": "m11-l3-a3",
            "type": "open_response",
            "title": "Rewrite Your Script",
            "instruction": "Think of a recent situation where you either stayed silent or reacted poorly. Rewrite what you wish you had said — using 'I' language, clarity, and calm assertion.",
            "content": {

              "placeholder": "The situation was… What I wish I'd said is…",
              "minWords": 25
            },
            "tip": "Remember: You don't need to convince the other person. You only need to clearly state your position.",
            "saveToVault": true
          }
        ]
      },
      {
        "id": "module-11-lesson-4",
        "title": "Countermoves & Standing Your Ground",
        "description": "Understand why people resist your changes — and how to hold your new position without caving or escalating.",
        "estimatedMinutes": 15,
        "activities": [
          {
            "id": "m11-l4-a1",
            "type": "carousel",
            "title": "The Countermove Pattern",
            "instruction": "When you change your steps in a relationship dance, the other person will always push back. Here's what to expect.",
            "content": {
              "cards": [
                {
                  "title": "What Is a Countermove?",
                  "body": "When you set a boundary or change a pattern, the other person will try to restore the old dynamic. They may guilt-trip, withdraw, get angry, or tell you you've changed. This is a countermove.",
                  "icon": "lucide-refresh-cw"
                },
                {
                  "title": "Why It Happens",
                  "body": "Change creates anxiety in a relationship system. The other person isn't necessarily trying to hurt you — they're trying to restore the familiar equilibrium, even if it was unhealthy.",
                  "icon": "lucide-brain"
                },
                {
                  "title": "The Critical Moment",
                  "body": "This is where most people cave. The discomfort of the countermove feels worse than the original problem. But if you go back to your old pattern, you confirm that boundaries don't stick.",
                  "icon": "lucide-alert-triangle"
                },
                {
                  "title": "Hold Your Position",
                  "body": "Stay calm. Don't attack, defend, or over-explain. Simply restate your position: 'I understand this is hard. And this is what I need.' Then give the relationship time to adjust.",
                  "icon": "lucide-anchor"
                }
              ]
            },
            "saveToVault": false
          },
          {
            "id": "m11-l4-a2",
            "type": "sort",
            "title": "Countermove or Genuine Concern?",
            "instruction": "Drag each response into the correct category. Is it a countermove designed to restore the old pattern, or genuine concern?",
            "content": {
              "categories": ["Countermove", "Genuine Concern"],
              "items": [
                { "text": "'You've changed. I don't even recognise you anymore.'", "correctCategory": "Countermove" },
                { "text": "'I'm worried this new distance between us means something is wrong.'", "correctCategory": "Genuine Concern" },
                { "text": "'Fine. Do whatever you want. I don't care anymore.'", "correctCategory": "Countermove" },
                { "text": "'I want to understand your needs. Can we talk about this more?'", "correctCategory": "Genuine Concern" },
                { "text": "'You're being selfish. You only think about yourself now.'", "correctCategory": "Countermove" },
                { "text": "'I feel hurt and I'd like to work through this together.'", "correctCategory": "Genuine Concern" }
              ]
            },
            "saveToVault": false
          },
          {
            "id": "m11-l4-a3",
            "type": "open_response",
            "title": "Your Countermove Plan",
            "instruction": "Think about a boundary you want to set (or have recently set). What countermove do you expect? How will you respond without caving or attacking?",

            },
            "tip": "Lerner: 'Countermoves are the other person's unconscious attempt to reinstate the status quo. They are not evidence that you are wrong.'",
            "saveToVault": true
          }
        ]
      },
      {
        "id": "module-11-lesson-5",
        "title": "Who's Responsible for What?",
        "description": "Untangle over-responsibility from under-responsibility — and learn to stay in your own lane.",
        "estimatedMinutes": 15,
        "activities": [
          {
            "id": "m11-l5-a1",
            "type": "carousel",
            "title": "The Responsibility Tangle",
            "instruction": "Understand how women often take on too much emotional responsibility — and how this blocks real change.",
            "content": {
              "cards": [
                {
                  "title": "Over-Functioning",
                  "body": "You do too much: managing, reminding, worrying, fixing. You carry the emotional load for the relationship. The more you do, the less the other person has to — creating a cycle of resentment.",
                  "icon": "lucide-loader"
                },
                {
                  "title": "Under-Functioning",
                  "body": "The counterpart to over-functioning. The more one person takes over, the more the other pulls back. Neither person is showing their full self — both are stuck in a polarised pattern.",
                  "icon": "lucide-moon"
                },
                {
                  "title": "Staying in Your Lane",
                  "body": "You are responsible for your own thoughts, feelings, and behaviour. You are NOT responsible for another adult's feelings, reactions, or choices. This distinction is the foundation of healthy boundaries.",
                  "icon": "lucide-milestone"
                }
              ]
            },
            "saveToVault": false
          },
          {
            "id": "m11-l5-a2",
            "type": "sort",
            "title": "My Responsibility or Theirs?",

            "content": {
              "categories": ["My Responsibility", "Not My Responsibility"],
              "items": [
                { "text": "How I communicate my needs", "correctCategory": "My Responsibility" },
                { "text": "Whether they feel hurt by my boundary", "correctCategory": "Not My Responsibility" },
                { "text": "Following through on my commitments", "correctCategory": "My Responsibility" },
                { "text": "Managing their emotional reaction", "correctCategory": "Not My Responsibility" },
                { "text": "Being honest about what I feel", "correctCategory": "My Responsibility" },
                { "text": "Making them happy", "correctCategory": "Not My Responsibility" },
                { "text": "Choosing how I respond to conflict", "correctCategory": "My Responsibility" },
                { "text": "Fixing their problems for them", "correctCategory": "Not My Responsibility" }
              ]
            },
            "saveToVault": false
          },
          {
            "id": "m11-l5-a3",
            "type": "open_response",
            "title": "Your Over-Functioning Audit",
            "instruction": "Identify one area where you chronically over-function. What would it look like to step back — not in anger, but with clarity and compassion?",
            "content": {
              "prompt": "Where do you over-function? What are you afraid would happen if you stopped? What would 'staying in your lane' look like here?",
              "placeholder": "I tend to over-function when it comes to…",
              "minWords": 30

            "tip": "Lerner: 'We cannot make another person change his or her steps to an old dance, but if we change our own steps, the dance no longer can continue in the same predictable pattern.'",
            "saveToVault": true
          },
          {
            "id": "m11-l5-a4",
            "type": "knowledge_check",
            "title": "Knowledge Check",
            "instruction": "Test your understanding before moving on.",
            "content": {
              "intro": "Let's check what you've learned about anger, boundaries, and self-definition.",
              "passMark": 3,
              "questions": [
                {
                  "question": "According to Harriet Lerner, what is the primary purpose of anger?",
                  "options": ["To motivate the other person to change their behaviour", "To signal that something is wrong, a need is unmet, or a boundary is being violated", "To release pent-up frustration and feel better", "To establish dominance in the relationship"],
                  "correct": 1,
                  "explanation": "Lerner's central thesis is that anger is information — a signal worth listening to. The goal isn't to express or suppress anger, but to decode what it's telling you and respond with clarity."
                },
                {
                  "question": "What does Lerner mean by 'de-selfing'?",
                  "options": ["Losing your physical identity in a relationship", "The gradual erosion of self that happens when you chronically put others' needs before your own", "Selfishly prioritising your own needs over your partner's", "Becoming too emotionally dependent on a partner"],
                  "correct": 1,
                  "explanation": "De-selfing is the chronic sacrifice of your own thoughts, feelings, and needs to maintain harmony. It leads to resentment and eventually to either explosion or shutdown — and it ultimately hurts the relationship."
                },
                {
                  "question": "What is a 'countermove' in the context of relationship change?",
                  "options": ["A helpful adjustment your partner makes when you set a boundary", "A therapeutic technique for managing anger", "The other person's resistance when you change a habitual pattern — their attempt to restore the old dynamic", "A deliberate manipulation tactic"],
                  "correct": 2,
                  "explanation": "A countermove is the other person's often-unconscious attempt to restore the relationship's familiar (even if unhealthy) equilibrium when you change your behaviour. It's not evidence you're wrong — it's evidence change is happening."

                {
                  "question": "What is the alternative to both people-pleasing silence and reactive explosions, according to Lerner?",

                  "correct": 2,
                  "explanation": "Lerner's 'third way' is self-definition — using calm, clear 'I' language to state your position and needs without attacking the other person or requiring their agreement. 'I am not comfortable with that' is a complete, powerful sentence."

            }
          }
        ]

    "subtitle": "Science-backed secrets from the Love Lab for becoming the partner she needs.",

    "icon": "lucide-shield",
    "estimatedMinutes": 75,
    "sources": ["The Man's Guide to Women — John Gottman, PhD, Julie Schwartz Gottman, PhD, Douglas Abrams & Rachel Carlton Abrams, MD"],
    "lessons": [
      {
        "id": "module-12-lesson-1",
        "title": "What Women Really Want: Trustworthiness",
        "description": "The #1 thing every woman is looking for — and it's not what most men think.",
        "estimatedMinutes": 15,
        "activities": [
          {
            "id": "m12-l1-a1",
            "type": "carousel",
            "title": "The Hero vs. The Zero",
            "instruction": "Swipe through to understand the core research findings from 40 years of studying 3,000+ couples in Gottman's Love Lab.",
            "content": {
              "cards": [
                {
                  "title": "Trustworthiness Is #1",
                  "body": "The number one thing women look for in a man isn't abs, money, or looks. It's trustworthiness: being who you say you are and doing what you say you'll do. Reliability. Accountability. Showing up as yourself.",
                  "icon": "lucide-shield-check"
                },
                {
                  "title": "Her Two Complaints",
                  "body": "Women's top two complaints: 'He is never there for me' and 'There isn't enough intimacy and connection.' These women feel alone even when in a relationship.",
                  "icon": "lucide-heart-crack"
                },
                {
                  "title": "His Two Complaints",
                  "body": "Men's top two complaints: 'There's too much fighting' and 'There's not enough sex.' Here's the breakthrough — these are causally related to hers. Fix hers and yours get fixed automatically.",
                  "icon": "lucide-zap"
                },
                {
                  "title": "The Key Variable: You",
                  "body": "Research shows that what men do in a relationship is, by a large margin, the crucial factor that separates a great relationship from a failed one. You have the power to make or break it.",
                  "icon": "lucide-key"
                }
              ]
            },
            "saveToVault": false
          },
          {
            "id": "m12-l1-a2",
            "type": "single_choice",
            "title": "Hero or Zero Self-Check",
            "instruction": "Be honest — which pattern sounds most like you right now?",
            "content": {
              "question": "When your partner is upset about something, what's your default response?",
              "options": [
                "I try to fix the problem immediately — offer solutions, suggest she look at it differently, or minimise it.",
                "I get defensive — I feel like she's attacking me so I counter-attack or shut down.",
                "I try to listen and understand what she's feeling before jumping to solutions.",
                "I check out — go on my phone, change the subject, or leave the room."
              ],
              "correctIndex": 2,
              "explanation": "Option 3 is the attunement response. The other three — fixing, defending, and withdrawing — are the most common patterns Gottman found in men whose relationships failed. The good news: attunement is a learnable skill."
            },
            "saveToVault": false
          },
          {
            "id": "m12-l1-a3",
            "type": "open_response",
            "title": "Your Trustworthiness Audit",
            "instruction": "Reflect honestly: In what ways are you showing up as trustworthy — and where are the gaps? Think about reliability, emotional availability, and consistency.",
            "content": {
              "prompt": "Consider: Do you follow through on what you say? Are you emotionally available when she needs you? Do you show up as your authentic self?",
              "placeholder": "The areas where I'm strong are… The areas where I could improve are…",
              "minWords": 25
            },
            "tip": "Gottman: 'Trustworthiness isn't just about fidelity. It's about being who you say you are and doing what you say you'll do.'",
            "saveToVault": true
          }
        ]
      },
      {
        "id": "module-12-lesson-2",
        "title": "A-TT-U-N-E: The Skill That Changes Everything",
        "description": "Learn the five-step attunement framework that Gottman's research proved leads to less fighting and more intimacy.",
        "estimatedMinutes": 15,
        "activities": [
          {
            "id": "m12-l2-a0",
            "type": "reaction_slider",
            "title": "Check In",
            "instruction": "Before learning the ATTUNE framework, reflect on how you currently respond when your partner is upset.",
            "content": {
              "question": "When your partner is emotionally distressed, how naturally do you attune to what they're feeling rather than trying to fix or dismiss it?",
              "options": [
                { "emoji": "😬", "label": "I immediately try to fix or minimise — feelings make me uncomfortable" },
                { "emoji": "😕", "label": "I try but often default to solutions or defensiveness" },
                { "emoji": "😐", "label": "Hit and miss — depends on my own stress level" },
                { "emoji": "🙂", "label": "Generally good at listening and empathising" },
                { "emoji": "🌟", "label": "Attuning is my natural first response" }
              ]
            }
          },
          {
            "id": "m12-l2-a1",
            "type": "carousel",
            "title": "The A-TT-U-N-E Framework",
            "instruction": "Master this five-step process. It's the single most important relationship skill from 40 years of research.",
            "content": {
              "cards": [
                {
                  "title": "A — Attend",
                  "body": "Give undivided attention. Turn off the game, put away the phone. Show through your actions that you care about what she's saying. Even if it seems trivial to you, it's important to her — and it's a bid for connection. Attention equals affection.",
                  "icon": "lucide-eye"
                },
                {
                  "title": "TT — Turn Toward",
                  "body": "Physically turn toward her. Women equate intimacy with face-to-face, eye-to-eye conversation. Men feel connected side-by-side — but unless you're about to take down a buffalo together, turn toward her while you talk.",
                  "icon": "lucide-rotate-ccw"
                },
                {
                  "title": "U — Understand",
                  "body": "Ask questions. Don't offer solutions, don't distract, don't minimise, don't joke. Seek to understand WHY this matters to her. It's not about saying 'I understand' — it's about showing genuine interest.",
                  "icon": "lucide-search"
                },
                {
                  "title": "N — Nondefensively Listen",
                  "body": "Don't react, don't counter-attack, don't justify. Any feeling is fact to the person feeling it. You have two ears and one mouth — use them in that ratio. Men who could calm themselves down had the great relationships.",
                  "icon": "lucide-ear"
                },
                {
                  "title": "E — Empathise",
                  "body": "Understanding is intellectual. Empathy is emotional. Try to FEEL how she feels. Let her know her feelings make sense. The emotional brain calms down when it feels connected and not alone. Show compassion — it's not about being right.",
                  "icon": "lucide-heart-handshake"
                }
              ]
            },
            "saveToVault": false
          },
          {
            "id": "m12-l2-a1b",
            "type": "flip_card",
            "title": "A-TT-U-N-E: The Five Steps",
            "instruction": "Flip each card to master the five components of emotional attunement.",
            "content": {
              "cards": [
                { "front": "A — Attend", "back": "Give undivided attention. Turn off the screen, put away the phone. Show through your actions that what your partner is saying matters. Attention equals affection — and its absence is felt immediately as disconnection, regardless of intent.", "emoji": "👁️", "tag": "ATTUNE" },
                { "front": "TT — Turn Toward", "back": "Physically orient toward your partner. Women especially equate emotional intimacy with face-to-face, eye-to-eye contact. Unless you're literally hunting together, turn your body toward her while you talk. This small physical shift signals genuine engagement.", "emoji": "↩️", "tag": "ATTUNE" },
                { "front": "U — Understand", "back": "Ask questions to understand WHY this matters to your partner, not what solution you should offer. 'Tell me more.' 'Why is this so important to you?' Understanding is the goal — not agreement, not advice. You can only help if you truly understand.", "emoji": "🔍", "tag": "ATTUNE" },
                { "front": "N & E — Nondefensively Listen & Empathise", "back": "Don't react, counter-attack, or justify. Any feeling is real to the person experiencing it. Then go one step further: try to FEEL how your partner feels. Empathy is not intellectual agreement — it's emotional resonance. 'That sounds really painful. I can see why you're hurt.'", "emoji": "❤️", "tag": "ATTUNE" }
              ]
            }
          },
          {
            "id": "m12-l2-a2",
            "type": "comparison",
            "title": "Zero vs. Hero Responses",
            "instruction": "Compare these two approaches. Notice how the Hero response uses ATTUNE while the Zero response shuts down connection.",
            "content": {
              "pairs": [

                },
                {
                  "left": { "label": "Zero", "text": "'Well maybe if you hadn't done X, Y wouldn't have happened. Here's what you should do…'" },
                  "right": { "label": "Hero", "text": "'I can see you're really hurt by this. What do you need from me right now? I'm here.'" }

                  "right": { "label": "Hero", "text": "*Puts phone down, turns toward her, makes eye contact* 'Hey — I can see something's bothering you. Talk to me.'" }
                }
              ]
            },
            "saveToVault": false

          {

            "type": "open_response",
            "title": "Your ATTUNE Practice",

            "content": {

      {
        "id": "module-12-lesson-3",
        "title": "Understanding Her Brain & Her Emotions",
        "description": "Why she experiences emotions differently — and why that's an opportunity, not a problem.",
        "estimatedMinutes": 15,
        "activities": [
          {
            "id": "m12-l3-a1",
            "type": "carousel",
            "title": "The Hopscotch Lesson",
            "instruction": "This story from the book perfectly illustrates the fundamental difference between how men and women relate to emotions.",
            "content": {
              "cards": [
                {
                  "title": "The Boys' Game",
                  "body": "When 8-year-old Brian cries because he never gets the ball, Gabe stops the game, gives Brian the ball, and play resumes. Problem solved. Emotions dispensed with. For boys, emotions are an interruption to the fun — like an unwelcome leech.",
                  "icon": "lucide-trophy"
                },
                {
                  "title": "The Girls' Game",
                  "body": "When Kathy cries during hopscotch, Lisa asks why. They talk about their friendship, plan a sleepover, decide to marry brothers. The game is forgotten — because the game was never the point. Emotions ARE the intimacy.",
                  "icon": "lucide-heart"
                },
                {
                  "title": "The Insight for Men",
                  "body": "When you ask 'What is she trying to accomplish by being emotional?' — that's a hopelessly male question. For women, there is no POINT to emotions. They just are. They're opportunities for connection. Stop trying to fix them.",
                  "icon": "lucide-lightbulb"
                },
                {
                  "title": "Fear Is Different Too",
                  "body": "When startled, men feel anger. Women feel fear. And women are more easily fear-conditioned — one bad experience creates future fear. Your touch (when she's happy with you) can shut down her brain's fear response entirely. Hold her hand.",
                  "icon": "lucide-hand-metal"
                }
              ]
            },
            "saveToVault": false
          },
          {
            "id": "m12-l3-a2",
            "type": "true_false",
            "title": "Myths vs. Research",
            "instruction": "Test your assumptions against what Gottman's Love Lab actually found.",
            "content": {
              "statements": [
                { "text": "Talking about negative emotions makes them worse.", "answer": false },

      {
        "id": "module-13-lesson-3",
        "title": "The Invalidation Triple Threat",
        "description": "The #1 marriage killer hiding in your everyday conversations — and you probably do it multiple times per week.",
        "estimatedMinutes": 15,
        "activities": [
          {
            "id": "m13-l3-a1",
            "type": "carousel",
            "title": "The Three Ways You Invalidate Your Partner",
            "instruction": "Fray calls this the world's leading cause of relationship failure. Learn to recognise all three forms.",
            "content": {
              "cards": [
                {
                  "title": "#1: Their Thoughts Are Wrong",
                  "body": "Your partner tells you something hurt them. Your response: 'That doesn't make sense. You're wrong to think that.' You correct their interpretation of reality instead of acknowledging their experience. You become the judge of whether their pain is legitimate.",
                  "icon": "lucide-x-circle"
                },
                {
                  "title": "#2: Their Feelings Are Wrong",
                  "body": "Your partner expresses pain. Your response: 'You shouldn't feel that way. I didn't mean it, so you shouldn't be hurt.' You tell them their emotional response is incorrect — as if feelings need your approval to exist.",
                  "icon": "lucide-heart-off"
                },
                {
                  "title": "#3: Their Character Is Wrong",
                  "body": "Your partner persists because they still feel unheard. Your response: 'You're too sensitive. You're always overreacting. You're crazy.' Now you've attacked WHO THEY ARE as a person — the most damaging invalidation of all.",
                  "icon": "lucide-user-x"
                },
                {
                  "title": "The Result: Death Spiral",
                  "body": "Each round of invalidation erodes trust. Your partner stops bringing things up. The silence isn't peace — it's surrender. They've concluded you'll never hear them. They start planning their exit. By the time you notice, it's usually too late.",

                }

            "content": {

                { title: "ACT: Values Over Resolution", body: "Acceptance and Commitment Therapy offers a powerful alternative: instead of waiting for resolution, you clarify your values and commit to living in alignment with them regardless of unresolved pain.                 { title: "Acceptance Is Not Approval", body: "In ACT, acceptance means allowing difficult thoughts and feelings to be present without struggling against them.                 { title: "Defusion: Stepping Back from Thoughts", body: "ACT's defusion techniques help you observe thoughts rather than be consumed by them.                 { title: "Grief as Part of Recovery", body: "Real grief — for the relationship that wasn't, for the time lost, for the version of yourself that didn't get to develop — is a necessary part of recovery. ## `src/data/exercise-animations.ts`

```ts
/**
 * SIGNAL Exercise Animation Registry
 * 
 * Architecture:
 * - One reusable SVG rig (ExerciseRig component)
 * - Animations defined at the EXERCISE level (not workout level)
 * - Each animation = lightweight JSON pose keyframes
 * - Workouts reference animations by exercise name via mapping layer
 * 
 * Adding a new exercise:
 * 1. Define pose keyframes (JointPose objects)
 * 2. Add entry to ANIMATION_REGISTRY
 * 3. Add name mapping(s) to EXERCISE_NAME_MAP
 */

// ── Joint pose type ──────────────────────────────────────────────────

export interface JointPose {
  headX: number; headY: number;
  neckX: number; neckY: number;
  shoulderLX: number; shoulderLY: number;
  shoulderRX: number; shoulderRY: number;
  hipX: number; hipY: number;
  hipLX: number; hipLY: number;
  hipRX: number; hipRY: number;
  elbowLX: number; elbowLY: number;
  elbowRX: number; elbowRY: number;
  handLX: number; handLY: number;
  handRX: number; handRY: number;
  kneeLX: number; kneeLY: number;
  kneeRX: number; kneeRY: number;
  footLX: number; footLY: number;
  footRX: number; footRY: number;
}

export type MovementType = "squat" | "hinge" | "lunge" | "push" | "pull" | "core" | "plank" | "bridge" | "isolation" | "compound" | "locomotion";
export type BodyOrientation = "standing" | "supine" | "prone" | "side" | "quadruped" | "kneeling";
export type LoopType = "ping-pong" | "loop" | "hold";

export interface ExerciseAnimationDef {
  key: string;
  name: string;
  category: string;
  movementType: MovementType;
  orientation: BodyOrientation;
  loopType: LoopType;
  unilateral: boolean;
  holdable: boolean;
  defaultTempo?: string;
  keyframes: JointPose[];
  cycleDuration: number;
}

// ── Base poses ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────

// Build a lookup map
const _registryMap = new Map<string, ExerciseAnimationDef>();
ANIMATION_REGISTRY.forEach(a => _registryMap.set(a.key, a));

export function getAnimationByKey(key: string): ExerciseAnimationDef | undefined {
  return _registryMap.get(key);
}

  "Bridge with Alternating Hip Flexion": "glute-bridge",
  "Plank with Knee Dips": "plank-shoulder-taps",
  "Single Toe Raise": "step-up",
  "Neutral Spine Sequence": "dead-bug",
};

/**
 * Look up animation for an exercise name from a workout.
 * Returns undefined if no animation exists.
 */
export function getAnimationForExercise(exerciseName: string): ExerciseAnimationDef | undefined {
  const key = EXERCISE_NAME_MAP[exerciseName];
  if (key) return _registryMap.get(key);
  
  // Fuzzy fallback: normalise and try partial match
  const normalised = exerciseName.toLowerCase().replace(/[^a-z0-9]/g, "-").replace(/-+/g, "-");
  for (const [k, anim] of _registryMap) {
    if (normalised.includes(k) || k.includes(normalised)) return anim;
  }
  return undefined;
}

```

const washingDishes: MeditationScript = {
  id: "gen-washing-dishes",
  title: "The Washing Dishes Meditation",
  subtitle: "Full presence in everyday tasks",
  category: "meditation",
  durationSec: 300,
  description: "Transform a mundane chore into meditative practice by fully engaging your senses and attention.",
  evidenceSource: "Thich Nhat Hanh, The Miracle of Mindfulness",
  tags: ["mindfulness", "everyday", "presence"],
  phase: "all",
  backgroundMusic: "gentle",
  ttsScript: `Welcome to the Washing Dishes Meditation.
Find a comfortable standing position at your sink, or imagine yourself there. This practice is about bringing our full, gentle awareness to a simple, everyday task. No need to rush, no need to think about what comes next. Just this moment.

Let's begin by taking a deep, calming breath together. Inhale slowly through your nose, feeling your lungs expand. And exhale gently through your mouth, letting go of any tension. Do this one more time. Inhale. And exhale.

Now, bring your attention to the water. Feel its temperature as it flows over your hands. Is it warm, cool, just right? Notice the sensation.
Perhaps you're holding a dish. Feel its shape, its weight. Is it smooth, or does it have a texture?
As you pick up the sponge, notice its softness, its absorbency. The gentle friction against your fingers.

Now, add a little soap. Watch as the bubbles begin to form. See their delicate iridescence, reflecting the light.
Begin to wash a dish. Slowly, mindfully. Feel the warm water, the slippery soap, the gentle rub of the sponge.
Notice the sound of the water, the quiet hum of the kitchen, or perhaps the complete stillness.

Allow your mind to stay with these sensations. If your thoughts drift to the past or the future, gently guide them back to the water, the soap, the dish in your hands. This is not about achieving a perfect state of mind, but about practicing gentle return.

Be fully present with each movement. The rinse, the way the water cascades off the clean surface. The feeling of the dish becoming clean and smooth.

There is no need to rush, no goal to achieve other than to be right here, right now, washing this dish. Each dish you wash is a moment of presence. Each stroke of the sponge, a gentle act of awareness.

As we come to the end of this short practice, take one more slow, mindful breath.
Feel the gratitude for this simple act, for the gift of your senses, and for the opportunity to find peace in the everyday.
When you're ready, you can gently open your eyes, or simply carry this quiet awareness with you into the rest of your day.`,

  ],
};

  ttsScript: `Welcome to the Tangerine Meditation.

Swallow deliberately, feeling the sensations in your throat. Take a moment after you've swallowed. What aftertastes linger?

This is what it means to eat mindfully. To bring our full attention to every aspect of the experience.

const coexistingTruths: MeditationScript = {
  id: "gen-coexisting-truths",
  title: "Coexisting Truths",
  subtitle: "Embracing your internal contradictions",
  category: "meditation",
  durationSec: 480,
  description: "A gentle exploration of the seemingly contradictory aspects within yourself, fostering acceptance and integration.",
  evidenceSource: "Brianna Wiest, The Human Element",
  tags: ["self-compassion", "acceptance", "inner-work", "brianna-wiest"],
  phase: "all",
  backgroundMusic: "gentle",
  ttsScript: `Welcome to Coexisting Truths.
Find a comfortable position, whether seated or lying down, where your body feels supported and at ease.
Gently close your eyes, or soften your gaze downwards.

Take a few deep, grounding breaths. Inhale slowly through your nose, feeling your belly and chest expand. And exhale completely through your mouth, letting go of any tension.
Allow your breath to settle into its natural rhythm. A gentle ebb and flow, creating a space of inner quiet.

Today, we're going to explore the beautiful complexity of being human — the way seemingly opposite truths can reside within us, simultaneously. There's no need to reconcile them, only to acknowledge them with compassion.

Bring to mind a situation or an aspect of yourself where you feel two conflicting things at once.
Perhaps you are both strong and vulnerable.
Perhaps you are both ambitious and in need of rest.
Perhaps you love someone deeply, and sometimes feel frustrated by them.
Or perhaps you desire growth, yet sometimes resist change.
Just allow one such pairing to surface, without judgment.

Now, let's hold this first truth. Acknowledge it gently within yourself.
If it's "I am strong," really feel into that strength. Where do you sense it in your body? What does it feel like?

And now, gently, without dismissing the first, acknowledge the coexisting truth.
"I am also vulnerable." Where do you sense your vulnerability? Perhaps a softening, a tender spot.

Notice how these two feelings, these two aspects, are both part of your experience. They don't negate each other.
The strength doesn't erase the vulnerability, and the vulnerability doesn't diminish the strength.
They simply exist. Like two sides of the same coin, two colours in a vibrant tapestry.

Perhaps you can even feel a sense of expansion as you hold both. You are bigger than any single label.
Offer yourself kindness for holding these complexities. It takes courage to acknowledge the full spectrum of who you are.

There is no need to make a choice between them. Both are real. Both are true for you.
Breathing into both, just as they are. This is not about fixing or changing, but about radically accepting.
This acceptance creates a wider container for your experience, allowing more of you to be seen and held.

As we bring this practice to a close, take a final deep breath, breathing in this sense of compassionate acceptance.
And as you exhale, release any lingering need to be one way or another.
When you're ready, gently bring your awareness back to the room, carrying this sense of inner spaciousness with you.`,

    { id: "s4", title: "Accept", body: "Breathe into radical acceptance of your complexity.", startTimeSec: 330, endTimeSec: 450 },
    { id: "s5", title: "Close", body: "Final breath and carry spaciousness forward.", startTimeSec: 450, endTimeSec: 480 },
  ],
};

  ttsScript: `Welcome to The Inner Light.

Turn your attention inward now.
Notice the sensations in your body. The gentle hum of your heart, the slight pressure where you meet the surface beneath you.

Now, imagine for a moment, that your physical body is like a beautiful vessel. It carries you through life, experiences the world, changes and grows. But beneath and beyond this vessel, there is something more.

Picture this essence as a soft, warm, luminous light within the very centre of your being.

This light represents your deepest self.
