            { heading: "Cap Before You Cut", body: "Before eliminating naps, try reducing duration:\n\u2022 Age 1\u20132.5: around 2 hours\n\u2022 Age 2.5: reduce to 1\u20131.5 hours\n\u2022 Age 3: maximum 1 hour\n\nIf capping doesn\u2019t solve night-time issues, it may be time to transition to quiet rest time instead." },
            { heading: "The Little-By-Little Sleep Plan", body: "For bedtime battles and teaching independent sleep:\n1. Place a chair next to their bed\n2. Stay quiet and boring \u2014 no engaging, singing, or back rubs\n3. Repeat your \u2018boring script\u2019: \u2018I\u2019m here, you\u2019re safe. Close your eyes.\u2019\n4. Each night, move the chair slightly further toward the door\n5. After ~2 weeks, you\u2019re at the door, then outside\n\nThis builds self-soothing without abandonment." },
          ]}},
          { id: "t-m10-l2-a2", type: "flip_card" as any, title: "Dropping the Nap: What You Need to Know", instruction: "Flip each card to understand when and how to transition away from napping.", content: { cards: [
            { front: "Signs It's Time", back: "Usually between ages 3–5 (rarely at 2.5). Signs: taking 20+ minutes to fall asleep at night, night wakings increasing, refusing 2+ naps per week consistently, early morning wake-ups. Don't rush it — try capping the nap first before dropping entirely.", emoji: "📋", tag: "Ready Signs" },
            { front: "Cap Before You Cut", back: "Before eliminating naps, reduce duration: Age 1–2.5: around 2 hours. Age 2.5: reduce to 1–1.5 hours. Age 3: maximum 1 hour. If capping doesn't solve night-time issues, transition to quiet rest time instead of a full nap.", emoji: "✂️", tag: "Gradual Approach" },
            { front: "Quiet Rest Time", back: "When the nap ends, replace it with quiet rest time (30–60 mins): child stays in their room with books, puzzles, or soft toys. This maintains the rhythm of the day, gives parents a break, and helps the child avoid becoming overtired.", emoji: "📚", tag: "What Comes Next" },
            { front: "The Bedtime-Nap Connection", back: "When dropping the nap, temporarily move bedtime EARLIER (30–60 mins) to compensate for lost sleep. Without this, overtiredness sets in by 3pm and both nap resistance and bedtime battles worsen. After 2–3 weeks, gradually shift bedtime back.", emoji: "🔗", tag: "Bedtime Adjustment" },
          ] } },
          { id: "t-m10-l2-a3", type: "knowledge_check" as any, title: "Knowledge Check", instruction: "Test what you've learned before moving on.", content: { intro: "Let's check your understanding of the nap transition.", passMark: 3, questions: [
            { question: "At what age do most children typically drop their nap?", options: ["Age 1–2", "Age 2–2.5", "Age 3–5", "Age 6–7"], correct: 2, explanation: "Most children naturally drop their nap between ages 3–5. Dropping before this (especially at age 2) is usually too early and can lead to overtiredness, worse behaviour, and increased night waking." },
            { question: "What should you try BEFORE fully eliminating the nap?", options: ["Stopping the nap suddenly on one day", "Capping the nap duration at a shorter length first", "Moving nap time to later in the day", "Eliminating the nap every other day"], correct: 1, explanation: "Capping (reducing nap duration) is the recommended first step. It allows the child to gradually adjust to less daytime sleep without the abrupt change that full elimination creates. Many families cap for several weeks before fully transitioning." },
            { question: "When a toddler drops their nap, what bedtime adjustment helps prevent overtiredness?", options: ["Move bedtime 1–2 hours later to tire them out more", "Keep bedtime exactly the same as before", "Move bedtime 30–60 minutes earlier temporarily", "Skip bedtime routine on non-nap days"], correct: 2, explanation: "Without the nap's restorative sleep, toddlers accumulate sleep pressure faster. Temporarily moving bedtime earlier (30–60 minutes) prevents overtiredness — which paradoxically makes toddlers harder to settle. After 2–3 weeks, gradually shift back." },
            { question: "What is 'quiet rest time' and why is it used?", options: ["Forced nap time where the child must sleep", "A designated period in the child's room with quiet activities — maintaining the rest rhythm without requiring sleep", "Sitting still at the dinner table", "TV time to wind down"], correct: 1, explanation: "Quiet rest time (30–60 minutes with books, puzzles, or soft toys in their room) replaces the nap's structure without requiring sleep. It gives both child and parent a restorative break and helps prevent afternoon overtiredness during the transition period." },
          ] } },
          { id: "t-m10-l2-a4", type: "true_false" as any, title: "Nap Check", content: { statement: "Most children should stop napping by age 2.", isTrue: false, explanation: "Most children still benefit from naps until age 3\u20135. Dropping too early often leads to overtiredness and worse behaviour. Look for consistent signs over several weeks before making the change." }},
        ]
      },
      {
        id: "toddler-m10-l3",
        title: "Kindergarten Readiness",
        description: "Preparing your child (and yourself!) for the big school transition",
        activities: [
          { id: "t-m10-l3-a0", type: "reaction_slider" as any, title: "How Are You Feeling?", instruction: "Before we begin, take a moment to reflect.", content: { question: "How ready do you feel for your child's transition to kindergarten or school?", options: [
            { emoji: "😰", label: "Very anxious about it" },
            { emoji: "😕", label: "Somewhat worried" },
            { emoji: "😐", label: "Mixed feelings" },
            { emoji: "🙂", label: "Fairly ready" },
            { emoji: "🌟", label: "Excited and prepared" },
          ] } },
          { id: "t-m10-l3-a1", type: "info_carousel" as any, title: "Ready for School", content: { slides: [
            { heading: "Focus on Independence, Not ABCs", body: "It\u2019s tempting to worry about counting and letters. But the skill that matters most is independence:\n\u2022 Can they open their lunchbox?\n\u2022 Can they ask when they need something?\n\u2022 Can they use the toilet on their own?\n\u2022 Can they put on shoes and jacket?\n\nPractise these through play and low-pressure games." },
            { heading: "PREP for Drop-Off", body: "Use PREP to walk through every detail before the first day. Role-play school life with dolls. Read school-themed books together.\n\nAt drop-off: stay calm, stay confident. Your feelings are contagious! If you waver, they\u2019ll worry something\u2019s wrong.\n\nGive a comfort anchor: a bracelet, a drawn heart on their hand, a note in their lunchbox." },
            { heading: "Expect After-School Meltdowns", body: "They\u2019ve been keeping it together all day in a new environment. That\u2019s exhausting! They\u2019ll melt down at home because YOU are their safe person.\n\nThe meltdown won\u2019t be about school \u2014 it\u2019ll be about crayons or bananas. Look beneath the surface and validate: \u2018You\u2019re feeling really upset. Sometimes I feel upset too.\u2019" },
          ]}},
          { id: "t-m10-l3-a2", type: "flip_card" as any, title: "Kindergarten Readiness: What Really Matters", instruction: "Flip each card to understand what actually prepares your child for their first school experience.", content: { cards: [
            { front: "Independence Over ABCs", back: "The skills that matter most: Can they open their lunchbox? Can they ask when they need something? Can they use the toilet alone? Can they put on shoes and jacket? Academic knowledge matters far less than self-help independence in the first months of school.", emoji: "🎒", tag: "True Readiness" },
            { front: "Prepare With PREP", back: "Before the first day, walk through every detail: Preview (what school looks like), Remind (what to do if scared), Explain (what happens if they miss you), Practise (role-play school with toys). Read school-themed books. Familiarity reduces fear.", emoji: "📖", tag: "PREP Method" },
            { front: "Your Calm Confidence Is Contagious", back: "At drop-off: stay calm, stay confident. Your feelings are contagious! If you waver, they'll worry something's wrong. Give a comfort anchor — a bracelet, a drawn heart on their hand, a note in their lunchbox. Keep the goodbye ritual brief, warm, and certain.", emoji: "💪", tag: "Drop-Off" },
            { front: "After-School Meltdowns Are Normal", back: "They've kept it together all day in a new environment. They'll melt down at home because YOU are their safe person. The meltdown won't be about school — it'll be about crayons or bananas. Look beneath the surface: 'You're feeling really upset. Big days are exhausting.'", emoji: "🌋", tag: "After School" },
          ] } },
          { id: "t-m10-l3-a3", type: "knowledge_check" as any, title: "Knowledge Check", instruction: "Test what you've learned before moving on.", content: { intro: "Let's check your understanding of kindergarten readiness.", passMark: 3, questions: [
            { question: "What is the MOST important skill for kindergarten readiness?", options: ["Knowing the alphabet and counting to 20", "Being able to write their name", "Independence skills — using the toilet alone, opening lunchbox, asking for help", "Being able to sit still for 30 minutes"], correct: 2, explanation: "Independence skills matter far more than academic knowledge in the first months of school. A child who can manage their own body, belongings, and needs — and ask for help when needed — adjusts to school far more easily than a child who knows their ABCs but can't open their lunchbox." },
            { question: "What does PREP stand for in preparing for school drop-off?", options: ["Prepare, Respond, Evaluate, Plan", "Preview, Remind, Explain, Practise", "Practice, Rest, Eat, Play", "Prepare, Reassure, Encourage, Praise"], correct: 1, explanation: "PREP (Preview what school looks like, Remind what to do if scared, Explain what happens if they miss you, Practise through role-play) reduces first-day fear by making the unknown familiar through preparation and rehearsal." },
            { question: "Why should a parent's goodbye be brief and confident, not long and emotional?", options: ["Long goodbyes make teachers' jobs harder", "Your emotional state is contagious — wavering signals to your child that there IS something to worry about", "Short goodbyes save time", "Children don't care how long goodbye takes"], correct: 1, explanation: "Children read parent emotion as information about safety. A warm, confident, brief goodbye communicates: 'This is safe. I'll be back. You've got this.' An emotional, drawn-out goodbye communicates: 'I'm worried too — maybe you should be too.'" },
            { question: "Why do after-school meltdowns happen, and what should parents do?", options: ["They're a sign the child isn't ready for school yet", "The child has been holding it together all day — they melt down at home because it's their safe space. Validate the emotion.", "They're manipulating parents for attention", "Parents should be firmer about the meltdown not being acceptable"], correct: 1, explanation: "After-school meltdowns happen because children expend enormous effort regulating themselves in a new, unfamiliar environment all day. Home — and you — is where they feel safe enough to release. This is a healthy sign of a secure attachment, not a problem." },
          ] } },
          { id: "t-m10-l3-a4", type: "open_response" as any, title: "School Readiness Plan", content: { prompt: "List 3 independence skills you can start practising with your child this week (opening containers, dressing themselves, asking for help). How will you make each one fun?", saveToVault: true }},
        ]
      }
    ]
  },
  {
    id: "toddler-m11",
    title: "Specific Situations",
    subtitle: "Hitting, biting, sharing, and other daily challenges",
    description: "Practical, in-the-moment strategies for the most common toddler behaviours that push buttons.",
    estimatedMinutes: 25,
    sources: ["Child Development Research", "Positive Discipline"],
    lessons: [
      {
        id: "toddler-m11-l1",
        title: "Hitting, Biting & Aggression",
        description: "Why it happens and what to do (and not do)",
        activities: [
          { id: "t-m11-l1-a0", type: "reaction_slider" as any, title: "How Are You Feeling?", instruction: "Before we begin, take a moment to reflect.", content: { question: "How do you feel when your toddler hits, bites, or is physically aggressive? Are you able to stay calm?", options: [
            { emoji: "😰", label: "Lose it completely" },
            { emoji: "😕", label: "Struggle a lot" },
            { emoji: "😐", label: "Sometimes okay" },
            { emoji: "🙂", label: "Usually calm" },
            { emoji: "💪", label: "Always calm" },
          ] } },
          { id: "t-m11-l1-a1", type: "info_carousel" as any, title: "Physical Aggression", content: { slides: [
            { heading: "Why They Hit/Bite", body: "Toddlers hit and bite because:\n\u2022 They can\u2019t express feelings in words yet\n\u2022 Their impulse control is undeveloped\n\u2022 They\u2019re testing cause-and-effect\n\u2022 They\u2019re overwhelmed\n\nIt\u2019s NOT because they\u2019re \u2018mean\u2019 or you\u2019re a bad parent." },
            { heading: "What to Do In the Moment", body: "1. Block/stop the behaviour: \u2018I won\u2019t let you hit\u2019\n2. Check the other child first (this also teaches empathy)\n3. Name the feeling: \u2018You were angry\u2019\n4. Offer the alternative: \u2018Hands are for gentle touch. You can stamp your feet when you\u2019re angry\u2019\n\nStay neutral \u2014 big reactions (positive OR negative) reinforce the behaviour." },
            { heading: "When Another Child Hits Yours", body: "This is hard! Model the response you\u2019d want:\n\u2022 Comfort your child first\n\u2022 Don\u2019t shame the other child\n\u2022 \u2018That hurt. We need to use gentle hands\u2019\n\u2022 Remove your child from the situation if needed\n\u2022 Don\u2019t force your child to \u2018hit back\u2019" },
          ]}},
          { id: "t-m11-l1-a2", type: "flip_card" as any, title: "Hitting & Biting: Key Concepts", instruction: "Flip each card to understand why toddlers hit and what actually works.", content: { cards: [
            { front: "Why They Hit & Bite", back: "Toddlers hit and bite because: they can't express feelings in words yet, impulse control is undeveloped, they're testing cause-and-effect, or they're overwhelmed. It's NOT because they're 'mean' or you're a bad parent. It's a communication failure, not a character flaw.", emoji: "🧠", tag: "The Why" },
            { front: "The 4-Step Response", back: "1. BLOCK: 'I won't let you hit.' 2. CHECK the other child first (models empathy). 3. NAME the feeling: 'You were angry.' 4. OFFER the alternative: 'You can stamp your feet when you're angry.' Stay neutral — big reactions reinforce the behaviour.", emoji: "📋", tag: "What to Do" },
            { front: "Big Reactions Backfire", back: "Both shock/horror AND laughing reinforce hitting. Toddlers are cause-and-effect experimenters — a dramatic parental reaction is very interesting and motivating to repeat. Stay neutral, brief, and matter-of-fact. Less reaction = less repetition.", emoji: "🎭", tag: "Reaction Matters" },
            { front: "Teaching the Alternative", back: "Saying 'don't hit' without an alternative leaves the toddler with the same overwhelming feeling and no acceptable outlet. Always pair the limit ('I won't let you hit') with an alternative ('you can squeeze this pillow / stamp your feet / use your words').", emoji: "🔄", tag: "Offer an Alternative" },
          ] } },
          { id: "t-m11-l1-a3", type: "knowledge_check" as any, title: "Knowledge Check", instruction: "Test what you've learned before moving on.", content: { intro: "Let's check your understanding of handling toddler hitting and biting.", passMark: 3, questions: [
            { question: "Why do toddlers hit and bite?", options: ["Because they are naturally aggressive", "Because they can't express feelings in words and have undeveloped impulse control — it's communication, not cruelty", "Because parents haven't set enough consequences", "Because they watched it on TV"], correct: 1, explanation: "Toddler physical aggression is almost always communication — expressing overwhelm, frustration, or excitement without the language to do so. Understanding this changes the parent's response from moral outrage to problem-solving." },
            { question: "Why do dramatic reactions (shock, shouting) make hitting WORSE?", options: ["They upset the parent", "Toddlers are cause-and-effect explorers — an interesting reaction is motivating to repeat", "They confuse the toddler", "They teach the toddler that hitting is funny"], correct: 1, explanation: "Toddlers are experimenting with cause and effect. A dramatic, emotional parental reaction is highly interesting and motivating to repeat. A neutral, brief, matter-of-fact response removes the interesting consequence and reduces repetition." },
            { question: "In the 4-step response to hitting, why do you check the other child FIRST?", options: ["Because the other child is more hurt", "Because it models empathy and connects the toddler's action with its impact on others", "Because parents need to assess the injury", "Because the hitting child needs time alone"], correct: 1, explanation: "Checking on the other child first models empathy in action — showing the toddler that their actions affect others. It also briefly removes the parental attention that sometimes reinforces hitting." },
            { question: "What must you ALWAYS pair with 'I won't let you hit'?", options: ["A time-out", "An explanation of why hitting is wrong", "An alternative acceptable behaviour for expressing the same feeling", "A consequence like losing a toy"], correct: 2, explanation: "Teaching the alternative is essential. 'Don't hit' without a replacement leaves the toddler with the same overwhelming feeling and no acceptable outlet. Offering an alternative (stamping, squeezing, using words) builds emotional regulation skills." },
          ] } },
          { id: "t-m11-l1-a4", type: "open_response" as any, title: "Your Plan", content: { prompt: "Write a specific script you\u2019ll use next time your toddler hits. Include what you\u2019ll say to them AND what you\u2019ll do with your body (get low, hold hands, etc.).", saveToVault: true }},
        ]
      },
      {
        id: "toddler-m11-l2",
        title: "Sharing & Turn-Taking",
        description: "Why forced sharing doesn\u2019t work and what to do instead",
        activities: [
          { id: "t-m11-l2-a0", type: "reaction_slider" as any, title: "How Are You Feeling?", instruction: "Before we begin, take a moment to reflect.", content: { question: "How confident are you in handling sharing conflicts between toddlers without forcing them to share?", options: [
            { emoji: "😰", label: "Very unsure" },
            { emoji: "😕", label: "Quite lost" },
            { emoji: "😐", label: "Somewhat okay" },
            { emoji: "🙂", label: "Fairly confident" },
            { emoji: "✅", label: "Very confident" },
          ] } },
          { id: "t-m11-l2-a1", type: "info_carousel" as any, title: "The Sharing Myth", content: { slides: [
            { heading: "Forced Sharing Doesn\u2019t Teach Sharing", body: "Imagine someone at work took your coffee and said \u2018You need to share!\u2019 You\u2019d be furious. Forced sharing teaches that other people can take your things whenever they want. True generosity comes from choice, not force." },
            { heading: "What to Do Instead", body: "\u2022 Teach turn-taking: \u2018When you\u2019re finished, then it\u2019s their turn\u2019\n\u2022 Use a timer for popular toys\n\u2022 Protect their right to finish: \u2018She\u2019s still using that. You can have it when she\u2019s done\u2019\n\u2022 Model generosity: \u2018Would you like to share some of my snack?\u2019\n\u2022 Praise genuine sharing when it naturally occurs" },
          ]}},
          { id: "t-m11-l2-a2", type: "flip_card" as any, title: "Sharing & Turn-Taking: What Actually Works", instruction: "Flip each card to understand why forced sharing backfires and what to do instead.", content: { cards: [
            { front: "Why Forced Sharing Backfires", back: "Imagine someone at work took your coffee and said 'You need to share!' Forced sharing teaches: other people can take your things whenever they want. True generosity comes from choice, not force — and choice doesn't develop until ages 3–4.", emoji: "☕", tag: "The Problem" },
            { front: "Turn-Taking Instead", back: "'When you're finished, then it's their turn.' Use a timer for popular toys. Protect their right to finish: 'She's still using that. You can have it when she's done.' This teaches: your turn will come — an important lesson in delayed gratification.", emoji: "⏱️", tag: "Turn-Taking" },
            { front: "When Sharing IS Real", back: "Sharing skills genuinely develop between ages 3–4. 43% of parents expect it before age 3 — when it's simply not developmentally possible. Praise genuine voluntary sharing ('I noticed you gave her a turn — that was really kind') to reinforce when it naturally occurs.", emoji: "🎁", tag: "Real Sharing" },
            { front: "Model Generosity", back: "Offer your child a bit of your snack. Let them see you share with others. Say 'I'd like to share some of my...' around them. Children learn generosity by watching it demonstrated, not by being forced to perform it.", emoji: "👀", tag: "Modelling" },
          ] } },
          { id: "t-m11-l2-a3", type: "knowledge_check" as any, title: "Knowledge Check", instruction: "Test what you've learned before moving on.", content: { intro: "Let's check your understanding of sharing and turn-taking.", passMark: 3, questions: [
            { question: "Why doesn't forced sharing teach real generosity?", options: ["Children are naturally selfish", "Forced sharing teaches 'others can take your things whenever they want' — the opposite of voluntary generosity", "Children need to learn that sharing is required", "Parents are not consistent enough"], correct: 1, explanation: "True generosity is voluntary — it comes from wanting to give, not from having things taken. Forced sharing teaches children to be more protective of possessions, not less — and it doesn't develop the internal motivation that real generosity requires." },
            { question: "At what age do sharing skills genuinely develop?", options: ["Age 1–2", "Age 2–2.5", "Age 3–4", "Age 5+"], correct: 2, explanation: "Sharing skills develop between ages 3–4. Before this, the cognitive and emotional capacity for voluntary sharing simply isn't there. Understanding this prevents frustration from expecting behaviour a child cannot yet produce." },
            { question: "What is the best approach when two toddlers want the same toy?", options: ["Take the toy away so neither child gets it", "Give it to the younger/more upset child", "Teach turn-taking: 'When you're finished, then it's their turn' — protecting each child's right to finish", "Insist the child shares immediately"], correct: 2, explanation: "Turn-taking respects each child's rights while teaching delayed gratification — a crucial skill. 'When you're done, then it's their turn' communicates: you will get your turn, and your turn will come to an end too." },
            { question: "How do children best learn to be genuinely generous?", options: ["Through consistent forced sharing", "By being rewarded for sharing", "By watching adults model generosity voluntarily in everyday life", "By being told sharing is important"], correct: 2, explanation: "Children learn generosity through observation — watching adults voluntarily share, offer, and give. Modelling 'I'd like to share some of my...' creates an internal template for generosity that children naturally replicate over time." },
          ] } },
          { id: "t-m11-l2-a4", type: "decision_point" as any, title: "What Would You Do?", content: { scenario: "Your child is having a full meltdown in the supermarket because you said no to a toy. Other shoppers are staring. What do you do?", options: [{ label: "Get down to their level and validate: 'You really wanted that toy. It's hard when we can't have something we want.'", outcome: "Validating the emotion doesn't mean giving in. Your child feels heard, and the intensity often drops. You can then offer a choice: 'Would you like to help me pick the apples or the bananas?'" }, { label: "Firmly say 'Stop it — you're embarrassing yourself' and keep walking", outcome: "Shaming during a meltdown escalates it. Your child can't access rational thinking during emotional flooding. They need co-regulation first, boundaries second." }, { label: "Give in and buy the toy to stop the scene", outcome: "This teaches: meltdowns = getting what I want. Short-term peace, long-term pattern. The next meltdown will be bigger." }] }},
        ]
      }
    ]
  },
  {
    id: "toddler-m12",
    title: "The BREATHE Method",
    subtitle: "A seven-step framework for navigating tantrums and meltdowns",
    description: "When a tantrum hits, you need a clear, step-by-step process. BREATHE gives you seven anchoring steps to stay calm, connect with your child, and guide them through their biggest feelings.",
    estimatedMinutes: 25,
    lessons: [
      {
        id: "toddler-m12-l1",
        title: "The Seven Steps of BREATHE",
        description: "Your complete tantrum navigation system",
        activities: [
          { id: "t-m12-l1-a0", type: "reaction_slider" as any, title: "How Are You Feeling?", instruction: "Before we begin, take a moment to check in.", content: { question: "When your toddler has a major meltdown, how calm are YOU able to stay?", options: [
            { emoji: "😰", label: "Completely lose it" },
            { emoji: "😕", label: "Often reactive" },
            { emoji: "😐", label: "Sometimes calm" },
            { emoji: "🙂", label: "Usually calm" },
            { emoji: "🧘", label: "Very calm" },
          ] } },
          { id: "t-m12-l1-a1", type: "info_carousel" as any, title: "B.R.E.A.T.H.E.", content: { slides: [
            { heading: "B \u2014 Be Clear Ahead of Time", body: "Before a tantrum even starts, set your child up for success. Use PREP to explain what\u2019s happening, what\u2019s expected, and what comes next. When children know the plan, they feel safer and tantrums reduce dramatically.\n\nR \u2014 Release Your Reaction When It Begins\nWhen the tantrum starts, YOUR first job is to regulate yourself. Take a breath. Drop your shoulders. Unclench your jaw. Your child is a sponge for your energy \u2014 if you escalate, they will too." },
            { heading: "E \u2014 Eye Level & A \u2014 Allow the Feels", body: "Get down to their level physically. This is powerful body language that says \u2018I\u2019m here, I\u2019m safe, I\u2019m not a threat.\u2019 Keep your voice low and calm.\n\nAllow the feelings to flow without trying to fix, distract, or shut them down. Tantrums aren\u2019t the time to teach \u2014 they\u2019re the time to CONNECT. \u2018You\u2019re really upset right now. I\u2019m right here.\u2019" },
            { heading: "T.H.E. \u2014 Tell, Highlight, Echo", body: "T \u2014 Tell Them Where the Bumpers Are: Once calming, set the boundary: \u2018It\u2019s not okay to throw things. I\u2019ll keep you safe.\u2019\n\nH \u2014 Highlight a Yes: Redirect to what they CAN do: \u2018You can\u2019t throw the blocks, but you CAN stomp your feet!\u2019\n\nE \u2014 Echo the Same Thing Over and Over: Repeat your calm phrase like a broken record. Repetition is soothing and helps their overwhelmed brain process." },
          ]}},
          { id: "t-m12-l1-a2", type: "flip_card" as any, title: "The BREATHE Method: Key Concepts", instruction: "Flip each card to master each step of the BREATHE tantrum navigation system.", content: { cards: [
            { front: "B & R: Before & Release", back: "B — BE CLEAR AHEAD OF TIME: Use PREP to set expectations before situations that trigger tantrums. R — RELEASE YOUR REACTION: When it starts, regulate YOURSELF first. Take a breath, drop your shoulders, unclench your jaw. Your child is a sponge for your energy — if you escalate, they will too.", emoji: "🅱️", tag: "Steps B & R" },
            { front: "E & A: Eye Level & Allow", back: "E — EYE LEVEL: Get down to their physical level — powerful body language that says 'I'm here, I'm safe, I'm not a threat.' A — ALLOW THE FEELS: Let feelings flow without fixing, distracting, or shutting them down. 'You're really upset right now. I'm right here.'", emoji: "👁️", tag: "Steps E & A" },
            { front: "T & H: Tell & Highlight", back: "T — TELL THEM THE BOUNDARIES: Once calming begins, set the limit: 'It's not okay to throw things. I'll keep you safe.' H — HIGHLIGHT A YES: Redirect to what they CAN do: 'You can't throw the blocks, but you CAN stomp your feet!'", emoji: "📢", tag: "Steps T & H" },
            { front: "E: Echo", back: "E — ECHO THE SAME THING OVER AND OVER: Repeat your calm phrase like a broken record. 'I know you're upset. I'm here. I know you're upset. I'm here.' Repetition is soothing and helps an overwhelmed brain process. Don't change the script — consistency is the medicine.", emoji: "🔁", tag: "Step E: Echo" },
          ] } },
          { id: "t-m12-l1-a3", type: "knowledge_check" as any, title: "Knowledge Check", instruction: "Test what you've learned before moving on.", content: { intro: "Let's check your understanding of the BREATHE method.", passMark: 3, questions: [
            { question: "In the BREATHE method, what does the FIRST step 'B' stand for?", options: ["Breathe in, breathe out", "Be clear ahead of time — use PREP to set expectations before triggering situations", "Be calm no matter what", "Block the behaviour immediately"], correct: 1, explanation: "B stands for 'Be Clear Ahead of Time.' Many tantrums are preventable when children know what's coming. Using PREP before transitions, unfamiliar situations, or places with temptations significantly reduces meltdown frequency." },
            { question: "Why is getting to the child's eye level (the 'E' step) so powerful?", options: ["It helps parents see the situation from the child's perspective", "It signals 'I'm here, I'm safe, I'm not a threat' through body language — physical positioning communicates safety", "It prevents the child from running away", "It makes it easier to talk quietly"], correct: 1, explanation: "Physical positioning communicates before words. Getting to eye level — rather than looming over a distressed child — signals in a primal, body-level way: 'I am with you, I am safe, I am not threatening you.' This helps the child's nervous system begin to settle." },

            { front: "Temperature", back: "Room temperature should be 16–20°C (61–68°F). Overheating is a SIDS risk factor. Dress baby in one more layer than you'd wear. Check baby's chest temperature, not hands or feet.", emoji: "🌡️", tag: "Temperature" },
          ] } },
          { id: "b-m1-l2-a3", type: "true_false" as any, title: "Safety Check", content: { statement: "A baby who sleeps on their tummy is at no increased risk as long as the mattress is firm.", isTrue: false, explanation: "Back sleeping is the single most important safe sleep practice. Always place your baby on their back for every sleep. Once they can roll independently (usually 5–6 months), it's safe to let them find their own position." }},
          { id: "b-m1-l2-a4", type: "knowledge_check" as any, title: "Knowledge Check", instruction: "Test your understanding of safe sleep before moving on.", content: { intro: "Let's check your knowledge of safe sleep essentials.", passMark: 3, questions: [
            { question: "Which of the following is an essential safe sleep practice?", options: ["Place baby on their tummy to help them sleep longer", "Always place baby on their back for every sleep", "Use a soft mattress with a pillow for comfort", "Keep the room at 24°C to keep baby warm"], correct: 1, explanation: "Back sleeping for every sleep is the single most important safe sleep practice and significantly reduces the risk of SIDS." },
            { question: "When is it safe for baby to sleep in a completely separate room?", options: ["From birth, as long as you have a monitor", "After the first week when you need rest", "After at least 6 months in your room", "Whenever the baby starts sleeping through the night"], correct: 2, explanation: "Room sharing (baby in their own cot in your room) is recommended for at least the first 6 months and ideally 12 months. It reduces SIDS risk by up to 50%." },
            { question: "What items should be in baby's sleep space?", options: ["A fitted sheet, small pillow and rolled towel for comfort", "Only a firm mattress with a fitted sheet", "Soft bumpers to prevent rolling and head knocks", "A light blanket tucked firmly under the mattress"], correct: 1, explanation: "The sleep space should contain only a firm, flat mattress with a fitted sheet. No pillows, bumpers, loose bedding, or soft toys." },
            { question: "Swaddling should stop when:", options: ["Baby reaches 3 months of age", "Baby shows signs of rolling", "Baby can lift their head during tummy time", "Baby starts sleeping through the night"], correct: 1, explanation: "Swaddling should stop when baby shows signs of rolling, as a swaddled baby who rolls to their tummy cannot reposition safely. This is typically around 3–4 months." },
          ] } },
        ]
      },
      {
        id: "baby-m1-l3",
        title: "Week-by-Week Sleep & Feed Guide",
        description: "Your structured daily schedule from birth to 6 months",
        activities: [
          { id: "b-m1-l3-a1", type: "info_carousel" as any, title: "Your Roadmap", content: { slides: [
            { heading: "How to Use the Schedule", body: "The weekly schedules on the next screen are a GUIDE, not a rigid timetable. Every baby is different. Use them as a framework and adjust based on your baby's hunger cues and sleep signals. The key principles: structured day → better night." },
            { heading: "Feed Amounts", body: "Breastfeeding: time on each breast is listed as a guide. Let baby fully drain one breast before switching. Bottle-feeding: amounts are calculated at roughly 150ml per kg of body weight per day, divided across feeds. Adjust up or down based on your baby's needs." },
            { heading: "Awake Windows", body: "0–4 weeks: 45–60 minutes\n4–8 weeks: 1–1.5 hours\n8–12 weeks: 1.5–2 hours\n3–4 months: 2–2.5 hours\n4–6 months: 2–2.5 hours\n\nWatch for sleepy cues: yawning, eye rubbing, fussiness. Put down BEFORE they're overtired." },
          ]}},
          { id: "b-m1-l3-a2", type: "open_response" as any, title: "Track Your Baby", content: { prompt: "Note your baby's current age and approximate schedule. Where does it differ from the guide? What's one adjustment you could try this week?", saveToVault: true }},
        ]
      }
    ]

  {
    id: "baby-m2",
    title: "Feeding Foundations",
    subtitle: "Breast, bottle, or combo — making it work for your family",
    description: "Evidence-based feeding guidance without the guilt. Whether you breastfeed, formula-feed, or combine both, learn how to nourish your baby and protect your own wellbeing.",
    estimatedMinutes: 25,
    sources: ["Lactation Science", "Paediatric Nutrition"],
    lessons: [
      {
        id: "baby-m2-l1",
        title: "Breastfeeding Success",
        description: "Positioning, latch, supply, and troubleshooting",
        activities: [
          { id: "b-m2-l1-a0", type: "reaction_slider" as any, title: "Feeding Confidence Check", instruction: "Before we begin, check in with how you're feeling about feeding.", content: { question: "How confident do you feel about your current approach to feeding your baby?", options: [
            { emoji: "😰", label: "Very unsure" },
            { emoji: "😕", label: "Struggling a bit" },
            { emoji: "😐", label: "Getting there" },
            { emoji: "🙂", label: "Mostly confident" },
            { emoji: "🌟", label: "Very confident" },
          ] } },
          { id: "b-m2-l1-a1", type: "info_carousel" as any, title: "Getting It Right", content: { slides: [
            { heading: "The Latch", body: "A good latch is the foundation of comfortable, effective breastfeeding. Baby should have a wide mouth covering the areola (not just the nipple), their chin tucked into the breast, nose clear, and you should hear rhythmic swallowing. Pain beyond mild discomfort in the first 30 seconds is a sign of poor latch — break suction and try again." },
            { heading: "Building Supply", body: "Milk production works on supply and demand. To build supply:\n• Feed frequently (8–12 times in 24 hrs initially)\n• Fully drain one breast before switching\n• Express/pump after morning feeds\n• Stay hydrated and well-nourished\n• Rest when baby rests\n\nThe morning is when supply is naturally highest." },
            { heading: "One Bottle a Day", body: "Introducing one bottle of expressed milk per day from week 2–4 gives flexibility, lets your partner bond through feeding, and ensures baby can take a bottle if needed. This does NOT harm breastfeeding when done correctly. Express the same volume to maintain supply." },
          ]}},
          { id: "b-m2-l1-a2", type: "flip_card" as any, title: "Breastfeeding Key Concepts", instruction: "Flip each card to understand the essentials of successful breastfeeding.", content: { cards: [
            { front: "A Good Latch", back: "Baby's mouth should cover the areola (not just the nipple), chin tucked into breast, nose clear. You should hear rhythmic swallowing. Ongoing pain beyond mild initial discomfort signals a poor latch — break suction and retry.", emoji: "🤱", tag: "Latch" },
            { front: "Supply & Demand", back: "Milk production is driven by demand. Feed 8–12 times per 24 hours to build supply. Fully drain one breast before switching. Express after morning feeds to increase output. Morning is when supply peaks naturally.", emoji: "🍼", tag: "Supply" },
            { front: "Foremilk vs Hindmilk", back: "Foremilk (at the start of a feed) is watery and thirst-quenching. Hindmilk (at the end) is richer and more calorie-dense. Let baby fully drain one breast to ensure they get both, especially the calorie-rich hindmilk.", emoji: "💧", tag: "Milk" },
            { front: "Growth Spurts", back: "Babies cluster-feed during growth spurts (around 3 weeks, 6 weeks, 3 months). This feels like constantly feeding and often triggers supply worries. It's the baby's way of boosting your supply — trust the process and feed on demand.", emoji: "📈", tag: "Growth" },
          ] } },
          { id: "b-m2-l1-a3", type: "open_response" as any, title: "Your Feeding Plan", content: { prompt: "What's your current feeding approach and what's your biggest challenge? Write down one question you'd like answered.", saveToVault: true }},
          { id: "b-m2-l1-a4", type: "knowledge_check" as any, title: "Knowledge Check", instruction: "Test what you've learned about breastfeeding success.", content: { intro: "Let's check your understanding of breastfeeding foundations.", passMark: 3, questions: [
            { question: "What is the key sign of a good breastfeeding latch?", options: ["Baby only has the nipple in their mouth", "Baby's mouth covers the nipple and most of the areola", "You feel significant pain throughout the feed", "Baby feeds for exactly 10 minutes each side"], correct: 1, explanation: "A good latch involves baby's mouth covering the areola, not just the nipple. This prevents nipple pain and ensures effective milk transfer." },
            { question: "How many times should a newborn typically feed in 24 hours?", options: ["4–6 times", "6–8 times", "8–12 times", "14–16 times"], correct: 2, explanation: "Newborns typically need 8–12 feeds per 24 hours. Frequent feeding builds milk supply and ensures adequate nutrition for rapid early growth." },
            { question: "When is breast milk supply naturally at its highest?", options: ["Late afternoon around 4pm", "After baby's longest sleep", "In the morning", "At bedtime after cluster feeding"], correct: 2, explanation: "Prolactin (the milk-producing hormone) peaks in the early morning, which is why morning feeds are most effective for expressing extra milk to build a supply stash." },
            { question: "What should you do when introducing a bottle of expressed milk?", options: ["Replace the breast feed entirely with the bottle", "Express the same volume given in the bottle to protect supply", "Stop breastfeeding that day to avoid confusion", "Only introduce bottles after 6 months"], correct: 1, explanation: "When giving a bottle of expressed milk, express the same volume to signal to your body that the demand hasn't changed. This protects your supply while giving feeding flexibility." },
          ] } },
        ]
      },
      {
        id: "baby-m2-l2",
        title: "Bottle-Feeding With Confidence",
        description: "Whether formula or expressed milk — doing it well",
        activities: [
          { id: "b-m2-l2-a1", type: "info_carousel" as any, title: "Bottle Basics", content: { slides: [
            { heading: "Calculating Amounts", body: "General guide: 150ml per kg of body weight per day, divided across feeds.\n\nExample: 4kg baby = 600ml/day ÷ 6 feeds = 100ml per feed\n\nThis is a STARTING POINT. Some babies need more, some less. Watch for hunger and fullness cues rather than fixating on exact amounts." },
            { heading: "Paced Bottle Feeding", body: "Hold baby semi-upright (not lying flat). Hold bottle horizontal so milk doesn't flow too fast. Let baby draw milk in at their own pace. Pause every few minutes to burp. A feed should take 15–20 minutes (not 5 minutes of guzzling). This prevents overfeeding and gas." },
            { heading: "Combination Feeding", body: "Many families combine breast and bottle successfully. The key: maintain breast stimulation by expressing whenever you give a bottle. This protects supply while giving you flexibility. No guilt — fed is best, and your mental health matters." },
          ]}},
          { id: "b-m2-l2-a2", type: "find_the_pair" as any, title: "Match the Method", content: { instruction: "Match each feeding method with its key principle.", pairs: [["Paced bottle feeding", "Hold baby semi-upright, let them control pace"], ["Calculating amounts", "150ml per kg of body weight per day"], ["Combination feeding", "Express when giving a bottle to protect supply"], ["Burping technique", "Pause every few minutes during feed"]] }},
        ]
      }
    ]
  },
  {
    id: "baby-m4",
    title: "Baby Brain Development & Play",
    subtitle: "Wiring a growing brain through everyday interaction",
    description: "Every nappy change, eye-contact moment, and tummy time session is literally building your baby's brain. Understand the sensory milestones from birth to 12 months, and how responsive play creates the neural foundations for everything that follows.",
    estimatedMinutes: 30,
    sourceBooks: ["What's Going On In There? — Lise Eliot", "The Wonder Weeks — Hetty van de Rijt & Frans Plooij"],
    sources: ["Infant Neuroscience", "Developmental Psychology"],
    lessons: [
      {
        id: "baby-m4-l1",
        title: "How Your Baby's Brain Grows",
        description: "One million new neural connections per second — what's actually happening",
        activities: [
          { id: "b-m4-l1-a0", type: "reaction_slider" as any, title: "Brain Development Check-In", instruction: "Take a moment to reflect before we explore how your baby's brain is growing.", content: { question: "How aware do you feel of the ways everyday interactions are building your baby's brain?", options: [
            { emoji: "😰", label: "Not at all aware" },
            { emoji: "😕", label: "Slightly aware" },
            { emoji: "😐", label: "Somewhat aware" },
            { emoji: "🙂", label: "Quite aware" },
            { emoji: "🌟", label: "Very aware" },
          ] } },
          { id: "b-m4-l1-a1", type: "info_carousel" as any, title: "The Building Brain", content: { slides: [
            { heading: "1 Million Connections Per Second", body: "In the first year of life, your baby's brain creates approximately 1 million new neural connections every second. This is faster than at any other time in their life. The experiences you provide — or fail to provide — literally shape which pathways get wired and which get pruned.\n\nThis isn't pressure — it's empowering. Normal, loving parenting is brain-building parenting." },
            { heading: "Serve & Return", body: "The single most powerful brain-building interaction is 'serve and return' — your baby initiates (looks, babbles, reaches) and you respond (eye contact, copy their sound, name what they're doing). Repeat.\n\nThis back-and-forth is the foundation of language, emotional regulation, and secure attachment. It happens naturally in loving care — but knowing it's happening means you'll do more of it." },
            { heading: "What 'Enrichment' Actually Means", body: "You don't need flashcards, educational toys, or screen programs. Research is clear: babies benefit most from:\n• Human faces, especially yours\n• Real conversation (not baby-talk shows)\n• Responsive interaction\n• Varied sensory experience (textures, sounds, light)\n• Safe exploration\n\nThe expensive stuff is for adults who feel guilty. The free stuff is what actually works." },
          ]}},
          { id: "b-m4-l1-a2", type: "flip_card" as any, title: "Brain Building Concepts", instruction: "Flip each card to understand the key ideas behind your baby's brain development.", content: { cards: [
            { front: "Serve & Return", back: "The most powerful brain-building interaction: baby initiates (looks, babbles, reaches) and you respond (eye contact, copy their sound, name what they're doing). This back-and-forth wires language, emotional regulation, and secure attachment.", emoji: "🔄", tag: "Interaction" },
            { front: "Neural Pruning", back: "Babies are born with more neural connections than they'll ever need. The brain strengthens pathways that are used frequently and prunes unused ones. Rich, varied experiences literally shape which brain pathways survive.", emoji: "✂️", tag: "Neuroscience" },
            { front: "Serve & Return Mismatch", back: "When a parent doesn't respond to a baby's bid for connection (the 'still face'), babies first try harder, then show distress, then turn inward. This shows how profoundly responsive interaction matters for emotional development.", emoji: "😶", tag: "Connection" },
            { front: "Enrichment Myth", back: "Babies don't need expensive educational toys or apps. Research is clear: human faces, real conversation, responsive interaction, varied sensory experience, and safe exploration are the most powerful brain-builders — all free.", emoji: "💡", tag: "Reality" },
          ] } },
          { id: "b-m4-l1-a3", type: "true_false" as any, title: "Reality Check", content: { statement: "Educational baby videos and apps are beneficial for brain development in the first year.", isTrue: false, explanation: "The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends no screen time for children under 18-24 months (video calls with family excepted). Babies learn language through LIVE interaction, not screens — the two-way responsiveness is irreplaceable." }},
          { id: "b-m4-l1-a4", type: "knowledge_check" as any, title: "Knowledge Check", instruction: "Test your understanding of baby brain development before moving on.", content: { intro: "Let's check your understanding of how your baby's brain grows through interaction.", passMark: 3, questions: [
            { question: "How many new neural connections does a baby's brain create per second in the first year?", options: ["About 1,000", "About 10,000", "About 100,000", "About 1 million"], correct: 3, explanation: "A baby's brain creates approximately 1 million new neural connections every second in the first year — the fastest rate of brain development in a human lifetime." },
            { question: "What is 'serve and return' in the context of baby brain development?", options: ["Feeding baby and burping them afterward", "Baby initiates interaction and parent responds, back and forth", "Offering a toy and taking it back to build attention", "A method for introducing solid foods"], correct: 1, explanation: "Serve and return is the back-and-forth interaction where baby initiates (looks, babbles, reaches) and the parent responds. This builds the neural foundations for language, emotional regulation, and attachment." },
            { question: "What does the American Academy of Pediatrics recommend about screens for babies under 18 months?", options: ["Up to 1 hour of quality educational content daily", "30 minutes of educational programming is fine", "No screen time except video calls with family", "Screens are fine as long as parents watch together"], correct: 2, explanation: "The AAP recommends avoiding screen media for children under 18–24 months, with the exception of video calls with family. Babies learn language through live, responsive interaction that screens cannot replicate." },
            { question: "Which of these is the most effective brain-building activity for babies?", options: ["Playing educational YouTube videos", "Using flashcards to teach shapes and colours", "Making eye contact and copying baby's sounds and expressions", "Buying age-rated educational toys"], correct: 2, explanation: "Responsive human interaction — particularly serve-and-return exchanges involving eye contact, mirroring, and responding to baby's cues — is the most powerful brain-builder available, and it costs nothing." },
          ] } },
        ]
      },
      {
        id: "baby-m4-l2",
        title: "Sensory Milestones & Tummy Time",
        description: "Month-by-month development and how to support it",
        activities: [
          { id: "b-m4-l2-a1", type: "info_carousel" as any, title: "Month by Month", content: { slides: [
            { heading: "Birth–3 Months: High Contrast & Faces", body: "Vision: blurry beyond 20-30cm — hold your face close. Loves high-contrast black/white patterns. Hearing: can recognise your voice from birth (heard it in the womb). Smell: recognises mother's milk scent.\n\nWhat to do: talk to them constantly. Make eye contact during feeds. Hold black/white images at close range. Play music and sing (pitch matters less than connection)." },
            { heading: "3–6 Months: Reaching & Rolling", body: "Hands discover objects. Reaching and mouthing begins — this IS how they learn. Vision develops colour. Begin to push up on tummy. Laugh appears around 4 months.\n\nWhat to do: Offer objects of different textures, weights, and shapes. Let them grasp your finger, a soft toy, a rattle. More tummy time — aim for 30 min/day total across sessions." },
            { heading: "6–12 Months: Crawling & Babbling", body: "Sitting unsupported arrives (around 6–8 months). Crawling begins. Object permanence develops — peekaboo is suddenly HILARIOUS because they now know you exist even when hidden.\n\nBabbling starts ('ba-ba', 'ma-ma'). Respond to every babble as if it's a word. The back-and-forth of 'conversation' is how language wires in." },
          ]}},
          { id: "b-m4-l2-a2", type: "info_carousel" as any, title: "The Tummy Time Toolkit", content: { slides: [
            { heading: "Why Tummy Time Matters", body: "Since the 'Back to Sleep' campaign (essential for SIDS prevention), babies spend less time on their tummies. This means tummy time must be intentional. It builds:\n• Neck, back and shoulder muscles\n• Head control (essential for crawling and walking)\n• Reduces flat head syndrome\n• Develops visual perspective\n\nStart from day 1 — even a few seconds counts." },
            { heading: "Tummy Time Troubleshooting", body: "If they hate it:\n• Do it straight after a nappy change (fresher and more alert)\n• Get down at their level — your face is motivation\n• Place on YOUR chest (tummy-to-chest)\n• Use a rolled towel under their chest for support\n• High-contrast mat or mirror in front of them\n• Build up slowly — 1 minute at a time\n\nGoal: 30 minutes total per day across multiple sessions by 3 months." },
            { heading: "Play Ideas by Age", body: "0–3m: Tummy time, mobiles, talking faces, high-contrast cards\n3–6m: Soft rattles, textured toys, peekaboo, floor mat exploration\n6–9m: Object permanence toys, soft stacking cups, bath play, treasure basket (everyday objects of different textures)\n9–12m: Push/pull toys, simple shape sorters, board books, finger foods as sensory play" },
          ]}},
        ]
      },
      {
        id: "baby-m4-l3",
        title: "Wonder Weeks — Developmental Leaps",
        description: "Understanding the 10 'stormy periods' of the first year",
        activities: [
          { id: "b-m4-l3-a1", type: "info_carousel" as any, title: "The Mental Leaps", content: { slides: [
            { heading: "What Wonder Weeks Are", body: "Van de Rijt and Plooij's research identified predictable developmental 'leaps' — periods when babies' brains are doing intensive reorganisation work. During a leap, babies often:\n• Become clingier, fussier, and harder to settle\n• Have disrupted sleep\n• Feed more frequently\n• Seem to 'forget' skills they had\n\nThis is NOT regression. It's advancement. The leap is followed by a burst of new abilities." },
            { heading: "The First 5 Leaps (Birth–6 months)", body: "Leap 1 (~5 weeks): Notices changing sensations — suddenly 'sees' light and patterns.\nLeap 2 (~8 weeks): Recognises patterns in the world.\nLeap 3 (~12 weeks): Transitions — finds that actions create change.\nLeap 4 (~19 weeks): Events — understands that actions are connected in a series.\nLeap 5 (~26 weeks): Relationships — starts understanding distance, depth, boundaries." },
            { heading: "When They're Stormy", body: "During a leap, the three Cs become more intense: Clingy, Cranky, Crying.\n\nWhat helps:\n• More skin contact and holding (you can't 'spoil' a baby in a leap)\n• Offer the breast/bottle more — sucking is genuinely soothing\n• Simplify the environment — less stimulation, more comfort\n• Name what's happening: 'You're learning so much. This is hard work for your brain.'\n• Trust that the storm passes — usually within days to a couple of weeks" },
          ]}},
          { id: "b-m4-l3-a2", type: "open_response" as any, title: "Track Your Baby", content: { prompt: "How old is your baby and what have you noticed them doing that's new this week? How does knowing about developmental leaps change how you feel about a fussy period?", saveToVault: true }},
        ]
      }
    ]
  },
  {
    id: "baby-m5",
    title: "Introducing Solids",
    subtitle: "First foods, baby-led weaning, and building a healthy relationship with eating",
    description: "The transition to solid food is one of the most exciting and confusing milestones of the first year. Whether you choose purees, baby-led weaning, or a combination — this guide gives you the evidence-based framework to do it confidently.",
    estimatedMinutes: 30,
    sourceBooks: ["Baby-Led Weaning — Gill Rapley & Tracey Murkett"],
    sources: ["Paediatric Nutrition", "Infant Feeding Guidelines"],
    lessons: [
      {
        id: "baby-m5-l1",
        title: "When & How to Start",
        description: "Signs of readiness and first-food principles",
        activities: [
          { id: "b-m5-l1-a0", type: "reaction_slider" as any, title: "Solids Readiness Check-In", instruction: "Before we start, take a moment to reflect on where you're at.", content: { question: "How confident do you feel about introducing solid foods to your baby?", options: [
            { emoji: "😰", label: "Very unsure" },
            { emoji: "😕", label: "A bit nervous" },
            { emoji: "😐", label: "Somewhat ready" },
            { emoji: "🙂", label: "Mostly ready" },
            { emoji: "🌟", label: "Very confident" },
          ] } },
          { id: "b-m5-l1-a1", type: "info_carousel" as any, title: "Starting Solids", content: { slides: [
            { heading: "Signs of Readiness (Not Just Age)", body: "NHS, WHO, and most paediatric bodies recommend starting around 6 months — but look for all THREE readiness signs:\n1. Can sit up with minimal support and hold their head steady\n2. Has lost the tongue-thrust reflex (no longer automatically pushes food out with tongue)\n3. Shows interest in food — reaching, watching intently\n\nNOT signs of readiness: waking at night (babies can wake for many reasons), sucking fists (normal newborn behaviour)." },
            { heading: "The Division of Responsibility", body: "Ellyn Satter's principle applies from day one of solids: YOUR job is to decide WHAT is offered, WHEN, and WHERE. YOUR BABY'S job is to decide WHETHER to eat and HOW MUCH.\n\nNever: force food, play aeroplane to distract, make them eat 'one more bite.' This overrides their natural hunger/fullness signals and can contribute to disordered eating later.\n\nTrust: babies are born with excellent appetite regulation. Honour it." },
            { heading: "Milk First (Until 12 Months)", body: "Until 12 months, breast milk or formula remains the PRIMARY nutrition source. Solids are complimentary — they're about exploring flavours, textures, and building skills, not replacing nutrition.\n\nThe NHS recommendation: offer solids about an hour AFTER a milk feed in the beginning (so hunger doesn't drive frustration). As they get older and more competent, shift toward meals before milk." },
          ]}},
          { id: "b-m5-l1-a2", type: "flip_card" as any, title: "Solid Food Readiness Concepts", instruction: "Flip each card to understand the key ideas behind starting solids safely.", content: { cards: [
            { front: "Readiness Signs", back: "All three signs must be present: (1) can sit with minimal support and hold head steady, (2) tongue-thrust reflex has faded (doesn't push food straight back out), (3) shows interest in food — reaching, watching intently.", emoji: "✅", tag: "Readiness" },
            { front: "Division of Responsibility", back: "From day one of solids: YOUR job is what is offered, when, and where. BABY'S job is whether to eat and how much. Never force, distract, or bribe with food — it overrides their natural hunger signals.", emoji: "⚖️", tag: "Feeding Philosophy" },
            { front: "Milk Remains Primary", back: "Until 12 months, breast milk or formula is the PRIMARY nutrition source. Solids are complementary — about exploring flavours, textures, and skills. Offer solids about an hour after a milk feed initially.", emoji: "🍼", tag: "Nutrition" },
            { front: "Iron Priority", back: "Iron is the most critical nutrient when starting solids because breastmilk iron decreases. Offer iron-rich foods (red meat, legumes, fortified cereal) twice daily from the start of solids.", emoji: "🥩", tag: "Nutrition" },
          ] } },
          { id: "b-m5-l1-a3", type: "survey" as any, title: "Your Approach", content: { question: "Which approach to starting solids are you planning?", options: ["Traditional purees", "Baby-led weaning", "Combination (both)", "Not sure yet"] }},
          { id: "b-m5-l1-a4", type: "knowledge_check" as any, title: "Knowledge Check", instruction: "Test your understanding of when and how to start solids.", content: { intro: "Let's check your understanding of the key principles for introducing solid food.", passMark: 3, questions: [
            { question: "Which of the following is NOT a sign that baby is ready for solids?", options: ["Can sit with minimal support and hold head steady", "Tongue-thrust reflex has faded", "Waking more frequently at night", "Shows interest in food by watching and reaching"], correct: 2, explanation: "Waking more at night is NOT a readiness sign — babies wake for many reasons. The three true signs are: sitting with support, faded tongue-thrust reflex, and interest in food." },
            { question: "When starting solids, which nutrient should be prioritised from day one?", options: ["Calcium", "Vitamin C", "Iron", "Vitamin D"], correct: 2, explanation: "Iron is the most critical nutrient when starting solids because breast milk iron decreases and the baby's iron stores deplete around 6 months. Offer iron-rich foods twice daily from the start." },
            { question: "What is the primary role of solids until 12 months?", options: ["To replace breast milk or formula as the main nutrition source", "To complement milk feeds while exploring flavours and textures", "To help baby sleep longer through the night", "To prevent picky eating by offering variety early"], correct: 1, explanation: "Until 12 months, breast milk or formula remains the primary nutrition source. Solids are complementary — about skill development and flavour exposure, not replacing milk nutrition." },
            { question: "According to Ellyn Satter's Division of Responsibility, who decides HOW MUCH baby eats?", options: ["The parent, to ensure adequate nutrition", "The paediatrician, based on weight charts", "The baby, following their own hunger and fullness cues", "Both parent and baby should negotiate each meal"], correct: 2, explanation: "The baby decides whether to eat and how much. The parent decides what is offered, when, and where. Overriding baby's hunger and fullness signals can contribute to disordered eating later in life." },
          ] } },
        ]
      },
      {
        id: "baby-m5-l2",
        title: "Baby-Led Weaning vs Purees",
        description: "Understanding both approaches and choosing yours",
        activities: [
          { id: "b-m5-l2-a1", type: "info_carousel" as any, title: "Approaches Compared", content: { slides: [
            { heading: "Baby-Led Weaning (BLW)", body: "Gill Rapley's approach: skip purees entirely and offer soft, appropriately sized pieces of real food from the start. Baby feeds themselves.\n\nAdvantages:\n• Develops self-feeding skills immediately\n• Exposes baby to varied textures from the start (less picky eating)\n• Baby controls how much they eat\n• Family mealtimes are easier\n\nRequires: sitting independently, patience with mess, understanding of gagging vs choking." },
            { heading: "Traditional Purees", body: "Starting with smooth purees and gradually increasing texture.\n\nAdvantages:\n• More control over exact quantities and nutrients\n• Lower stress around gagging\n• Can be prepared in bulk and frozen\n• Well-established method with generational confidence behind it\n\nRequires: gradual texture progression (lumps by 7–8 months — texture avoidance is a risk of purees only)." },
            { heading: "Combination (Most Families)", body: "Most families blend both approaches: purees for iron-rich foods and nutrient density, soft finger foods for texture experience and self-feeding development.\n\nThe most important thing isn't your approach — it's texture progression. Research shows babies who are still on smooth purees at 9+ months are significantly more likely to be picky eaters at 7 years. Lumpy and finger foods by 7–9 months matter." },
          ]}},
          { id: "b-m5-l2-a2", type: "find_the_pair" as any, title: "Match the Food to the Stage", content: { instruction: "Match each food to the stage it's appropriate for.", pairs: [["6 months — first foods", "Broccoli floret, mashed sweet potato, iron-fortified infant cereal"], ["7–9 months — texture progression", "Soft cooked pasta, minced meat, mashed banana pieces, cheese"], ["9–12 months — family food", "Soft pieces of whatever the family eats, minus salt, honey, whole nuts"], ["6–12 months — iron priority", "Red meat, legumes, fortified cereal — offer twice daily"]] }},
        ]
      },
      {
        id: "baby-m5-l3",
        title: "Allergens, Gagging & Food Safety",
        description: "What you need to know to do this confidently",
        activities: [
          { id: "b-m5-l3-a1", type: "info_carousel" as any, title: "Safe Solids", content: { slides: [
            { heading: "Allergen Introduction", body: "Current evidence shows introducing common allergens EARLY (starting at 6 months) reduces the risk of allergy development — the opposite of what was previously advised.\n\nIntroduce one at a time, 3–5 days apart, watching for reactions:\n• Peanut (smooth peanut butter thinned with warm water)\n• Tree nuts (same method)\n• Egg (well-cooked)\n• Dairy (cheese, yoghurt — not cow's milk as a main drink until 12 months)\n• Wheat, fish, shellfish\n\nIf family history of severe allergy: discuss with your paediatrician first." },
            { heading: "Gagging vs Choking", body: "GAGGING is normal, safe, and protective. The gag reflex in babies is positioned far forward on the tongue — it triggers frequently and dramatically but is the body doing its job. Signs: loud, retching noise, red face, eyes watering. Action: stay calm, don't interfere.\n\nCHOKING is different: silent, distressed, blue colour, ineffective breathing. Action: learn infant choking first aid BEFORE starting solids. Every parent should know this.\n\nKnowing the difference transforms your confidence." },
            { heading: "Foods to Avoid Before 12 Months", body: "Never before 12 months:\n• Honey (risk of botulism)\n• Whole cow's milk as main drink\n• Salt (kidneys can't handle it)\n• Added sugar\n• Whole nuts (choking risk)\n• Raw shellfish\n• Unpasteurised cheese\n• Shark, marlin, swordfish (high mercury)\n\nAfter 12 months: honey is fine, cow's milk becomes the drink, and most restrictions lift. Focus shifts to a varied, balanced family diet." },
          ]}},
          { id: "b-m5-l3-a2", type: "true_false" as any, title: "Safety Check", content: { statement: "If your baby gags dramatically on a piece of food, you should immediately remove the food from their mouth with your finger.", isTrue: false, explanation: "Gag reflex is protective — let it do its job. Inserting your finger can actually push food further back. Stay calm, watch, and let them work through it. Act only if signs of actual choking appear: silence, ineffective breathing, blue colour. Learn infant first aid — it's the best preparation." }},
        ]
      }
    ]
