          { id: "kt-m14-l1-a0", type: "reaction_slider" as any, title: "How Are You Feeling?", instruction: "Before we begin, take a moment to reflect.", content: { question: "How would you rate your child's motivation and engagement with their own education right now?", options: [
            { emoji: "😰", label: "Very disengaged" },
            { emoji: "😕", label: "Mostly passive" },
            { emoji: "😐", label: "Somewhat engaged" },
            { emoji: "🙂", label: "Fairly motivated" },
            { emoji: "🌟", label: "Highly motivated" },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-m14-l1-a1", type: "info_carousel" as any, title: "Internal Drive", content: { slides: [
            { heading: "The Ownership Shift", body: "Children who see education as THEIR project (not yours) are more motivated. Stop asking 'Did you do your homework?' and start asking 'What's your plan for tonight?' The shift from monitoring to coaching changes everything." },
            { heading: "The Switch Point Metaphor", body: "Every small decision is like a railway switch — just three inches of steel that sends you hundreds of miles in one direction or another. Help your teen see that daily choices about study, effort, and showing up are switch points for their future. Not dramatic — just true." },
            { heading: "When They're Failing", body: "Before you panic:\n• Ask: 'What's going on?' (not 'Why are you failing?')\n• Investigate: learning difficulty? social issue? depression? wrong subject?\n• Separate the person from the grade: 'You are not your marks'\n• Problem-solve together: 'What would help? A tutor? A study group? A different approach?'\n• Let natural consequences teach when appropriate" },
          ]}},
          { id: "kt-m14-l1-a2", type: "flip_card" as any, title: "School Motivation: Key Concepts", instruction: "Flip each card to discover what drives genuine academic engagement.", content: { cards: [
            { front: "Ownership vs Monitoring", back: "Children who see education as THEIR project are more motivated than those whose parents monitor and push. Shift from 'Did you do your homework?' to 'What's your plan for tonight?' This moves from monitoring to coaching — and changes everything.", emoji: "🎯", tag: "Ownership" },
            { front: "The Switch Point", back: "Every small daily decision is like a railway switch — just three inches of steel that sends you hundreds of miles in a different direction. Help your teen see that daily choices about effort and showing up are switch points for their future.", emoji: "🔀", tag: "Daily Choices" },
            { front: "Performance vs Mastery", back: "Performance-oriented students ('I need an A') burn out faster — every test becomes a judgment of worth. Mastery-oriented students ('I want to understand this') are more resilient because they're driven by curiosity, not fear. Shift 'What did you get?' to 'What did you learn?'", emoji: "📚", tag: "Learning Mindset" },
            { front: "When They're Struggling", back: "Before panicking about poor grades: Ask 'What's going on?' (not 'Why are failing?'). Investigate whether there's a learning difficulty, social issue, mental health concern, or wrong subject. Separate the person from the grade: 'You are not your marks.'", emoji: "🤝", tag: "When It's Hard" },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-m14-l1-a3", type: "single_choice" as any, title: "Scenario", content: { question: "Your 14-year-old says 'School is pointless, I'm going to be a YouTuber.' Best response?", options: [
            { label: "'That's not a real career. Focus on your studies.'", isCorrect: false },
            { label: "'Tell me more about what you'd create. What skills would you need?'", isCorrect: true },
            { label: "'Fine, but you still need to pass.'", isCorrect: false },
          ], explanation: "Curiosity opens dialogue. When you explore their interest, you can naturally connect it to real skills (editing, marketing, communication, business) that school CAN support. Dismissing dreams closes the conversation entirely." }},
          { id: "kt-m14-l1-a4", type: "knowledge_check" as any, title: "Knowledge Check", instruction: "Test what you've learned before moving on.", content: { intro: "Let's check your understanding of helping your child thrive at school.", passMark: 3, questions: [
            { question: "What does 'The Ownership Shift' mean in the context of school motivation?", options: ["Parents take more responsibility for homework", "The child sees education as their own project, not their parents'", "The school takes ownership of the child's success", "The teacher shifts their approach to teaching"], correct: 1, explanation: "When children own their education — seeing it as their project — motivation is internal and sustainable. When parents own it (monitoring, pushing, doing), children disengage because there's no need for their own initiative." },
            { question: "What is the difference between a performance-oriented and mastery-oriented student?", options: ["Performance-oriented students work harder", "Mastery-oriented students care about marks more", "Performance-oriented students base worth on grades; mastery-oriented students focus on understanding and curiosity", "There is no meaningful difference"], correct: 2, explanation: "Performance orientation ('I need an A') ties self-worth to grades and leads to burnout. Mastery orientation ('I want to understand this') builds resilience because learning itself is the reward." },
            { question: "When a teen says 'School is pointless,' the best response is:", options: ["'Focus on your studies — career dreams come later'", "'You're right, but you still have to go'", "'Tell me more about what you'd do instead — what skills would that need?'", "'School is the most important thing right now'"], correct: 2, explanation: "Curiosity opens dialogue. Exploring their interest lets you naturally connect it to skills school can support. Dismissing dreams immediately closes the conversation and increases disengagement." },
            { question: "Before panicking about poor grades, what should a parent investigate first?", options: ["Which subject to drop", "Whether there's a learning difficulty, social issue, or mental health concern", "How to get a private tutor", "Whether the teacher is the problem"], correct: 1, explanation: "Poor grades can indicate a learning difficulty, social problem, depression, wrong subject, or other underlying issue. Understanding the cause is essential before reacting — 'What's going on?' opens this investigation better than 'Why are you failing?'" },
          ] } },
        ]
      },
      {
        id: "kt-m14-l2",
        title: "Finding Their Voice",
        description: "Helping your child discover what lights them up",
        activities: [
          { id: "kt-m14-l2-a0", type: "reaction_slider" as any, title: "How Are You Feeling?", instruction: "Before we begin, take a moment to reflect.", content: { question: "How well do you know what truly lights your child up — beyond grades and performance?", options: [
            { emoji: "😰", label: "Not at all sure" },
            { emoji: "😕", label: "Have some idea" },
            { emoji: "😐", label: "Somewhat clear" },
            { emoji: "🙂", label: "Fairly clear" },
            { emoji: "🌟", label: "Very clear" },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-m14-l2-a1", type: "info_carousel" as any, title: "Discover Their Spark", content: { slides: [
            { heading: "Beyond Academics", body: "Not every child thrives in traditional schooling. Help them find their 'thing':\n• What do they lose track of time doing?\n• What topics do they choose to read/watch about?\n• What would they do if no one was watching or judging?\n• What problem in the world bothers them most?\n\nTheir 'thing' might be music, coding, cooking, sport, art, activism — it doesn't have to look like a traditional career path." },
            { heading: "The 10-Year Vision", body: "Try this exercise with your teen: 'Introduce yourself as you'd like to be 10 years from now. Where do you live? What do you do? What matters to you?'\n\nThis isn't about pressure — it's about possibility. When they can see a future worth working toward, daily motivation follows naturally." },
          ]}},
          { id: "kt-m14-l2-a2", type: "flip_card" as any, title: "Discovering Your Child's Spark", instruction: "Flip each card to explore how to help your child find what lights them up.", content: { cards: [
            { front: "Beyond Traditional School", back: "Not every child thrives in traditional schooling. Ask: What do they lose track of time doing? What topics do they choose to learn about unprompted? Their 'thing' might be music, coding, cooking, sport, art, or activism — it doesn't have to look like a conventional career path.", emoji: "✨", tag: "Finding the Spark" },
            { front: "The 10-Year Vision", back: "Try this exercise with your teen: 'Introduce yourself as you'd like to be 10 years from now. Where do you live? What do you do? What matters to you?' This isn't about pressure — it's about possibility. When they can see a future worth working toward, daily motivation follows.", emoji: "🔭", tag: "Future Thinking" },
            { front: "Connect Interest to Skills", back: "Whatever your teen is passionate about connects to real, marketable skills. Gaming: strategy, teamwork, coding. YouTube: communication, editing, marketing. Cooking: creativity, business, nutrition. Help them see the path from passion to competence.", emoji: "🔗", tag: "Passion to Path" },
            { front: "Purpose Fuels Motivation", back: "Purpose doesn't have to be grand. A teenager who volunteers at a dog shelter, builds a community garden, or tutors younger students finds meaning — and motivation follows meaning. Help them connect to something bigger than grades.", emoji: "🌱", tag: "Finding Purpose" },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-m14-l2-a3", type: "knowledge_check" as any, title: "Knowledge Check", instruction: "Test what you've learned before moving on.", content: { intro: "Let's check your understanding of helping your child discover their spark.", passMark: 3, questions: [
            { question: "What question best helps a teenager identify what they're passionate about?", options: ["'What subject will earn you the most money?'", "'What do your teachers say you're good at?'", "'What do you lose track of time doing?'", "'What do your friends think you should do?'"], correct: 2, explanation: "The question 'What do you lose track of time doing?' bypasses performance anxiety and gets to genuine interest and flow — a much better indicator of passion than external feedback or earning potential." },
            { question: "What is the purpose of the '10-Year Vision' exercise?", options: ["To create pressure for future achievement", "To help teens connect to a future worth working toward, making daily motivation more natural", "To identify career limitations early", "To compare your child's goals to peers"], correct: 1, explanation: "The 10-Year Vision creates possibility, not pressure. When teens can see a compelling future self, the daily effort to get there becomes meaningful rather than arbitrary." },
            { question: "Why does purpose fuel motivation more than grades or rewards?", options: ["Because teenagers don't care about grades", "Because external rewards are always temporary motivators", "Because connecting to something meaningful makes effort feel worthwhile rather than imposed", "Because purpose is easier to achieve than academic success"], correct: 2, explanation: "When effort connects to something that genuinely matters — helping others, creating something, building a skill — motivation becomes intrinsic. Grades and rewards are external and temporary; purpose is sustained from within." },
            { question: "A teenager obsessed with gaming can be redirected toward:", options: ["Reducing screen time to improve grades", "Seeing gaming as a waste of time", "Understanding how gaming connects to real skills like strategy, teamwork, coding, and communication", "Choosing a different hobby entirely"], correct: 2, explanation: "Gaming connects to genuine skills — strategic thinking, teamwork, coding, communication, and even business (streaming, content creation). Connecting passion to competence builds engagement rather than breeding resentment." },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-m14-l2-a4", type: "open_response" as any, title: "Your Child's Spark", content: { prompt: "What activities make your child come alive? When do you see them most engaged? How could you create more opportunities for that spark this month?", saveToVault: true }},
        ]
      }
    ]
  },
  // ─── MODULE 15: MAKING & KEEPING GOOD FRIENDS (teen friendship skills) ──
  {

    title: "Making & Keeping Good Friends",
    subtitle: "Teaching your teen to choose wisely and be a true friend",
    description: "Friendships are one of the biggest influences on your teenager's choices. These strategies help them choose friends who lift them up, handle friendship drama, and stand up to peer pressure.",
    estimatedMinutes: 30,
    sourceBooks: ["The 6 Most Important Decisions You'll Ever Make — Sean Covey", "How to Talk So Teens Will Listen — Adele Faber"],
    sources: ["Social Psychology", "Adolescent Development"],
    lessons: [
      {
        id: "kt-m15-l1",
        title: "The Friendship Filter",
        description: "Choosing friends who make you better, not worse",
        activities: [
          { id: "kt-m15-l1-a0", type: "reaction_slider" as any, title: "How Are You Feeling?", instruction: "Before we begin, take a moment to reflect.", content: { question: "How confident are you in helping your child choose friends who are a positive influence?", options: [
            { emoji: "😰", label: "Very unsure" },
            { emoji: "😕", label: "Quite lost" },
            { emoji: "😐", label: "Somewhat okay" },
            { emoji: "🙂", label: "Fairly confident" },
            { emoji: "💪", label: "Very confident" },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-m15-l1-a1", type: "info_carousel" as any, title: "Choosing Well", content: { slides: [
            { heading: "Steady vs Fickle Friends", body: "Teach your child the difference:\n\nSteady friends: like you for who you are, stick around when things are hard, keep your secrets, celebrate your wins without jealousy.\n\nFickle friends: like you for what you have or who you know, drop you when someone 'better' comes along, use your secrets as weapons.\n\nAsk: 'Would this person still be your friend if you lost everything popular about you?'" },
            { heading: "The Popularity Trap", body: "Popularity isn't good or bad — it depends on WHY someone is popular. Some people are well-liked because they're genuinely kind and capable. Others are 'popular' because people are afraid of them.\n\nHelp your teen see: real influence comes from character, not status. The kids who are comfortable being themselves — not trying to climb the social ladder — often end up happiest." },
            { heading: "Don't Centre Your Life on Friends", body: "Friends make a terrible 'centre of gravity' for your life — they're imperfect, changeable, and human. If your self-worth depends on your friend count or how they treat you today, you'll be an emotional rollercoaster.\n\nBetter centre: your own values. When you know what you stand for, friendships become something you enjoy — not something you desperately need." },
          ]}},
          { id: "kt-m15-l1-a2", type: "flip_card" as any, title: "Choosing Friends Wisely", instruction: "Flip each card to understand what makes a genuinely good friend.", content: { cards: [
            { front: "Steady vs Fickle Friends", back: "Steady friends: like you for who you are, stick around when things are hard, keep your secrets, celebrate your wins without jealousy. Fickle friends: like you for what you have or who you know, drop you when someone 'better' comes along, use your secrets as weapons.", emoji: "⚖️", tag: "Types of Friends" },
            { front: "The Popularity Trap", back: "Popularity isn't good or bad — it depends on WHY someone is popular. Some are liked because they're genuinely kind and capable. Others are 'popular' because people fear them. Real influence comes from character, not status.", emoji: "👑", tag: "Popularity" },
            { front: "Your Values as an Anchor", back: "Friends make a terrible 'centre of gravity' for your life — they're imperfect, changeable, and human. If self-worth depends on friend count, you'll be an emotional rollercoaster. Better centre: your own values. Then friendships become something you enjoy — not something you desperately need.", emoji: "⚓", tag: "Identity & Values" },
            { front: "The Real Question to Ask", back: "'Would this person still be your friend if you lost everything popular about you?' This question cuts through social performance and gets to the heart of genuine friendship.", emoji: "❓", tag: "The Test" },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-m15-l1-a3", type: "knowledge_check" as any, title: "Knowledge Check", instruction: "Test what you've learned before moving on.", content: { intro: "Let's check your understanding of helping your child choose friends wisely.", passMark: 3, questions: [
            { question: "What distinguishes a 'steady' friend from a 'fickle' friend?", options: ["Steady friends are always available; fickle friends are busy", "Steady friends like you for who you are; fickle friends like you for what you have or who you know", "Steady friends are more popular", "Fickle friends are more interesting"], correct: 1, explanation: "Steady friends remain loyal regardless of your social status, celebrate your wins without jealousy, and keep your secrets. Fickle friends are relationship opportunists — they stay as long as you're useful." },
            { question: "Why is 'popularity' not automatically a sign of genuine social health?", options: ["Popular kids don't have real friends", "Some people are 'popular' because others fear them, not because they're liked", "Popular kids are usually less kind", "Popularity only matters in school"], correct: 1, explanation: "Popularity based on social fear or status is very different from being genuinely well-liked for kindness and character. Help your child understand WHY someone is popular before looking up to them." },
            { question: "What is the problem with making friends your 'centre of gravity'?", options: ["It means you spend too much time socialising", "Friends are imperfect and changeable, so your self-worth becomes unstable", "It reduces academic performance", "It makes you too social"], correct: 1, explanation: "Basing self-worth on friendships creates emotional instability — because friends are human, they will sometimes fail, leave, or disappoint. A stable identity grounded in personal values is a much more reliable foundation." },
            { question: "The best test of whether a friendship is genuine is:", options: ["Whether they text you back quickly", "'Would this person still be your friend if you lost everything popular about you?'", "Whether they invite you to everything", "Whether your parents approve of them"], correct: 1, explanation: "This question strips away social performance and status. A genuine friend would remain loyal even without access to your popularity, possessions, or social capital — and that's the standard worth holding." },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-m15-l1-a4", type: "open_response" as any, title: "Friendship Audit", content: { prompt: "Think about your child's closest friends. Do they bring out the best in your child? Is there a friendship that concerns you? How could you have a conversation about it without banning anyone?", saveToVault: true }},
        ]
      },
      {
        id: "kt-m15-l2",
        title: "Handling Gossip, Bullying & Betrayal",
        description: "What to do when friends turn on you",
        activities: [
          { id: "kt-m15-l2-a0", type: "reaction_slider" as any, title: "How Are You Feeling?", instruction: "Before we begin, take a moment to reflect.", content: { question: "How comfortable are you coaching your child through serious friendship conflicts like betrayal or gossip?", options: [
            { emoji: "😰", label: "Very uncomfortable" },
            { emoji: "😕", label: "Quite unsure" },
            { emoji: "😐", label: "Somewhat okay" },
            { emoji: "🙂", label: "Fairly comfortable" },
            { emoji: "💪", label: "Very confident" },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-m15-l2-a1", type: "info_carousel" as any, title: "When It Goes Wrong", content: { slides: [
            { heading: "When a Friend Betrays You", body: "It happens to almost everyone. A trusted friend shares your secret, talks behind your back, or drops you for a new crowd. Coach your teen:\n\n• 'You have a right to feel hurt — that was a betrayal of trust'\n• 'You can't control what they did, only how you respond'\n• 'Would you want to confront them directly, or let the friendship go?'\n• 'What does this teach you about what you need in a friend?'" },
            { heading: "Responding to Gossip", body: "Two strategies for when people talk:\n\n1. Confront calmly: 'I've heard you've been saying things about me. I'd prefer if you talked to me directly.' (Takes courage, often shuts it down)\n\n2. Rise above: Sometimes the most powerful response is no response. When you stop reacting, gossip loses its fuel.\n\nBoth are valid — help your teen choose based on the situation." },
            { heading: "Forgive the Small Stuff", body: "Friends will annoy each other. They'll be thoughtless, competitive, moody. Before blowing up a friendship over a single incident, ask:\n• 'Is this a pattern or a one-off?'\n• 'Are they going through something hard?'\n• 'Is this worth losing the friendship over?'\n\nForgive the small quirks. Draw the line at repeated cruelty." },
          ]}},
          { id: "kt-m15-l2-a2", type: "flip_card" as any, title: "When Friendships Go Wrong", instruction: "Flip each card to understand how to support your child through friendship conflict and betrayal.", content: { cards: [
            { front: "When a Friend Betrays You", back: "Coach your teen: 'You have a right to feel hurt — that was a betrayal of trust.' 'You can't control what they did, only how you respond.' 'Would you want to confront them directly, or let the friendship go?' 'What does this teach you about what you need in a friend?'", emoji: "💔", tag: "Betrayal" },
            { front: "Two Strategies for Gossip", back: "1. Confront calmly: 'I've heard you've been saying things about me. I'd prefer if you talked to me directly.' 2. Rise above: Sometimes the most powerful response is no response — when you stop reacting, gossip loses its fuel. Both are valid — help your teen choose based on the situation.", emoji: "🗣️", tag: "Responding to Gossip" },
            { front: "Forgive the Small Stuff", back: "Friends will annoy each other — they'll be thoughtless, competitive, moody. Before ending a friendship over one incident, ask: 'Is this a pattern or a one-off?' 'Are they going through something hard?' 'Is this worth losing the friendship over?' Forgive quirks. Draw the line at repeated cruelty.", emoji: "🕊️", tag: "Forgiveness" },
            { front: "When to Step In as a Parent", back: "For most teen friendship dramas, coach your child to handle it themselves. Only step in when: there's persistent bullying, there are safety concerns, or the school needs to be involved. Premature parent involvement usually makes social situations worse.", emoji: "🛑", tag: "Parent Role" },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-m15-l2-a3", type: "decision_point" as any, title: "Friendship Betrayal", content: { scenario: "Your teen's best friend shared a private secret with the whole group. Your teen is devastated and says they'll never trust anyone again.", options: [{ label: "'That was a real betrayal. You have every right to feel hurt. What do you want to do about this friendship?'", outcome: "Validating the hurt and asking what THEY want teaches agency. They may choose to confront, forgive, or step back — all valid. Your job: support their choice." }, { label: "'Get over it — everyone gossips'", outcome: "Minimising betrayal teaches them their feelings don't matter. Trust violations hurt at any age and deserve acknowledgment." }, { label: "'I'll talk to their parents'", outcome: "For teen friendships, parent intervention usually makes things worse. Coach them to handle it, and step in only if there's bullying or safety concerns." }] }},
          { id: "kt-m15-l2-a4", type: "knowledge_check" as any, title: "Knowledge Check", instruction: "Test what you've learned before moving on.", content: { intro: "Let's check your understanding of helping teens handle friendship conflict.", passMark: 3, questions: [
            { question: "When your teen's friend betrays their trust, what should you do FIRST?", options: ["Call the other parent immediately", "Tell them to get over it", "Validate their hurt and ask what THEY want to do about the friendship", "Contact the school"], correct: 2, explanation: "Validating the hurt ('that was a real betrayal, you have every right to feel hurt') before exploring options teaches emotional literacy and agency. Your teen needs to feel heard before they can think clearly about next steps." },
            { question: "What are the two valid strategies when dealing with gossip about your teen?", options: ["Report it to school and ignore it", "Confront calmly or rise above by not reacting", "Fight back or withdraw from school", "Post about it on social media or tell their friends"], correct: 1, explanation: "Confronting directly ('I'd prefer if you talked to me directly') or choosing not to react (removing fuel from the fire) are both valid. The right choice depends on the specific situation and your teen's personality." },
            { question: "When should a parent intervene in their teenager's friendship conflicts?", options: ["Whenever their child is upset", "Immediately when they hear about a conflict", "Only when there's persistent bullying, safety concerns, or school involvement is needed", "Never — teens should handle everything themselves"], correct: 2, explanation: "For most teen friendship dramas, coaching from a distance is better than direct intervention. Parent involvement at this age usually escalates rather than resolves conflict. Reserve intervention for serious situations." },
            { question: "The question to ask before ending a friendship over a conflict is:", options: ["'Is this person popular enough to be worth keeping?'", "'Is this a pattern or a one-off? Are they going through something hard? Is this worth losing the friendship over?'", "'What do my friends think I should do?'", "'Will this affect my social status?'"], correct: 1, explanation: "These three questions provide perspective — distinguishing between a pattern of cruelty (worth addressing seriously) and a one-time mistake during a hard time (worth forgiving). Imperfect friendships deserve grace for normal human failures." },
          ] } },
        ]
      },
      {
        id: "kt-m15-l3",
        title: "Being a Good Friend",
        description: "The skills that make people want to be around you",
        activities: [
          { id: "kt-m15-l3-a0", type: "reaction_slider" as any, title: "How Are You Feeling?", instruction: "Before we begin, take a moment to reflect.", content: { question: "How well do you think your child models being a genuinely good friend to others?", options: [
            { emoji: "😰", label: "Needs a lot of work" },
            { emoji: "😕", label: "Struggling" },
            { emoji: "😐", label: "Average" },
            { emoji: "🙂", label: "Fairly good" },
            { emoji: "🌟", label: "Excellent" },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-m15-l3-a1", type: "info_carousel" as any, title: "Friendship Skills", content: { slides: [
            { heading: "The Emotional Bank Account", body: "Every relationship has an invisible 'trust bank account'. Deposits: keeping promises, being kind, listening, showing up. Withdrawals: gossip, flaking, selfishness, breaking trust.\n\nWhen the account is full, friendships can survive tough moments. When it's empty, one small conflict can end it.\n\nAsk your teen: 'Are you making more deposits or withdrawals in your friendships?'" },
            { heading: "Listen First", body: "The #1 friendship skill: genuinely listening. Not waiting for your turn to talk. Not looking at your phone. Actually hearing what someone is feeling.\n\nPractice at home:\n• 'Tell me about your day — I'm just going to listen'\n• Model putting your phone down during conversations\n• Reflect back: 'It sounds like you felt...' before offering advice" },
            { heading: "Stand Up, Don't Stand By", body: "A true friend doesn't just avoid being mean — they stand up when someone else IS being mean. Teach your teen:\n• 'If you see someone being excluded, invite them in'\n• 'If a friend is being talked about, change the subject or walk away'\n• 'Being a bystander IS a choice — and it's the wrong one'\n\nCourage in small moments builds character for big ones." },
          ]}},
          { id: "kt-m15-l3-a2", type: "flip_card" as any, title: "Being a Good Friend", instruction: "Flip each card to discover the skills that make people genuinely want to be around you.", content: { cards: [
            { front: "The Emotional Bank Account", back: "Every relationship has an invisible trust bank. Deposits: keeping promises, being kind, listening, showing up. Withdrawals: gossip, flaking, selfishness, breaking trust. When the account is full, friendships survive tough moments. When it's empty, one small conflict can end everything.", emoji: "🏦", tag: "Trust Account" },
            { front: "Listen First", back: "The number-one friendship skill is genuinely listening — not waiting for your turn to talk, not looking at your phone, but actually hearing what someone is feeling. Practise at home: put phones down, reflect back 'It sounds like you felt...' before offering any advice.", emoji: "👂", tag: "Listening" },
            { front: "Stand Up, Don't Stand By", back: "A true friend doesn't just avoid being mean — they stand up when someone else IS being mean. If you see someone being excluded, invite them in. If a friend is being talked about, change the subject or walk away. Being a bystander IS a choice — and it's the wrong one.", emoji: "🦁", tag: "Courage" },
            { front: "Courage in Small Moments", back: "Standing up for someone takes courage every time. But courage in small moments (defending someone in conversation, including the left-out kid) builds character for big ones. These small acts matter far more than they appear.", emoji: "⚡", tag: "Small Brave Acts" },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-m15-l3-a3", type: "knowledge_check" as any, title: "Knowledge Check", instruction: "Test what you've learned before moving on.", content: { intro: "Let's check your understanding of what it takes to be a genuinely good friend.", passMark: 3, questions: [
            { question: "What is the 'Emotional Bank Account' metaphor?", options: ["A system for tracking friend debts", "Trust is built through deposits (kindness, loyalty) and depleted by withdrawals (gossip, flaking) — the balance determines relationship resilience", "A way to decide whether friendships are worth keeping", "A school counselling tool"], correct: 1, explanation: "The Emotional Bank Account illustrates that trust is built incrementally through small acts of kindness, loyalty, and reliability — and depleted by gossip, selfishness, and broken promises. A full account can weather conflict; an empty one cannot." },
            { question: "What is identified as the number-one friendship skill?", options: ["Being funny and entertaining", "Genuinely listening — not waiting for your turn, not looking at your phone", "Knowing lots of people", "Being available 24/7"], correct: 1, explanation: "Genuine listening — where you actually hear and reflect what someone is feeling before offering advice or opinions — is the foundation of deep friendship. It signals: you matter, I'm here, your feelings are real." },
            { question: "What does 'standing up, not standing by' mean?", options: ["Defending yourself physically", "Speaking up or acting when you see someone being excluded or bullied — not being a passive bystander", "Standing next to your friend in difficult moments", "Reporting bullying to teachers immediately"], correct: 1, explanation: "Being a bystander — seeing someone being hurt or excluded and doing nothing — is a choice. True friends include the left-out person, redirect conversations when friends are being talked about, and act with courage even when it's uncomfortable." },
            { question: "Why do 'small acts' of courage in friendship matter?", options: ["They don't really matter — only big gestures count", "They build character incrementally, preparing you for larger moments of courage", "They're a way to impress people", "They're required to be popular"], correct: 1, explanation: "Small brave acts — including someone, standing up in conversation, being honest — build the character and courage needed for much bigger moments. Character is built incrementally, one small decision at a time." },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-m15-l3-a4", type: "survey" as any, title: "Reflect", content: { question: "Which friendship skill does your family need to practise most?", options: ["Listening without fixing", "Being loyal when it's hard", "Forgiving small stuff", "Standing up for others"] }},
        ]
      }
    ]
  },
  // ─── MODULE 16: AVOIDING ADDICTIONS ─────────────────────────────────────
  {
    id: "kt-m16",
    title: "Addiction-Proofing Your Child",
    subtitle: "Honest conversations about substances, screens, and habits",
    description: "Addiction doesn't start with hard drugs — it starts with coping patterns. These strategies help you have honest, effective conversations about substances, screen dependency, and building healthy habits.",
    estimatedMinutes: 30,
    sourceBooks: ["The 6 Most Important Decisions You'll Ever Make — Sean Covey", "The Teenage Brain — Frances E. Jensen", "Raising Mentally Strong Kids — Daniel Amen"],
    sources: ["Addiction Psychology", "Adolescent Neuroscience"],
    lessons: [
      {
        id: "kt-m16-l1",
        title: "Three Hard Truths About Addiction",
        description: "What every parent and teen needs to understand",
        activities: [
          { id: "kt-m16-l1-a0", type: "reaction_slider" as any, title: "How Are You Feeling?", instruction: "Before we begin, take a moment to reflect.", content: { question: "How confident do you feel having honest conversations with your teen about substances and addiction?", options: [
            { emoji: "😰", label: "Very unsure" },
            { emoji: "😕", label: "Quite nervous" },
            { emoji: "😐", label: "Somewhat okay" },
            { emoji: "🙂", label: "Fairly confident" },
            { emoji: "💪", label: "Very confident" },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-m16-l1-a1", type: "info_carousel" as any, title: "Addiction Reality", content: { slides: [
            { heading: "Truth 1: It's Progressive", body: "Nobody plans to become addicted. It starts small and grows slowly. First it's fun, then it's fun with problems, then it's just problems. The teenage brain is especially vulnerable because the reward system is hypersensitive while the 'brake system' (prefrontal cortex) is still developing.\n\nThis isn't a moral failing — it's neuroscience." },
            { heading: "Truth 2: Addiction Replaces Connection", body: "People don't become addicted to substances — they become addicted to the relief substances provide. Loneliness, anxiety, boredom, pain — substances numb these. The antidote isn't willpower — it's CONNECTION.\n\nThe strongest protective factor against addiction: a teen who feels genuinely connected to their family and has at least one trusted adult they can talk to." },
            { heading: "Truth 3: It Can Happen to Anyone", body: "Addiction doesn't discriminate by income, intelligence, or family type. Risk factors include:\n• Family history of addiction\n• Untreated anxiety or depression\n• Early exposure (before age 15)\n• Trauma\n• Social isolation\n• Peer group that normalises substance use\n\nProtective factors: strong family bond, clear boundaries, emotional literacy, meaningful activities, delayed first exposure." },
          ]}},
          { id: "kt-m16-l1-a2", type: "flip_card" as any, title: "Three Truths About Addiction", instruction: "Flip each card to understand the key facts every parent and teen needs to know.", content: { cards: [
            { front: "It's Progressive", back: "Nobody plans to become addicted. It starts small: first it's fun, then it's fun with problems, then it's just problems. The teenage brain's reward system is hypersensitive while the prefrontal 'brake system' is still developing — making teens uniquely vulnerable. This is neuroscience, not moral failure.", emoji: "📈", tag: "How It Progresses" },
            { front: "Connection Is the Antidote", back: "People don't become addicted to substances — they become addicted to the RELIEF substances provide: from loneliness, anxiety, boredom, or pain. The antidote isn't willpower — it's connection. The strongest protective factor: a teen who feels genuinely connected to family and has a trusted adult.", emoji: "🤝", tag: "The Real Antidote" },
            { front: "It Can Happen to Anyone", back: "Risk factors: family history of addiction, untreated anxiety or depression, early exposure (before 15), trauma, social isolation, peer group that normalises use. Protective factors: strong family bond, clear values, emotional literacy, meaningful activities, delayed first exposure.", emoji: "⚠️", tag: "Risk & Protection" },
            { front: "Cannabis & the Teen Brain", back: "Cannabis is not safe for teenagers. Regular use before age 25 can impair memory, motivation, and attention, and increase psychosis risk in those predisposed. The developing brain is uniquely vulnerable. 'Natural' does not mean safe for a brain under construction.", emoji: "🧠", tag: "Drug Facts" },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-m16-l1-a3", type: "true_false" as any, title: "Fact Check", content: { statement: "Cannabis is completely safe for teenagers because it's a natural plant.", isTrue: false, explanation: "Cannabis significantly affects the developing teenage brain. Research shows regular use before age 25 can impair memory, motivation, attention, and increase risk of psychosis in those predisposed. 'Natural' does not mean safe for a developing brain." }},
          { id: "kt-m16-l1-a4", type: "knowledge_check" as any, title: "Knowledge Check", instruction: "Test what you've learned before moving on.", content: { intro: "Let's check your understanding of the key truths about addiction.", passMark: 3, questions: [
            { question: "Why is the teenage brain especially vulnerable to addiction?", options: ["Teenagers make bad decisions on purpose", "The reward system is hypersensitive while the prefrontal cortex (the 'brake') is still developing", "Teenagers don't understand consequences", "Peer pressure is always the cause"], correct: 1, explanation: "The teenage brain has a highly sensitive reward system that responds intensely to substances, but the prefrontal cortex — responsible for impulse control and long-term thinking — isn't fully developed until around age 25. This biological mismatch creates real vulnerability." },
            { question: "What is identified as the strongest protective factor against teen substance abuse?", options: ["Strict rules and consequences", "Zero-tolerance policies at school", "A teen who feels genuinely connected to family and has at least one trusted adult", "Keeping teens busy with activities"], correct: 2, explanation: "Connection is the antidote to addiction. Teens who feel genuinely loved, known, and connected — and who have a trusted adult they can talk to — are dramatically less likely to turn to substances to manage difficult emotions." },
            { question: "Addiction is best understood as:", options: ["A moral failing that reflects poor character", "A choice that teenagers make when they're bored", "Progressive dependence that starts small and grows, often driven by a need to escape emotional pain", "Something that only happens to children from difficult families"], correct: 2, explanation: "Addiction is progressive — nobody plans to become dependent. It starts as relief (from pain, loneliness, anxiety) and gradually becomes the main problem. It's a neurological and psychological process, not a character flaw." },
            { question: "Which of the following is a PROTECTIVE factor against addiction?", options: ["Early exposure to alcohol 'to teach moderation'", "Keeping substance conversations off-limits", "Meaningful activities and emotional literacy", "Highly permissive parenting"], correct: 2, explanation: "Protective factors include: strong family bonds, clear values, emotional literacy, meaningful activities (sport, creative work, volunteering), and delayed first exposure to substances. These build resilience against the pull of addictive coping." },
          ] } },
        ]
      },
      {
        id: "kt-m16-l2",
        title: "Screen & Social Media Dependency",
        description: "When the phone becomes the problem",
        activities: [
          { id: "kt-m16-l2-a0", type: "reaction_slider" as any, title: "How Are You Feeling?", instruction: "Before we begin, take a moment to reflect.", content: { question: "How concerned are you about your child's current relationship with screens and social media?", options: [
            { emoji: "😰", label: "Very concerned" },
            { emoji: "😕", label: "Somewhat worried" },
            { emoji: "😐", label: "Neutral" },
            { emoji: "🙂", label: "Mostly okay" },
            { emoji: "✅", label: "Not concerned" },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-m16-l2-a1", type: "info_carousel" as any, title: "Digital Dependency", content: { slides: [
            { heading: "The Dopamine Loop", body: "Social media, gaming, and short-form video are engineered to be addictive. Every notification, like, and new video triggers a dopamine hit in your teen's already-sensitive reward system.\n\nSigns of dependency:\n• Anxiety when phone is taken away\n• Can't go 10 minutes without checking\n• Mood crashes after scrolling\n• Choosing screen over real-life activities\n• Sleep disruption from late-night use" },
            { heading: "Boundaries That Work", body: "Negotiate boundaries WITH them (not imposed on them):\n• No phones at meals or in bedrooms after a set time\n• Screen-free first hour after waking\n• Weekly screen time review together (not as punishment — as awareness)\n• Model it yourself (if you're always on YOUR phone, why shouldn't they be?)\n• Replace screen time with something better, not just nothing" },
            { heading: "The Comparison Trap", body: "Social media creates a distorted mirror. Everyone's life looks better, easier, more exciting. Help your teen see:\n• 'People post their highlights, not their hard days'\n• 'How do you feel AFTER 30 minutes of scrolling? Better or worse?'\n• 'What would you have done with that hour if you didn't have a phone?'\n\nAwareness is the first step. Don't lecture — help them notice the pattern themselves." },
          ]}},
          { id: "kt-m16-l2-a2", type: "flip_card" as any, title: "Screen & Social Media Dependency", instruction: "Flip each card to understand digital dependency and how to create boundaries that work.", content: { cards: [
            { front: "The Dopamine Loop", back: "Social media, gaming, and short-form video are engineered to be addictive — every notification, like, and new video triggers a dopamine hit in the teen's already-sensitive reward system. Signs of dependency: anxiety when phone is taken, can't go 10 minutes without checking, mood crashes after scrolling.", emoji: "🔁", tag: "How It Works" },
            { front: "Boundaries That Stick", back: "Negotiate boundaries WITH your teen, not impose them on them. No phones at meals or in bedrooms after a set time. Screen-free first hour after waking. Weekly screen time review together. Model it yourself — if you're always on your phone, why shouldn't they be?", emoji: "📵", tag: "Creating Boundaries" },
            { front: "The Comparison Trap", back: "Social media creates a distorted mirror. Everyone's life looks better, easier, more exciting online. Help your teen see: 'People post their highlights, not their hard days.' Ask: 'How do you feel AFTER 30 minutes of scrolling? Better or worse?' Awareness is the first step.", emoji: "🪞", tag: "Social Comparison" },
            { front: "Replace, Don't Just Remove", back: "Removing screen time without replacing it with something better creates resentment, not change. Replace with connection, physical activity, creative projects, or outdoor time. The goal is to make healthy alternatives as accessible and appealing as screens.", emoji: "🔄", tag: "What Works" },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-m16-l2-a3", type: "knowledge_check" as any, title: "Knowledge Check", instruction: "Test what you've learned before moving on.", content: { intro: "Let's check your understanding of screen dependency and digital boundaries.", passMark: 3, questions: [
            { question: "Why are social media and short-form video particularly addictive for teenagers?", options: ["Teenagers have poor self-control", "They're engineered to trigger dopamine responses in an already hypersensitive teenage reward system", "Teenagers are bored and have nothing else to do", "Parents don't set enough rules"], correct: 1, explanation: "Platforms are deliberately designed to maximise engagement through dopamine feedback loops — notifications, likes, infinite scroll. For the teenage brain (with a highly sensitive reward system), this engineering creates powerful dependency." },
            { question: "What makes screen boundaries more likely to stick?", options: ["Making rules without discussion", "Negotiating them WITH your teen, applying them to everyone including parents", "Removing all devices immediately", "Using parental controls without explanation"], correct: 1, explanation: "Boundaries negotiated WITH teens have more buy-in than rules imposed on them. Applying the same rules to yourself as a parent eliminates the 'do as I say, not as I do' contradiction that teenagers quickly identify and resent." },
            { question: "What does the social media 'comparison trap' do to teenagers?", options: ["It motivates them to do better", "It creates a distorted view where everyone else's life seems better, causing anxiety and lowered self-worth", "It has no real effect if parents talk to them enough", "It only affects girls"], correct: 1, explanation: "Social media presents highlight reels as normal life. Constant comparison to curated content erodes self-worth, creates anxiety about missing out, and generates a distorted sense of how other people actually live." },
            { question: "When setting screen time limits, what should you do alongside removing screen time?", options: ["Nothing — the removal itself is enough", "Replace it with something better, not just with nothing", "Explain why screens are dangerous", "Monitor their digital activity closely"], correct: 1, explanation: "Removing screen time without replacing it with engaging alternatives creates resistance and resentment. The goal is to make healthy options — connection, activity, creativity — as accessible and rewarding as screens, not just to eliminate the problematic behaviour." },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-m16-l2-a4", type: "open_response" as any, title: "Family Digital Audit", content: { prompt: "How much screen time does your family consume daily? Be honest about YOUR usage too. What's one boundary you could introduce this week that applies to everyone — including you?", saveToVault: true }},
        ]
      },
      {
        id: "kt-m16-l3",
        title: "Striking at the Root",
        description: "Addressing the WHY behind unhealthy coping",
        activities: [
          { id: "kt-m16-l3-a0", type: "reaction_slider" as any, title: "How Are You Feeling?", instruction: "Before we begin, take a moment to reflect.", content: { question: "How well do you think you understand the emotional needs driving any unhealthy coping habits your child may have?", options: [
            { emoji: "😰", label: "Not at all" },
            { emoji: "😕", label: "Barely" },
            { emoji: "😐", label: "Somewhat" },
            { emoji: "🙂", label: "Fairly well" },
            { emoji: "🌟", label: "Very well" },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-m16-l3-a1", type: "info_carousel" as any, title: "Root Causes", content: { slides: [
            { heading: "Ask Why, Not What", body: "Instead of focusing on WHAT they're doing (drinking, vaping, endless scrolling), ask WHY:\n• What are they trying to escape from?\n• What emotion are they trying to manage?\n• What need is being met by this behaviour?\n\n'I'm not asking to judge — I'm asking because I care about what's driving this.'" },
            { heading: "Build Alternative Coping", body: "Your teen needs healthy ways to handle:\n• Stress → physical activity, breathing, journaling\n• Loneliness → genuine connection, community, pets\n• Boredom → creative projects, nature, learning something new\n• Pain → therapy, talking, processing with a safe adult\n\nThe goal: make healthy coping as accessible and rewarding as the unhealthy option." },
            { heading: "If They're Already Struggling", body: "If you suspect substance use or serious dependency:\n• Don't panic publicly (process your fear with another adult first)\n• Approach with care: 'I've noticed some changes. I'm worried, not angry.'\n• Listen more than you talk\n• Seek professional help early (GP, counsellor, addiction service)\n• NZ: Alcohol Drug Helpline 0800 787 797\n• Remember: early intervention dramatically improves outcomes" },
          ]}},
          { id: "kt-m16-l3-a2", type: "flip_card" as any, title: "Addressing the Root Causes of Unhealthy Coping", instruction: "Flip each card to understand what drives unhealthy habits and how to address them effectively.", content: { cards: [
            { front: "Ask Why, Not What", back: "Instead of focusing on WHAT your teen is doing (drinking, vaping, endless scrolling), ask WHY. What are they trying to escape from? What emotion are they trying to manage? What need is being met? 'I'm not asking to judge — I'm asking because I care about what's driving this.'", emoji: "🔍", tag: "Root Cause" },
            { front: "Build Alternative Coping", back: "Teens need healthy ways to handle stress, loneliness, boredom, and pain. Stress: physical activity, breathing, journaling. Loneliness: genuine connection, community, pets. Boredom: creative projects, nature. Pain: therapy, processing with a safe adult. The goal: make healthy coping as accessible as unhealthy options.", emoji: "🛠️", tag: "Alternatives" },
            { front: "If They're Already Struggling", back: "Don't panic publicly — process your fear with another adult first. Approach with care: 'I've noticed some changes. I'm worried, not angry.' Listen more than you talk. Seek professional help early. NZ Alcohol Drug Helpline: 0800 787 797. Early intervention dramatically improves outcomes.", emoji: "🆘", tag: "Getting Help" },
            { front: "Connection Is Treatment", back: "Research consistently shows that family connection is one of the most powerful protective and recovery factors for substance issues. A teenager who knows they are genuinely loved and unconditionally accepted is far more likely to seek help and recover.", emoji: "❤️", tag: "The Core" },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-m16-l3-a3", type: "sort" as any, title: "Healthy Coping Order", content: { instruction: "When your teen is struggling emotionally, rank these coping strategies from most to least sustainable:", items: ["Talk to a trusted person about what's wrong", "Physical activity or time in nature", "Creative outlet (music, art, writing)", "Scrolling social media for distraction", "Substances to numb the feeling"], correctOrder: ["Talk to a trusted person about what's wrong", "Physical activity or time in nature", "Creative outlet (music, art, writing)", "Scrolling social media for distraction", "Substances to numb the feeling"] }},
          { id: "kt-m16-l3-a4", type: "knowledge_check" as any, title: "Knowledge Check", instruction: "Test what you've learned before moving on.", content: { intro: "Let's check your understanding of addressing the root causes of unhealthy coping.", passMark: 3, questions: [
            { question: "When your teen is engaging in unhealthy coping, what is the most important question to ask?", options: ["'What exactly are you doing?'", "'Why are you doing this — what are you trying to escape or manage?'", "'How long has this been going on?'", "'Who told you this was okay?'"], correct: 1, explanation: "Focusing on WHAT they're doing addresses symptoms. Understanding WHY — what emotion, need, or pain they're trying to manage — gets to the root. From there, you can help them find healthier ways to meet the same need." },
            { question: "Which of the following is a healthy alternative coping strategy for stress?", options: ["Spending more time gaming alone", "Physical activity, breathing exercises, or journaling", "Avoiding the situation causing stress", "Venting on social media"], correct: 1, explanation: "Physical activity, breathing, and journaling are all evidence-based stress management strategies that address the physiological stress response without creating dependency or avoidance patterns." },
            { question: "When you suspect your teen is struggling with substance use, the first step is:", options: ["Search their room immediately", "Ground them from all activities", "Process your own fear with another adult first, then approach with care: 'I'm worried, not angry'", "Call the school"], correct: 2, explanation: "Reacting from panic typically pushes teens further away. Processing your own emotions first means you can approach with genuine concern rather than fear-driven anger. Starting with 'I'm worried, not angry' opens dialogue rather than closing it." },
            { question: "What does research show is one of the most powerful protective and recovery factors for substance issues in teens?", options: ["Strict consequences and monitoring", "Removing all social activities", "Genuine family connection and unconditional love", "Comprehensive drug education programs at school"], correct: 2, explanation: "Family connection is consistently identified as one of the strongest protective factors against addiction and one of the most powerful supports for recovery. Teens who know they are genuinely loved and accepted are far more likely to seek help and successfully recover." },
          ] } },
        ]
      }
    ]
  },
  // ─── MODULE 17: BUILDING SELF-WORTH ─────────────────────────────────────
  {
    id: "kt-m17",
    title: "Building Unshakeable Self-Worth",
    subtitle: "Helping your child like who they are — from the inside out",
    description: "Self-worth is the foundation everything else is built on. These strategies help your child develop genuine confidence based on character and competence — not likes, looks, or popularity.",
    estimatedMinutes: 30,
    sourceBooks: ["The 6 Most Important Decisions You'll Ever Make — Sean Covey", "Good Inside — Becky Kennedy", "Raising Girls Who Like Themselves — Kasey Edwards"],
    sources: ["Self-Esteem Research", "Positive Psychology"],
    lessons: [
      {
        id: "kt-m17-l1",
        title: "The Two Mirrors",
        description: "Teaching your child to see themselves clearly",
        activities: [
          { id: "kt-m17-l1-a0", type: "reaction_slider" as any, title: "How Are You Feeling?", instruction: "Before we begin, take a moment to reflect.", content: { question: "How would you rate your child's current level of self-worth and genuine confidence?", options: [
            { emoji: "😰", label: "Very low" },
            { emoji: "😕", label: "Struggling" },
            { emoji: "😐", label: "Average" },
            { emoji: "🙂", label: "Fairly healthy" },
            { emoji: "🌟", label: "Very strong" },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-m17-l1-a1", type: "info_carousel" as any, title: "Mirrors of Self-Worth", content: { slides: [
            { heading: "The Social Mirror", body: "The 'social mirror' is what the world reflects back at your child: peer opinions, social media likes, grades, appearance comments. This mirror is distorted — it changes daily, it's based on others' insecurities, and it never gives an accurate picture.\n\nIf your child bases their worth on this mirror, they'll always be searching for validation." },
            { heading: "The True Mirror", body: "The 'true mirror' reflects who they actually are: their values, their effort, their kindness, their growth. This mirror is stable — it doesn't change based on who's looking.\n\nHelp them build this mirror by regularly reflecting THEIR qualities back to them:\n• 'I noticed you helped that kid who was sitting alone. That takes courage.'\n• 'You didn't give up on that project even when it was hard. That's persistence.'\n• 'The way you handled that disagreement showed real maturity.'" },
            { heading: "Character + Competence", body: "True confidence comes from two sources:\n\n1. CHARACTER: Who you are when no one's watching. Integrity, kindness, resilience.\n2. COMPETENCE: Getting good at something through effort. Sport, art, music, academics, cooking, fixing things.\n\nHelp your child develop BOTH. Character without skill feels hollow. Skill without character feels empty." },
          ]}},
          { id: "kt-m17-l1-a2", type: "flip_card" as any, title: "Building Self-Worth: Key Concepts", instruction: "Flip each card to understand the foundations of genuine confidence.", content: { cards: [
            { front: "The Social Mirror", back: "The 'social mirror' is what the world reflects back: peer opinions, social media likes, grades, appearance comments. This mirror is distorted — it changes daily, based on others' insecurities, and never gives an accurate picture. Children who base worth on this mirror will always be searching for validation.", emoji: "📱", tag: "Social Mirror" },
            { front: "The True Mirror", back: "The 'true mirror' reflects who they actually are: their values, effort, kindness, and growth. It's stable — it doesn't change based on who's looking. Help your child build it by reflecting their qualities back: 'I noticed you helped that kid who was sitting alone. That takes courage.'", emoji: "🪞", tag: "True Mirror" },
            { front: "Character + Competence", back: "True confidence comes from two sources: CHARACTER (who you are when no one's watching — integrity, kindness, resilience) and COMPETENCE (getting genuinely good at something through effort). Develop both. Character without skill feels hollow. Skill without character feels empty.", emoji: "⚡", tag: "The Two Pillars" },
            { front: "Anti-Comparison Practice", back: "Comparison is the thief of joy — especially for teenagers. Help them shift from 'Why am I not as good as them?' to 'Am I better than I was yesterday?' Progress is personal. Create a family practice: each person shares one thing they improved at this week, no matter how small.", emoji: "📊", tag: "Healthy Progress" },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-m17-l1-a3", type: "knowledge_check" as any, title: "Knowledge Check", instruction: "Test what you've learned before moving on.", content: { intro: "Let's check your understanding of building genuine self-worth.", passMark: 3, questions: [
            { question: "What is the 'social mirror' and why is it problematic for children's self-worth?", options: ["It refers to mirrors used in social settings", "It is peer opinions, likes, grades, and appearance comments — distorted and constantly changing, making self-worth unstable", "It is a positive reflection of social success", "It refers to social media profiles"], correct: 1, explanation: "The social mirror reflects external validation — grades, peer approval, social media engagement. It's distorted (based on others' insecurities) and constantly changes, making any self-worth based on it inherently unstable." },
            { question: "What makes the 'true mirror' more reliable for self-worth?", options: ["It comes from teachers and coaches", "It reflects fixed traits like intelligence", "It reflects values, effort, kindness, and growth — qualities that are stable and within the child's control", "It is based on achievement and performance"], correct: 2, explanation: "The true mirror reflects who your child actually is — their character, effort, and values — not how they perform or what others think of them. Because it's based on internal qualities, it's consistent and stable." },
            { question: "True confidence comes from:", options: ["Always winning and succeeding", "Being praised frequently", "Character (who you are) AND competence (what you can do through effort)", "Having many friends and being popular"], correct: 2, explanation: "Genuine confidence has two foundations: character (integrity, kindness, resilience — who you are when no one's watching) and competence (developing real skills through effort and practice). Both are needed — one without the other produces hollow confidence." },
            { question: "The 'anti-comparison practice' shifts focus from:", options: ["Other people to your own past performance", "Grades to sport", "School to family", "Your own performance to others' successes"], correct: 0, explanation: "Rather than comparing to others ('Why am I not as good as them?'), the anti-comparison practice focuses on personal growth ('Am I better than I was yesterday?'). Progress is measured against your own past self, not against others — making improvement feel achievable and motivating." },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-m17-l1-a4", type: "open_response" as any, title: "Reflect", content: { prompt: "Which mirror does your child look at most — the social mirror or the true mirror? What's one thing you could say this week to strengthen their true mirror?", saveToVault: true }},
        ]
      },
      {
        id: "kt-m17-l2",
        title: "Conquering Their Personal Challenge",
        description: "Everyone has a thing they struggle with — help them face it",
        activities: [
          { id: "kt-m17-l2-a0", type: "reaction_slider" as any, title: "How Are You Feeling?", instruction: "Before we begin, take a moment to reflect.", content: { question: "How well do you think your child faces personal challenges rather than avoiding them?", options: [
            { emoji: "😰", label: "Avoids everything" },
            { emoji: "😕", label: "Struggles a lot" },
            { emoji: "😐", label: "Sometimes faces it" },
            { emoji: "🙂", label: "Usually faces it" },
            { emoji: "💪", label: "Takes it head on" },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-m17-l2-a1", type: "info_carousel" as any, title: "Facing the Fear", content: { slides: [
            { heading: "Everyone Has One", body: "Every child has something that feels like their biggest obstacle — their personal dragon to slay. It might be:\n• Speaking up in class\n• Making friends\n• A learning difficulty\n• Body image\n• A family situation\n• Anxiety\n• Not fitting in\n\nThe size of the challenge doesn't matter. What matters is that they face it, not avoid it." },
            { heading: "Small Wins Build Confidence", body: "Confidence doesn't come from affirmations or pep talks. It comes from DOING hard things and surviving. Help your child:\n\n1. Name the challenge (what specifically scares them?)\n2. Break it into tiny steps\n3. Celebrate each step (not just the outcome)\n4. Normalise setbacks ('Everyone falls. Getting up is the skill.')\n5. Model your own struggles ('I was nervous about that presentation too')" },
            { heading: "The Anti-Comparison Practice", body: "Comparison is the thief of joy — especially for teenagers. Help them shift:\n\nFROM: 'Why am I not as good/pretty/smart/popular as them?'\nTO: 'Am I better than I was yesterday?'\n\nCreate a family practice: each person shares one thing they improved at this week, no matter how small. Progress is personal." },
          ]}},
          { id: "kt-m17-l2-a2", type: "flip_card" as any, title: "Conquering Your Child's Personal Challenge", instruction: "Flip each card to understand how to help your child face and overcome their biggest obstacle.", content: { cards: [
            { front: "Everyone Has a Dragon", back: "Every child has something that feels like their biggest obstacle — speaking up in class, making friends, body image, a learning difficulty, anxiety. The size of the challenge doesn't matter. What matters is that they FACE it, not avoid it. Avoidance always makes things bigger.", emoji: "🐉", tag: "Personal Dragons" },
            { front: "Small Wins Build Confidence", back: "Confidence doesn't come from affirmations or pep talks. It comes from doing hard things and surviving. Help your child: name the challenge, break it into tiny steps, celebrate each step (not just outcomes), normalise setbacks, and model your own struggles.", emoji: "🏆", tag: "Building Confidence" },
            { front: "Normalise Setbacks", back: "'Everyone falls. Getting up is the skill.' Share your own failures and how you recovered. When children see adults handle failure with resilience rather than shame, they learn that setbacks are normal — not proof that they're incapable.", emoji: "🔄", tag: "Resilience" },
            { front: "The Anti-Comparison Shift", back: "FROM: 'Why am I not as good/smart/popular as them?' TO: 'Am I better than I was yesterday?' Create a family practice: each person shares one thing they improved this week, no matter how small. Progress is personal and self-referenced, not comparative.", emoji: "↗️", tag: "Growth Focus" },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-m17-l2-a3", type: "knowledge_check" as any, title: "Knowledge Check", instruction: "Test what you've learned before moving on.", content: { intro: "Let's check your understanding of helping your child face their personal challenges.", passMark: 3, questions: [
            { question: "Where does genuine confidence actually come from?", options: ["Being told you're great by parents and teachers", "Doing hard things, surviving, and building competence over time", "Avoiding situations where you might fail", "Being naturally talented at something"], correct: 1, explanation: "Confidence is built through action — doing scary or hard things and surviving the experience. This creates an internal evidence base: 'I've done hard things before, I can do them again.' Affirmations and praise don't build this in the same way." },
            { question: "When a child is facing a significant personal challenge, what is the most helpful approach?", options: ["Remove the challenge so they don't have to face it", "Tell them to toughen up and get on with it", "Break the challenge into tiny steps, celebrate each one, and normalise setbacks", "Wait until they're older and more capable"], correct: 2, explanation: "Breaking challenges into small, achievable steps creates early wins that build momentum and belief. Celebrating progress (not just outcomes) and normalising setbacks removes the threat of failure as a catastrophe." },
            { question: "What happens when children consistently avoid their personal challenges?", options: ["They feel better and the fear fades naturally", "The challenge gets smaller with time", "Avoidance reinforces fear — making challenges feel larger and more threatening", "It protects their self-worth"], correct: 2, explanation: "Avoidance provides short-term relief but long-term, it reinforces the message that the challenge is too big to face. Each avoided situation makes the fear stronger. Gentle, gradual exposure — facing the challenge in small steps — is the evidence-based approach." },
            { question: "Why is sharing your own failures with your child valuable?", options: ["It lowers their expectations of you", "It demonstrates that failure is a normal part of life that adults also experience and recover from", "It makes them feel better about failing", "It shows you understand what they're going through"], correct: 1, explanation: "When children see adults fail and recover without shame, they learn that setbacks are survivable — not proof of being broken or incapable. Modelling recovery from failure normalises the process and demonstrates resilience in action." },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-m17-l2-a4", type: "survey" as any, title: "Your Child's Challenge", content: { question: "What do you think your child struggles with most?", options: ["Social confidence", "Academic pressure", "Body image", "Family situation", "Finding their identity", "Anxiety or worry"] }},
        ]
      }
    ]
  },
  // ─── MODULE 18: MINDFUL PARENTING (Clarke-Fields) ──────────────────────
  {
    id: "kt-m18",
    title: "Mindful Parenting",
    subtitle: "Breaking reactive cycles & responding with intention",
    description: "You can't pour from an empty cup. Hunter Clarke-Fields' approach helps you recognise your own triggers, break generational patterns of reactivity, and show up as the parent you want to be — even on the hard days.",
    estimatedMinutes: 35,
    sourceBooks: ["Raising Good Humans — Hunter Clarke-Fields"],
    sources: ["Mindfulness Research", "Attachment Theory"],
    lessons: [
      {
        id: "kt-m18-l1",
        title: "Your Triggers Aren't About Your Child",
        description: "Understanding why YOU react the way you do",
        activities: [
          { id: "kt-m18-l1-a0", type: "reaction_slider" as any, title: "How Are You Feeling?", instruction: "Before we begin, take a moment to check in with yourself.", content: { question: "How reactive do you feel you are as a parent right now — how often do you react without pausing to choose your response?", options: [
            { emoji: "😰", label: "Very reactive" },
            { emoji: "😕", label: "Often reactive" },
            { emoji: "😐", label: "Sometimes" },
            { emoji: "🙂", label: "Usually calm" },
            { emoji: "🧘", label: "Very mindful" },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-m18-l1-a1", type: "info_carousel" as any, title: "Trigger Awareness", content: { slides: [
            { heading: "The Autopilot Problem", body: "Clarke-Fields explains that most parenting reactions are on autopilot — we default to whatever WE experienced growing up. Yelling, threatening, shaming, withdrawing — these aren't conscious choices. They're conditioned responses from our own childhood. The first step to changing is noticing: 'I'm reacting, not responding.'" },
            { heading: "Mapping Your Triggers", body: "Common parental triggers and what's underneath:\n• Child whining → 'I can't handle being needed constantly' (overwhelm)\n• Child defying → 'I'm not respected/in control' (powerlessness)\n• Child crying → 'I was told crying was weakness' (inherited shame)\n• Sibling fighting → 'I need peace to function' (sensory overload)\n• Child lying → 'I can't trust anyone' (betrayal wound)\n\nYour trigger reveals YOUR unmet need, not your child's flaw." },
            { heading: "The STOP Practice", body: "When you feel the surge of reactivity:\n\nS — Stop. Physically pause. Don't speak.\nT — Take a breath. One deep breath reactivates your prefrontal cortex.\nO — Observe. What am I feeling? What's my body doing? What story am I telling myself?\nP — Proceed. Now choose your response consciously.\n\nThis takes 10 seconds. Those 10 seconds change everything." },
            { heading: "Repair Over Perfection", body: "You WILL lose it sometimes. Clarke-Fields says the magic isn't in never making mistakes — it's in how you repair. After you've calmed down:\n• 'I yelled at you and that wasn't okay. I'm sorry.'\n• 'You didn't deserve that. I was feeling overwhelmed and I handled it badly.'\n• 'What can I do to make this right?'\n\nRepair teaches your child: mistakes are human, accountability matters, and relationships can heal." },
          ]}},
          { id: "kt-m18-l1-a2", type: "flip_card" as any, title: "Trigger Awareness: Key Concepts", instruction: "Flip each card to understand what's beneath your reactive moments.", content: { cards: [
            { front: "The Autopilot Problem", back: "Most parenting reactions are on autopilot — we default to whatever we experienced growing up. Yelling, threatening, shaming, withdrawing — these are conditioned responses from our own childhood, not conscious choices. The first step to changing is noticing: 'I'm reacting, not responding.'", emoji: "🤖", tag: "Autopilot" },
            { front: "Triggers Reveal YOUR Needs", back: "Your trigger isn't about your child — it reveals your unmet need. Child whining = overwhelm. Child defying = powerlessness. Child crying = inherited shame around emotions. Child lying = betrayal wound. When you identify the need underneath, you can address it rather than exploding at your child.", emoji: "🎯", tag: "What Triggers Reveal" },
            { front: "The STOP Practice", back: "When you feel the surge of reactivity: S — Stop. Physically pause. T — Take a breath (one deep breath reactivates the prefrontal cortex). O — Observe. What am I feeling? What story am I telling myself? P — Proceed. Now choose your response consciously. This takes 10 seconds and changes everything.", emoji: "🛑", tag: "STOP Practice" },
            { front: "Repair Over Perfection", back: "You WILL lose it sometimes. The magic isn't in never making mistakes — it's in how you repair: 'I yelled at you and that wasn't okay. I'm sorry. You didn't deserve that. What can I do to make this right?' Repair teaches children: mistakes are human, accountability matters, and relationships heal.", emoji: "🔧", tag: "Repair" },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-m18-l1-a3", type: "knowledge_check" as any, title: "Knowledge Check", instruction: "Test what you've learned before moving on.", content: { intro: "Let's check your understanding of your own triggers and mindful parenting.", passMark: 3, questions: [
            { question: "According to Clarke-Fields, why do most parents react the way they do under stress?", options: ["Because their children are genuinely difficult", "Because parenting is overwhelming", "Because reactions are on autopilot — conditioned by their own childhood experiences", "Because they haven't read enough parenting books"], correct: 2, explanation: "Clarke-Fields explains that most stress reactions are conditioned autopilot responses from our own upbringing — not conscious choices. Noticing 'I'm reacting, not responding' is the crucial first step to changing the pattern." },
            { question: "What does a parenting trigger reveal about the parent?", options: ["That they're a bad parent", "Their child's bad behaviour", "An unmet need or wound being activated in the parent, not a flaw in the child", "That they need more sleep"], correct: 2, explanation: "Triggers point inward. A child whining triggers overwhelm (parent's unmet need for rest). A child defying triggers powerlessness (parent's need for respect). Identifying the underlying need allows you to address it rather than misdirecting it at your child." },
            { question: "What does the 'T' in the STOP practice stand for?", options: ["Think about the consequences", "Talk calmly to your child", "Take a breath", "Tell yourself to calm down"], correct: 2, explanation: "T stands for 'Take a breath.' One slow, deep breath physiologically reactivates the prefrontal cortex — the rational, decision-making part of the brain — giving you access to conscious choice rather than reactive impulse." },
            { question: "Why is 'repair' more important than 'perfection' in mindful parenting?", options: ["Because perfection is impossible anyway", "Because repair teaches children that mistakes are human, accountability matters, and relationships can heal", "Because children forget quickly", "Because apologies are easy"], correct: 1, explanation: "Clarke-Fields says the magic of mindful parenting isn't in never losing it — it's in how you repair. A genuine apology ('I yelled, that wasn't okay, I'm sorry') models accountability and shows children that relationships can survive and heal from conflict." },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-m18-l1-a4", type: "open_response" as any, title: "Trigger Map", content: { prompt: "What are your top 3 parenting triggers? For each one, can you identify what's UNDERNEATH it — what need or wound is being activated? Write honestly; this is just for you.", saveToVault: true }},
        ]
      },
      {
        id: "kt-m18-l2",
        title: "Breaking Generational Patterns",
        description: "You don't have to parent the way you were parented",
        activities: [
          { id: "kt-m18-l2-a0", type: "reaction_slider" as any, title: "How Are You Feeling?", instruction: "Before we begin, take a moment to reflect.", content: { question: "How aware are you of generational parenting patterns you might be unconsciously repeating?", options: [
            { emoji: "😰", label: "Not at all aware" },
            { emoji: "😕", label: "Vaguely aware" },
            { emoji: "😐", label: "Somewhat aware" },
            { emoji: "🙂", label: "Fairly aware" },
            { emoji: "🌟", label: "Very aware" },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-m18-l2-a1", type: "info_carousel" as any, title: "Breaking the Cycle", content: { slides: [
            { heading: "The Inheritance", body: "Clarke-Fields is clear: we parent the way we were parented UNLESS we consciously choose otherwise. The phrases that come out under stress — 'Because I said so,' 'Stop crying or I'll give you something to cry about,' 'You're being ridiculous' — those are echoes. They're your parents' voices coming through your mouth. Noticing this is the beginning of change." },
            { heading: "The Inner Child Work", body: "When your child's behaviour triggers an outsized reaction, ask: 'How old do I feel right now?' Often the answer isn't your actual age — it's 6, or 10, or 14. Your wounded inner child is reacting to their wounded inner child. Two hurt kids can't solve anything. The adult needs to show up first." },
            { heading: "Choosing Your Legacy", body: "Write two lists:\n1. What I received from my parents that I want to KEEP: (love of reading, family dinners, work ethic...)\n2. What I received that I want to CHANGE: (criticism, emotional unavailability, yelling, comparison...)\n\nYou are the transition generation. The patterns that stop with you don't reach your grandchildren." },
