            { heading: "Daily Mindfulness Practice", body: "Clarke-Fields recommends just 5 minutes daily:\n• Morning: set a parenting intention ('Today I will pause before reacting')\n• During conflict: one conscious breath before speaking\n• Evening: reflect without judgment — 'What went well? What would I do differently?'\n\nMindfulness isn't about being calm all the time. It's about being AWARE of when you're not calm — and choosing what to do next." },
          ]}},
          { id: "kt-m18-l2-a2", type: "flip_card" as any, title: "Breaking Generational Patterns", instruction: "Flip each card to understand how to identify and change inherited parenting patterns.", content: { cards: [
            { front: "The Inheritance", back: "We parent the way we were parented UNLESS we consciously choose otherwise. Phrases that come out under stress — 'Because I said so,' 'Stop crying,' 'You're being ridiculous' — are echoes. They're your parents' voices coming through your mouth. Noticing this is the beginning of change.", emoji: "🔄", tag: "The Pattern" },
            { front: "The Inner Child Moment", back: "When your child's behaviour triggers an outsized reaction, ask: 'How old do I feel right now?' Often the answer is 6, 10, or 14 — not your actual age. Your wounded inner child is reacting to their struggling child. Two hurt children can't solve anything. The adult needs to show up first.", emoji: "👶", tag: "Inner Child" },
            { front: "Your Legacy Lists", back: "Write two lists: 1. What I received that I want to KEEP (love of reading, family dinners, work ethic). 2. What I received that I want to CHANGE (criticism, yelling, emotional unavailability, comparison). You are the transition generation — what stops with you doesn't reach your grandchildren.", emoji: "📝", tag: "Your Legacy" },
            { front: "Daily Mindfulness Practice", back: "Just 5 minutes daily: Morning — set a parenting intention ('Today I will pause before reacting'). During conflict — one conscious breath before speaking. Evening — reflect without judgment: 'What went well? What would I do differently?' This isn't about being calm all the time — it's about noticing when you're not.", emoji: "🧘", tag: "Daily Practice" },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-m18-l2-a3", type: "knowledge_check" as any, title: "Knowledge Check", instruction: "Test what you've learned before moving on.", content: { intro: "Let's check your understanding of breaking generational parenting patterns.", passMark: 3, questions: [
            { question: "According to Clarke-Fields, what determines how parents default to responding under stress?", options: ["Their parenting philosophy", "Their child's temperament", "How they were parented — unless they consciously choose otherwise", "How well-rested they are"], correct: 2, explanation: "Clarke-Fields is clear: we parent the way we were parented unless we make a conscious choice to do differently. Stress reactions in particular reveal inherited patterns — phrases and behaviours absorbed in our own childhood." },
            { question: "When you react to your child with disproportionate emotion, asking 'How old do I feel right now?' helps you:", options: ["Identify how tired you are", "Recognise that a younger, wounded part of yourself is reacting — not your adult self", "Understand your child's developmental stage", "Track your emotional patterns over time"], correct: 1, explanation: "Outsized reactions often come from a younger, hurt part of ourselves being triggered. Recognising 'I feel 8 right now' allows the adult self to step in and respond with maturity rather than from old wound." },
            { question: "What does 'You are the transition generation' mean?", options: ["You are the first generation to use mindful parenting", "The patterns that stop with you don't get passed down to your grandchildren", "You need to transition between different parenting styles", "Your generation has different challenges than previous ones"], correct: 1, explanation: "'Transition generation' means you are consciously choosing to end harmful cycles. The patterns — criticism, shame, emotional unavailability — that you interrupt stop here. They don't continue to your children's children. This is one of the most profound contributions a parent can make." },
            { question: "What is the minimum daily mindfulness Clarke-Fields recommends?", options: ["30 minutes of formal meditation", "Just 5 minutes: morning intention, one breath during conflict, evening reflection", "Weekly therapy sessions", "Daily journaling for an hour"], correct: 1, explanation: "Clarke-Fields recommends a minimal but consistent practice: setting a parenting intention each morning, taking one conscious breath before responding in conflict, and a brief evening reflection. Small, consistent practice is more effective than occasional intensive effort." },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-m18-l2-a4", type: "survey" as any, title: "Self-Awareness", content: { question: "Which reactive pattern do you most want to break?", options: ["Yelling when overwhelmed", "Withdrawing/shutting down", "Over-controlling/micromanaging", "Using guilt or shame", "Comparing my kids to others", "Dismissing their emotions"] }},
        ]
      },
      {
        id: "kt-m18-l3",
        title: "Responding vs Reacting",
        description: "Practical scripts for the moments that test you most",
        activities: [
          { id: "kt-m18-l3-a0", type: "reaction_slider" as any, title: "How Are You Feeling?", instruction: "Before we begin, take a moment to reflect.", content: { question: "How consistently do you respond to your children with intention rather than reacting automatically?", options: [
            { emoji: "😰", label: "Almost never" },
            { emoji: "😕", label: "Sometimes" },
            { emoji: "😐", label: "About half the time" },
            { emoji: "🙂", label: "Often" },
            { emoji: "🌟", label: "Most of the time" },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-m18-l3-a1", type: "info_carousel" as any, title: "Response Scripts", content: { slides: [
            { heading: "Instead of Yelling", body: "REACTIVE: 'HOW MANY TIMES DO I HAVE TO TELL YOU?!'\nRESPONSIVE: 'I notice this keeps happening. Let's figure out a system that works for both of us.'\n\nREACTIVE: 'STOP IT RIGHT NOW!'\nRESPONSIVE: 'I can see you're struggling. I'm going to take a breath, and then we'll work this out.'\n\nThe shift: from controlling THEM to regulating YOURSELF." },
            { heading: "Instead of Shaming", body: "REACTIVE: 'What is WRONG with you?'\nRESPONSIVE: 'That behaviour isn't okay. You're a good person having a hard moment.'\n\nREACTIVE: 'You always do this!'\nRESPONSIVE: 'This happened today. What was going on for you?'\n\nREACTIVE: 'You're being such a brat!'\nRESPONSIVE: 'I can see big feelings are in charge right now. I'm here when you're ready.'" },
            { heading: "Instead of Threatening", body: "REACTIVE: 'If you don't stop, I'm taking everything away!'\nRESPONSIVE: 'Here's what's going to happen: [clear, calm consequence]. You choose.'\n\nREACTIVE: 'Wait till your father gets home!'\nRESPONSIVE: 'We're going to deal with this now, together, calmly.'\n\nThe principle: consequences should be related, respectful, and reasonable — not punitive." },
            { heading: "The 24-Hour Rule", body: "Clarke-Fields suggests: for any non-urgent issue, wait 24 hours before having the conversation. Most things feel less catastrophic after sleep. You'll be calmer, they'll be calmer, and the conversation will be productive rather than punitive.\n\nExceptions: safety issues require immediate action. Everything else can wait." },
          ]}},
          { id: "kt-m18-l3-a2", type: "flip_card" as any, title: "Responding vs Reacting: Scripts That Work", instruction: "Flip each card to learn the shift from reactive to responsive parenting language.", content: { cards: [
            { front: "Instead of Yelling", back: "REACTIVE: 'HOW MANY TIMES DO I HAVE TO TELL YOU?!' RESPONSIVE: 'I notice this keeps happening. Let's figure out a system that works for both of us.' The shift: from controlling THEM to regulating YOURSELF.", emoji: "📢", tag: "Yelling" },
            { front: "Instead of Shaming", back: "REACTIVE: 'What is WRONG with you?' RESPONSIVE: 'That behaviour isn't okay. You're a good person having a hard moment.' REACTIVE: 'You always do this!' RESPONSIVE: 'This happened today. What was going on for you?'", emoji: "🚫", tag: "Shaming" },
            { front: "Instead of Threatening", back: "REACTIVE: 'If you don't stop, I'm taking everything away!' RESPONSIVE: 'Here's what's going to happen: [clear, calm consequence]. You choose.' Consequences should be related, respectful, and reasonable — not punitive.", emoji: "⚡", tag: "Threats" },
            { front: "The 24-Hour Rule", back: "For any non-urgent issue, wait 24 hours before having the conversation. Most things feel less catastrophic after sleep. You'll be calmer, they'll be calmer, and the conversation will be productive rather than punitive. Exception: safety issues require immediate action.", emoji: "⏰", tag: "Timing" },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-m18-l3-a3", type: "knowledge_check" as any, title: "Knowledge Check", instruction: "Test what you've learned before moving on.", content: { intro: "Let's check your understanding of mindful responses in challenging parenting moments.", passMark: 3, questions: [
            { question: "What is the key shift in 'responding instead of reacting' when you feel the urge to yell?", options: ["Speak more quietly", "Shift from trying to control your child's behaviour to regulating your own state first", "Send them to their room to cool down", "Explain your feelings calmly"], correct: 1, explanation: "The shift is internal — from trying to control the child (which escalates) to managing your own emotional state (which de-escalates). When you regulate yourself first, you model exactly what you're asking your child to do." },
            { question: "How should you reframe 'What is WRONG with you?' in responsive parenting?", options: ["'Why are you always like this?'", "'I'm very disappointed in you'", "'That behaviour isn't okay — and you're a good person having a hard moment'", "'Go to your room and think about what you've done'"], correct: 2, explanation: "This response separates the behaviour (not okay) from the person (still good). It names the issue without attacking identity — which is the foundation of discipline that teaches rather than shames." },
            { question: "What principle should guide consequences in responsive parenting?", options: ["They should be as severe as possible to deter future behaviour", "They should be related, respectful, and reasonable — not punitive", "They should be decided in the heat of the moment", "Consequences aren't needed if you talk enough"], correct: 1, explanation: "Clarke-Fields and other gentle discipline experts agree: consequences are most effective when related to the behaviour, respectful of the child's dignity, and reasonable for their age. Punitive consequences may stop behaviour short-term but don't teach." },
            { question: "When does the 24-Hour Rule NOT apply?", options: ["When the child is a teenager", "When you're angry", "When there are safety concerns requiring immediate action", "When the child has broken a rule before"], correct: 2, explanation: "The 24-hour rule — waiting before non-urgent conversations — applies to most discipline situations. Safety concerns (a child in danger, immediate risk) require immediate action. Everything else benefits from the calm perspective that comes after sleep." },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-m18-l3-a4", type: "open_response" as any, title: "Script Practice", content: { prompt: "Think of the last time you reacted instead of responded. Rewrite the moment: what did you say, and what could you have said instead? How might the outcome have changed?", saveToVault: true }},
        ]
      }
    ]
  },
  // ─── MODULE 19: GENTLE DISCIPLINE (Ockwell-Smith) ──────────────────────
  {
    id: "kt-m19",
    title: "Gentle Discipline",
    subtitle: "Setting boundaries with empathy, not punishment",
    description: "Sarah Ockwell-Smith's gentle discipline approach proves you can have firm boundaries AND deep connection. Discipline means 'to teach' — not 'to punish.' These strategies work with your child's brain, not against it.",
    estimatedMinutes: 35,
    sourceBooks: ["Gentle Discipline — Sarah Ockwell-Smith"],
    sources: ["Developmental Psychology", "Attachment Research"],
    lessons: [
      {
        id: "kt-m19-l1",
        title: "Why Punishment Doesn't Work",
        description: "The science behind why traditional discipline backfires",
        activities: [
          { id: "kt-m19-l1-a0", type: "reaction_slider" as any, title: "How Are You Feeling?", instruction: "Before we begin, take a moment to reflect.", content: { question: "How do you feel about your current approach to discipline — do you feel it's teaching your child or mainly controlling them?", options: [
            { emoji: "😰", label: "Mostly controlling" },
            { emoji: "😕", label: "More control than teaching" },
            { emoji: "😐", label: "About equal" },
            { emoji: "🙂", label: "More teaching than control" },
            { emoji: "🌟", label: "Mostly teaching" },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-m19-l1-a1", type: "info_carousel" as any, title: "Beyond Punishment", content: { slides: [
            { heading: "Punishment vs Discipline", body: "Ockwell-Smith draws a critical distinction:\n\nPUNISHMENT: Making a child suffer for a mistake. Goal: compliance through fear.\nDISCIPLINE: Teaching a child to make better choices. Goal: understanding through connection.\n\nPunishment stops behaviour in the moment. Discipline changes behaviour for life. The question isn't 'How do I make them stop?' — it's 'What do I want them to LEARN?'" },
            { heading: "Why Time-Outs Often Fail", body: "Traditional time-outs isolate a dysregulated child — exactly when they need connection most. Ockwell-Smith explains that when a child is in fight/flight, their learning brain is offline. They can't reflect on what they did wrong from a 'naughty step.' They can only feel rejected.\n\nAlternative: 'Time-IN' — sit with them, help them calm, THEN discuss what happened." },
            { heading: "The Punishment-Rebellion Cycle", body: "Research shows punishment creates one of three outcomes:\n1. Compliance through fear (breaks the relationship)\n2. Sneakiness (they learn to not get caught)\n3. Rebellion (they push back harder)\n\nNone of these teach the child to make good decisions when you're not watching. Gentle discipline builds INTERNAL motivation — they do the right thing because they understand WHY, not because they're afraid." },
            { heading: "Behaviour Is Communication", body: "Every challenging behaviour is trying to tell you something:\n• Hitting = 'I don't have words for how I feel'\n• Whining = 'I need connection/attention'\n• Defiance = 'I need some control over my life'\n• Lying = 'I don't feel safe telling the truth'\n• Tantrums = 'My feelings are too big for my body'\n\nAddress the NEED underneath the behaviour, not just the behaviour itself." },
          ]}},
          { id: "kt-m19-l1-a2", type: "flip_card" as any, title: "Why Punishment Doesn't Work", instruction: "Flip each card to understand the science of discipline versus punishment.", content: { cards: [
            { front: "Punishment vs Discipline", back: "PUNISHMENT: Making a child suffer for a mistake. Goal — compliance through fear. DISCIPLINE: Teaching a child to make better choices. Goal — understanding through connection. Punishment stops behaviour in the moment. Discipline changes behaviour for life.", emoji: "⚖️", tag: "The Difference" },
            { front: "Why Time-Outs Often Fail", back: "Isolating a dysregulated child is exactly when they need connection most. When a child is in fight/flight, their learning brain is offline — they can't reflect from a 'naughty step.' They can only feel rejected. Alternative: 'Time-IN' — sit with them, help them calm, THEN discuss what happened.", emoji: "⏱️", tag: "Time-Outs" },
            { front: "The Punishment-Rebellion Cycle", back: "Research shows punishment creates one of three outcomes: compliance through fear (breaks the relationship), sneakiness (they learn not to get caught), or rebellion (they push back harder). None of these teach good decisions when you're not watching.", emoji: "🔄", tag: "The Cycle" },
            { front: "Behaviour Is Communication", back: "Every challenging behaviour is trying to tell you something. Hitting = 'I don't have words for this feeling.' Whining = 'I need connection.' Defiance = 'I need some control.' Lying = 'I don't feel safe telling the truth.' Address the NEED underneath.", emoji: "📣", tag: "What Behaviour Means" },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-m19-l1-a3", type: "single_choice" as any, title: "Check", content: { question: "Your 4-year-old hits their sibling. According to gentle discipline, the FIRST step is:", options: [
            { label: "Put them in time-out immediately", isCorrect: false },
            { label: "Take away a toy as consequence", isCorrect: false },
            { label: "Ensure the hurt child is safe, then connect with the hitter to understand what happened", isCorrect: true },
            { label: "Ignore it — they'll grow out of it", isCorrect: false },
          ], explanation: "Gentle discipline prioritises safety first (check on the hurt child), then connection (what's going on for the child who hit?), then teaching ('Hitting hurts. When you're angry, you can....'). Punishment skips the learning step entirely." }},
          { id: "kt-m19-l1-a4", type: "knowledge_check" as any, title: "Knowledge Check", instruction: "Test what you've learned before moving on.", content: { intro: "Let's check your understanding of why punishment doesn't work and what to do instead.", passMark: 3, questions: [
            { question: "What is the key difference between punishment and discipline?", options: ["Punishment is louder; discipline is quieter", "Punishment makes children suffer for mistakes; discipline teaches children to make better choices", "Punishment is physical; discipline is verbal", "There is no meaningful difference"], correct: 1, explanation: "Punishment aims for compliance through fear. Discipline aims to teach through connection and understanding. Punishment may stop behaviour immediately but doesn't create internal motivation to behave well when unsupervised." },
            { question: "Why do traditional time-outs often fail for young children?", options: ["They're too comfortable", "Children enjoy the alone time", "They isolate a dysregulated child exactly when they need connection most — and a brain in fight/flight cannot reflect and learn", "They're not long enough"], correct: 2, explanation: "When a child is dysregulated (in fight/flight mode), their thinking brain is offline. They cannot reflect from a naughty step — they can only feel abandoned and rejected. A 'time-in' (sitting with them calmly until they regulate) then discussing what happened is more effective." },
            { question: "When a child hits, gentle discipline says the underlying message is often:", options: ["They are naturally aggressive", "'I don't have words for how I feel right now'", "'I want to hurt my sibling'", "'I need stricter consequences'"], correct: 1, explanation: "Challenging behaviours communicate unmet needs or underdeveloped skills. Hitting usually means the child doesn't have emotional vocabulary or coping strategies yet. Addressing the need (teaching emotional expression) is more effective than punishing the behaviour." },
            { question: "What are the three typical outcomes of punishment-based discipline?", options: ["Learning, understanding, and change", "Compliance through fear, sneakiness, or rebellion — none of which teach good decisions", "Remorse, apology, and improvement", "Immediate change, long-term change, or no change"], correct: 1, explanation: "Research consistently shows punishment creates compliance through fear (damages relationship), sneakiness (learns to hide behaviour), or rebellion (escalates defiance). None builds the internal motivation to make good choices independently." },
          ] } },
        ]
      },
      {
        id: "kt-m19-l2",
        title: "Age-Appropriate Expectations",
        description: "Understanding what your child's brain can actually do",
        activities: [
          { id: "kt-m19-l2-a0", type: "reaction_slider" as any, title: "How Are You Feeling?", instruction: "Before we begin, take a moment to reflect.", content: { question: "How often do you find yourself expecting your child to do things they're developmentally not yet capable of?", options: [
            { emoji: "😰", label: "Very often" },
            { emoji: "😕", label: "Fairly often" },
            { emoji: "😐", label: "Sometimes" },
            { emoji: "🙂", label: "Rarely" },
            { emoji: "✅", label: "Almost never" },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-m19-l2-a1", type: "info_carousel" as any, title: "Brain Development", content: { slides: [
            { heading: "The Immature Brain", body: "Ockwell-Smith emphasises: most 'misbehaviour' is developmentally NORMAL. A 2-year-old grabbing toys isn't 'selfish' — they haven't developed theory of mind yet. A 5-year-old lying isn't 'manipulative' — they're testing reality. A teenager slamming doors isn't 'disrespectful' — their emotional regulation is under construction.\n\nMatching expectations to brain development prevents frustration on both sides." },
            { heading: "What to Expect & When", body: "0–2: Cannot share, cannot regulate emotions, cannot understand 'why'\n2–4: Beginning empathy, short impulse control, emotional flooding common\n4–7: Can follow rules but will forget under stress, developing conscience\n7–11: Can reason, understand consequences, still emotionally immature\n12+: Can think abstractly but prefrontal cortex still developing until ~25\n\nAsk: 'Is this something my child CAN'T do yet, or WON'T do?'" },
            { heading: "Reframing Challenging Phases", body: "• 'Terrible twos' → 'The age of autonomy' (they're learning independence)\n• 'Threenager' → 'The age of imagination' (testing boundaries = testing reality)\n• 'Difficult tween' → 'The age of identity' (they're figuring out who they are)\n• 'Impossible teenager' → 'The age of separation' (biologically designed to pull away)\n\nEvery frustrating phase serves a developmental purpose." },
          ]}},
          { id: "kt-m19-l2-a2", type: "flip_card" as any, title: "Age-Appropriate Expectations", instruction: "Flip each card to understand what children's developing brains can actually do at each stage.", content: { cards: [
            { front: "Immature Brains, Normal Behaviour", back: "Most 'misbehaviour' is developmentally NORMAL. A 2-year-old grabbing toys isn't selfish — they haven't developed theory of mind yet. A 5-year-old lying isn't manipulative — they're testing reality. Matching expectations to brain development prevents frustration on both sides.", emoji: "🧠", tag: "Brain Development" },
            { front: "What to Expect & When", back: "0–2: Cannot share, cannot regulate emotions. 2–4: Beginning empathy, short impulse control, emotional flooding. 4–7: Can follow rules but forgets under stress. 7–11: Can reason, still emotionally immature. 12+: Can think abstractly, but prefrontal cortex still developing until ~25.", emoji: "📅", tag: "Age Guide" },
            { front: "The CANT vs WON'T Question", back: "Before disciplining, ask: 'Is this something my child CAN'T do yet, or WON'T do?' A child who can't share at age 2 needs teaching, not punishment. A child who won't share at age 7 needs a different conversation. The distinction changes your response completely.", emoji: "❓", tag: "Can't vs Won't" },
            { front: "Reframe the Phases", back: "'Terrible twos' → Age of autonomy (learning independence). 'Threenager' → Age of imagination (testing reality). 'Difficult tween' → Age of identity (figuring out who they are). 'Impossible teenager' → Age of separation (biologically designed to pull away). Every frustrating phase serves a purpose.", emoji: "🔄", tag: "Reframing" },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-m19-l2-a3", type: "knowledge_check" as any, title: "Knowledge Check", instruction: "Test what you've learned before moving on.", content: { intro: "Let's check your understanding of age-appropriate expectations in discipline.", passMark: 3, questions: [
            { question: "Why is a 2-year-old grabbing toys NOT a sign of bad character?", options: ["It is a sign of bad character that needs discipline", "2-year-olds haven't developed theory of mind yet — sharing requires understanding other people's feelings", "They need more socialisation", "Parents are being too permissive"], correct: 1, explanation: "Theory of mind — the ability to understand that others have different thoughts and feelings — develops gradually between ages 3–5. Expecting a 2-year-old to share willingly means expecting a cognitive capacity they don't yet have." },
            { question: "The key question before disciplining a child is:", options: ["'How many times have I told them?'", "'What consequence should I use?'", "'Is this something they CAN'T do yet, or WON'T do?'", "'What would other parents think?'"], correct: 2, explanation: "Can't vs Won't is the crucial distinction. A child who literally cannot do something yet (due to brain development) needs teaching and support. A child who won't (choosing not to despite being capable) needs a different kind of engagement." },
            { question: "When is a teenager's prefrontal cortex (the reasoning, impulse-control brain) fully developed?", options: ["At age 13", "At age 16", "At age 18", "Around age 25"], correct: 3, explanation: "The prefrontal cortex — responsible for impulse control, long-term planning, and rational decision-making — isn't fully developed until approximately age 25. This is why teenage behaviour that looks 'unreasonable' to adults is often literally still developing." },
            { question: "Ockwell-Smith reframes the 'terrible twos' as:", options: ["A period of poor parenting outcomes", "The 'age of autonomy' — when children are learning independence", "A phase that can be avoided with consistent discipline", "Evidence that children need stricter boundaries"], correct: 1, explanation: "The 'terrible twos' reflect a child discovering autonomy and independence — a healthy, essential developmental stage. Reframing challenging phases as developmentally purposeful reduces parent frustration and promotes more effective, patient responses." },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-m19-l2-a4", type: "fill_blanks" as any, title: "Practice the Repair", content: { sentence: "After losing your temper, say: 'I ___ at you and that wasn't okay. I'm ___. You didn't ___ that. I was feeling ___ and I handled it badly.'", blanks: ["yelled", "sorry", "deserve", "overwhelmed"] }},
        ]
      },
      {
        id: "kt-m19-l3",
        title: "The Gentle Discipline Toolkit",
        description: "Practical strategies that maintain boundaries AND connection",
        activities: [
          { id: "kt-m19-l3-a0", type: "reaction_slider" as any, title: "How Are You Feeling?", instruction: "Before we begin, take a moment to reflect.", content: { question: "How confident are you in setting firm, loving boundaries WITHOUT resorting to threats or punishment?", options: [
            { emoji: "😰", label: "Not confident at all" },
            { emoji: "😕", label: "Quite unsure" },
            { emoji: "😐", label: "Somewhat okay" },
            { emoji: "🙂", label: "Fairly confident" },
            { emoji: "💪", label: "Very confident" },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-m19-l3-a1", type: "info_carousel" as any, title: "Practical Tools", content: { slides: [
            { heading: "Natural & Logical Consequences", body: "Natural consequences: 'You didn't wear your coat → you got cold' (the world teaches)\nLogical consequences: 'You threw the toy → the toy is put away for today' (related, respectful, reasonable)\n\nOckwell-Smith's test: Is the consequence RELATED to the behaviour? Is it RESPECTFUL of the child? Is it REASONABLE for their age? If any answer is no, it's punishment disguised as a consequence." },
            { heading: "The CALM Approach", body: "C — Connect first. Get on their level, make eye contact, use a calm voice.\nA — Acknowledge the feeling. 'I can see you're really frustrated.'\nL — Limit the behaviour. 'I won't let you hit. Hitting hurts.'\nM — Move to solution. 'What could you do instead when you feel this angry?'\n\nThis takes longer than yelling. But the learning lasts infinitely longer." },
            { heading: "Collaborative Problem-Solving", body: "For recurring issues, sit down OUTSIDE the moment and problem-solve together:\n1. 'I've noticed mornings are really stressful. What's hard about them for you?'\n2. 'What's hard about them for me is...'\n3. 'What could we try that works for both of us?'\n4. Write the plan together. Try it for a week. Review.\n\nChildren who help create solutions are far more likely to follow them." },
            { heading: "When You Need to Say No", body: "Gentle doesn't mean permissive. You CAN say no firmly and kindly:\n• 'I hear you want to stay up. The answer is no. Your body needs sleep.'\n• 'I understand you're disappointed. We're still leaving now.'\n• 'You can feel angry about the boundary. The boundary stays.'\n\nHold the limit with calm confidence. Empathy for their feelings doesn't mean changing the rule." },
          ]}},
          { id: "kt-m19-l3-a2", type: "flip_card" as any, title: "The Gentle Discipline Toolkit", instruction: "Flip each card to learn practical tools that maintain boundaries AND connection.", content: { cards: [
            { front: "Natural & Logical Consequences", back: "Natural: 'You didn't wear your coat → you got cold.' Logical: 'You threw the toy → the toy goes away today.' Ockwell-Smith's test: Is the consequence RELATED to the behaviour? RESPECTFUL of the child? REASONABLE for their age? If any answer is no, it's punishment disguised as a consequence.", emoji: "⚖️", tag: "Consequences" },
            { front: "The CALM Approach", back: "C — Connect first. Get on their level, make eye contact, use a calm voice. A — Acknowledge the feeling. 'I can see you're really frustrated.' L — Limit the behaviour. 'I won't let you hit. Hitting hurts.' M — Move to solution. 'What could you do instead when you feel this angry?'", emoji: "🌊", tag: "CALM Method" },
            { front: "Collaborative Problem-Solving", back: "For recurring issues, sit down OUTSIDE the moment: 'I've noticed mornings are really stressful. What's hard about them for you? What's hard for me is... What could we try that works for both of us?' Write the plan together, try it for a week, review it. Children who help create solutions follow them.", emoji: "🤝", tag: "Problem-Solving" },
            { front: "Gentle Doesn't Mean Permissive", back: "You CAN say no firmly and kindly: 'I hear you want to stay up. The answer is no. Your body needs sleep.' 'I understand you're disappointed. We're still leaving now.' 'You can feel angry about the boundary. The boundary stays.' Empathy for feelings doesn't mean changing the rule.", emoji: "🦁", tag: "Firm & Kind" },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-m19-l3-a3", type: "knowledge_check" as any, title: "Knowledge Check", instruction: "Test what you've learned before moving on.", content: { intro: "Let's check your understanding of the gentle discipline toolkit.", passMark: 3, questions: [
            { question: "What is a logical consequence according to Ockwell-Smith?", options: ["Any punishment that teaches a lesson", "A consequence that is related, respectful, and reasonable — connected to the actual behaviour", "Time-out in the child's room", "Taking away all screen time indefinitely"], correct: 1, explanation: "Logical consequences must pass three tests: RELATED (connected to the behaviour, not arbitrary), RESPECTFUL (preserving the child's dignity), and REASONABLE (appropriate for their age). Consequences that fail any of these tests are simply punishments with a different name." },
            { question: "In the CALM approach, what does the 'A' stand for?", options: ["Act calmly", "Acknowledge the feeling", "Ask what happened", "Address the behaviour"], correct: 1, explanation: "A stands for Acknowledge the feeling — 'I can see you're really frustrated.' Acknowledging the emotion BEFORE addressing the behaviour is crucial. A child who feels understood can then move into the 'L' (limit) and 'M' (move to solution) stages." },
            { question: "Why are children more likely to follow solutions they helped create?", options: ["They feel responsible for consequences", "They understand the rules better when explained", "They have greater ownership and buy-in when they were part of creating the solution", "They tend to be more cooperative than adults expect"], correct: 2, explanation: "Collaborative problem-solving builds genuine investment in solutions. When children help identify the problem, brainstorm options, and choose an approach, they feel respected and are far more motivated to follow through." },
            { question: "In gentle discipline, saying 'You can feel angry about the boundary — the boundary stays' demonstrates:", options: ["That parents don't care about children's feelings", "That empathy for feelings can coexist with firm boundaries — gentle doesn't mean permissive", "A failure to listen to the child", "Poor conflict resolution"], correct: 1, explanation: "One of the most important concepts in gentle discipline: validating a child's emotions does NOT mean changing your boundaries. You can fully acknowledge their anger while holding the limit firm — this models emotional regulation and boundary-setting simultaneously." },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-m19-l3-a4", type: "open_response" as any, title: "Reframe a Battle", content: { prompt: "Think of a recurring discipline issue in your home. Using the CALM approach, write out how you could handle it differently next time. What's the feeling underneath the behaviour?", saveToVault: true }},
        ]
      }
    ]
  },
  // ─── MODULE 20: TALKING ABOUT TOUGH TOPICS (Silverman/Faber) ──────────
  {
    id: "kt-m20",
    title: "Talking About Tough Topics",
    subtitle: "Having the conversations that matter — even when they're hard",
    description: "Dr Robyn Silverman and Adele Faber show that HOW you talk to your child matters as much as WHAT you say. These frameworks help you navigate the conversations about race, death, sex, money, mental health, and everything else that catches you off guard.",
    estimatedMinutes: 35,
    sourceBooks: ["How to Talk to Kids About Anything — Dr Robyn Silverman", "How to Talk So Kids Will Listen & Listen So Kids Will Talk — Adele Faber"],
    sources: ["Communication Research", "Child Psychology"],
    lessons: [
      {
        id: "kt-m20-l1",
        title: "The Art of Listening",
        description: "Why children stop talking and how to reopen the door",
        activities: [
          { id: "kt-m20-l1-a0", type: "reaction_slider" as any, title: "How Are You Feeling?", instruction: "Before we begin, take a moment to reflect.", content: { question: "How confident are you that your child feels they can talk to you about anything — including the hard stuff?", options: [
            { emoji: "😰", label: "Not confident" },
            { emoji: "😕", label: "Slightly confident" },
            { emoji: "😐", label: "Somewhat confident" },
            { emoji: "🙂", label: "Fairly confident" },
            { emoji: "🌟", label: "Very confident" },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-m20-l1-a1", type: "info_carousel" as any, title: "Listening Skills", content: { slides: [
            { heading: "Why Kids Stop Talking", body: "Faber identifies the conversation killers parents use daily without realising:\n• Denying feelings: 'You're fine!' 'There's nothing to be scared of'\n• Philosophising: 'Well, life isn't always fair'\n• Advising: 'What you should do is...'\n• Interrogating: 'Why did you do that? What were you thinking?'\n• Defending the other person: 'I'm sure they didn't mean it'\n\nEach one sends the message: your feelings aren't valid. Eventually, they stop sharing." },
            { heading: "The Faber Method: Accept Feelings", body: "Instead of fixing, try:\n1. LISTEN with full attention (put down your phone)\n2. ACKNOWLEDGE with a word: 'Oh...' 'Mmm...' 'I see...'\n3. NAME the feeling: 'That sounds really frustrating'\n4. GIVE the wish in fantasy: 'I wish I could make it not rain for your game'\n\nThis doesn't fix the problem. It does something better — it makes your child feel understood. A child who feels understood will come back." },
            { heading: "The Power of 'Tell Me More'", body: "Silverman's simplest tool: when your child mentions something — anything — say 'Tell me more about that.' Not 'why?' (feels interrogative). Not 'what happened?' (feels investigative). Just: 'Tell me more.'\n\nThis works with toddlers and teenagers. It signals genuine interest without pressure. It hands them control of the conversation. And it often reveals things you'd never have known to ask about." },
          ]}},
          { id: "kt-m20-l1-a2", type: "flip_card" as any, title: "The Art of Listening: Key Concepts", instruction: "Flip each card to understand what makes children stop talking — and how to reopen the door.", content: { cards: [
            { front: "What Kills Conversation", back: "Faber identifies daily conversation killers: Denying feelings ('You're fine!'), philosophising ('Life isn't always fair'), advising ('What you should do is...'), interrogating ('Why? What were you thinking?'), defending the other person ('I'm sure they didn't mean it'). Each sends the message: your feelings aren't valid.", emoji: "🚫", tag: "Conversation Killers" },
            { front: "The Faber Method", back: "Instead of fixing, try: 1. LISTEN with full attention (phone down). 2. ACKNOWLEDGE with a word: 'Oh... Mmm... I see...' 3. NAME the feeling: 'That sounds really frustrating.' 4. GIVE the wish in fantasy: 'I wish I could make it not rain for your game.' A child who feels understood will come back.", emoji: "👂", tag: "Faber Method" },
            { front: "The Power of 'Tell Me More'", back: "Silverman's simplest tool: when your child mentions anything, say 'Tell me more about that.' Not 'why?' (feels interrogative). Not 'what happened?' (feels investigative). Just: 'Tell me more.' Works with toddlers and teenagers. Signals genuine interest, hands them control of the conversation.", emoji: "💬", tag: "Tell Me More" },
            { front: "The Goal of Listening", back: "The goal of listening isn't to fix the problem. It's to make your child feel understood. A child who feels understood will keep talking, keep coming back, and eventually let you in to help. Advice without acknowledgment is wasted — understanding first unlocks everything else.", emoji: "🔑", tag: "The Real Goal" },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-m20-l1-a3", type: "single_choice" as any, title: "Practice", content: { question: "Your child says 'Nobody at school likes me.' Best first response?", options: [
            { label: "'Of course they do! You have lots of friends!'", isCorrect: false },
            { label: "'That sounds really lonely. Tell me more about what happened.'", isCorrect: true },
            { label: "'Maybe if you were nicer to people...'", isCorrect: false },
            { label: "'Do you want me to talk to your teacher?'", isCorrect: false },
          ], explanation: "Faber's approach: acknowledge the feeling first, then invite them to share more. Denying ('of course they do') invalidates. Advising and fixing skip the emotional step entirely." }},
          { id: "kt-m20-l1-a4", type: "knowledge_check" as any, title: "Knowledge Check", instruction: "Test what you've learned before moving on.", content: { intro: "Let's check your understanding of the art of listening.", passMark: 3, questions: [
            { question: "According to Faber, what happens when parents consistently use 'conversation killers'?", options: ["Children become better at arguing", "Children eventually stop sharing because they learn their feelings aren't valid", "Children become more independent", "Nothing — children always want to talk to their parents"], correct: 1, explanation: "Each conversation killer — denying feelings, immediately advising, interrogating — sends the message that the child's emotional experience is invalid or unwelcome. Over time, children learn to stop sharing because sharing feels pointless or unsafe." },
            { question: "In the Faber listening method, what is the FIRST step?", options: ["Name the feeling", "Offer a solution", "Listen with full attention — phone down, eyes up, body present", "Ask clarifying questions"], correct: 2, explanation: "The first step is undivided attention — putting the phone down, making eye contact, and being fully present. Before any words are spoken, your body language communicates whether you're genuinely interested or just going through the motions." },
            { question: "Why does Silverman recommend 'Tell me more' over 'Why?' or 'What happened?'", options: ["It's simpler to say", "'Why?' and 'What happened?' feel interrogative or investigative; 'Tell me more' signals pure interest and hands them control", "Children respond better to open-ended requests", "It avoids conflict"], correct: 1, explanation: "'Why?' puts children on the defensive (it implies they need to justify themselves). 'What happened?' feels like an investigation. 'Tell me more' is neutral, curious, and gives the child complete control over what they share and how." },
            { question: "What is the ultimate goal of empathic listening?", options: ["Gathering information to give good advice", "Making the child feel understood — which keeps them coming back and opens the door to eventual help", "Showing the child you care", "Solving their problems"], correct: 1, explanation: "Feeling understood is the prerequisite for being helped. A child who feels heard will keep talking, return to you when things get difficult, and eventually be open to your input. Advice without acknowledgment lands in a closed heart." },
          ] } },
        ]
      },
      {
        id: "kt-m20-l2",
        title: "Conversations About Bodies, Sex & Consent",
        description: "Age-appropriate honesty that builds safety",
        activities: [
          { id: "kt-m20-l2-a0", type: "reaction_slider" as any, title: "How Are You Feeling?", instruction: "Before we begin, take a moment to reflect.", content: { question: "How comfortable are you having age-appropriate conversations with your child about bodies, sex, and consent?", options: [
            { emoji: "😰", label: "Very uncomfortable" },
            { emoji: "😕", label: "Quite uneasy" },
            { emoji: "😐", label: "Somewhat okay" },
            { emoji: "🙂", label: "Fairly comfortable" },
            { emoji: "💪", label: "Very comfortable" },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-m20-l2-a1", type: "info_carousel" as any, title: "The Body Talk", content: { slides: [
            { heading: "Start Early, Stay Casual (Silverman)", body: "Silverman emphasises: the 'sex talk' should never be ONE big conversation. It should be hundreds of small, casual ones starting from toddlerhood.\n\nAge 2–4: Correct names for body parts. 'Your body belongs to you.'\nAge 5–8: How babies are made (simplified). Puberty preview. Good touch vs bad touch.\nAge 9–12: Detailed puberty. Consent. Healthy relationships. Online safety.\nAge 13+: Sex, contraception, consent, pornography literacy, healthy relationships." },
            { heading: "The Consent Conversation", body: "Consent education starts at 2, not 12:\n• 'Your body, your rules. No one touches you without permission.'\n• 'Ask before you hug your friend.'\n• 'Uncle Joe wants a hug. You can say no. A wave is fine.'\n• 'If someone touches you and it feels wrong, tell me. You will NEVER be in trouble.'\n\nAs they age: 'Consent is enthusiastic. Silence is not yes. Pressure is not okay. You can change your mind at any time.'" },
            { heading: "When They Find Pornography", body: "Average age of first exposure to pornography: 11. Silverman's approach — don't panic, educate:\n• 'You're not in trouble for seeing this.'\n• 'What you saw is not what real relationships/sex look like.'\n• 'Those are actors performing for a camera. Real intimacy involves caring about the other person's feelings.'\n• 'If you see something that makes you feel confused or uncomfortable, you can always talk to me.'\n\nThis conversation should happen BEFORE exposure, not after." },
          ]}},
          { id: "kt-m20-l2-a2", type: "flip_card" as any, title: "Body, Sex & Consent: Key Concepts", instruction: "Flip each card to understand how to approach these important conversations with your child.", content: { cards: [
            { front: "Start Early, Stay Casual", back: "The 'sex talk' should never be ONE big conversation — it should be hundreds of small, casual ones starting from toddlerhood. Age 2–4: correct body part names, 'your body belongs to you.' Age 5–8: how babies are made (simplified), good vs bad touch. Age 9–12: puberty, consent. Age 13+: sex, contraception, healthy relationships.", emoji: "📅", tag: "Age-Appropriate Talks" },
            { front: "Consent Starts at Age 2", back: "Consent education begins with toddlers: 'Your body, your rules — no one touches you without permission.' 'Ask before you hug your friend.' 'Uncle Joe wants a hug. You can say no. A wave is fine.' As they age: 'Consent is enthusiastic. Silence is not yes. You can change your mind at any time.'", emoji: "🛡️", tag: "Consent" },
            { front: "When They Find Pornography", back: "Average first exposure age: 11. Don't panic — educate: 'You're not in trouble for seeing this.' 'What you saw is not what real relationships look like.' 'Those are actors — real intimacy involves caring about the other person.' 'If you see something confusing, you can always talk to me.' Have this conversation BEFORE exposure.", emoji: "💻", tag: "Digital Reality" },
            { front: "The Goal: Safety Through Openness", back: "The entire goal of body safety conversations is this: your child knows they can come to you with anything and will not be in trouble. A child who knows this is vastly safer than a child kept ignorant. Discomfort on your part is worth it. Keep the door open.", emoji: "🔐", tag: "The Goal" },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-m20-l2-a3", type: "knowledge_check" as any, title: "Knowledge Check", instruction: "Test what you've learned before moving on.", content: { intro: "Let's check your understanding of having conversations about bodies, sex, and consent.", passMark: 3, questions: [
            { question: "According to Silverman, when should you start conversations about bodies and consent?", options: ["Age 10, when children can understand", "Age 13, at the start of high school", "From toddlerhood — many small, casual conversations rather than one big talk", "When they ask about it first"], correct: 2, explanation: "Silverman emphasises starting early and keeping conversations casual and ongoing. By the time parents attempt 'the talk,' children have often already formed impressions from peers or media. Early, normalised conversations are far more effective." },
            { question: "Which phrase correctly teaches consent to a 3-year-old?", options: ["'Be a good girl and give Grandma a kiss'", "'You don't have to hug anyone if you don't want to — your body belongs to you'", "'Give everyone a hug — it's polite'", "'Wait until you're older to worry about that'"], correct: 1, explanation: "Teaching 'your body belongs to you' and that your child can refuse any physical contact (even from relatives) is foundational consent education. Forcing affection — even well-intentioned — teaches children that others have the right to override their physical boundaries." },
            { question: "What is the recommended approach when a child is accidentally exposed to pornography?", options: ["React with strong moral disapproval so they know it's wrong", "Ignore it — they'll forget", "'You're not in trouble. What you saw doesn't represent real relationships — those are actors, and real intimacy involves caring about each other'", "Block all internet access immediately"], correct: 2, explanation: "Silverman recommends a calm, educational response. Shame or strong disapproval makes children afraid to come to you in the future. Education — this is not reality, real intimacy is different — provides the protective context they need." },
            { question: "The most important message to convey in all body safety conversations is:", options: ["Sexual information should be kept private", "Your body is shameful and private", "If anything happens or you see anything confusing, you can always tell me and you will never be in trouble", "These topics are for when you're older"], correct: 2, explanation: "Children who know they can come to a trusted adult without facing punishment are exponentially safer. Creating a 'no trouble' zone around body conversations means children are more likely to disclose abuse, seek information from you rather than peers, and come to you when things go wrong." },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-m20-l2-a4", type: "comparison" as any, title: "Your Legacy Lists", content: { title: "What You Received — What You'll Pass On", columnA: { label: "Keep (from my parents)", items: ["What did they do well?", "What traditions do you cherish?", "What values did they instil?", "What made you feel safe?"] }, columnB: { label: "Change (stops with me)", items: ["What caused you pain?", "What patterns do you repeat under stress?", "What would you never want your child to feel?", "What phrase still echoes in your head?"] }, reflection: "You are the transition generation. What stops with you doesn't reach your grandchildren." }},
        ]
      },
      {
        id: "kt-m20-l3",
        title: "Race, Privilege & Difference",
        description: "Helping your child understand and respect diversity",
        activities: [
          { id: "kt-m20-l3-a0", type: "reaction_slider" as any, title: "How Are You Feeling?", instruction: "Before we begin, take a moment to reflect.", content: { question: "How comfortable are you discussing topics like race, diversity, and inequality with your child?", options: [
            { emoji: "😰", label: "Very uncomfortable" },
            { emoji: "😕", label: "Quite uneasy" },
            { emoji: "😐", label: "Somewhat okay" },
            { emoji: "🙂", label: "Fairly comfortable" },
            { emoji: "💪", label: "Very comfortable" },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-m20-l3-a1", type: "info_carousel" as any, title: "Diversity Talks", content: { slides: [
            { heading: "Don't Be Colourblind (Silverman)", body: "Silverman cautions against 'We don't see colour' — children DO notice differences from age 3. Pretending differences don't exist teaches them it's shameful to notice or discuss them.\n\nInstead: 'People have different skin colours, like people have different eye colours. All are beautiful. What matters is how we treat each other.'" },
            { heading: "Answering Embarrassing Questions", body: "When your child points at someone and says loudly 'Why is that person in a wheelchair?'\n• Don't shush them (teaches that disability is shameful)\n• Answer simply: 'Their legs work differently, so they use a chair to help them move around.'\n• If appropriate, model friendly interaction\n\nSilverman says: children's curiosity about difference is healthy. Our discomfort is the problem, not their questions." },
            { heading: "Building Empathy Through Exposure", body: "Diverse books, friendships, media, and experiences teach empathy naturally. If your child's world is homogeneous, actively broaden it:\n• Books featuring characters from different backgrounds\n• Cultural events and festivals\n• Conversations about inequality: 'Not everyone has what we have. What could we do about that?'\n• Model inclusivity in your own friendships and choices" },
          ]}},
          { id: "kt-m20-l3-a2", type: "flip_card" as any, title: "Talking About Race, Privilege & Difference", instruction: "Flip each card to understand how to have honest, constructive conversations about diversity with your child.", content: { cards: [
            { front: "Don't Be Colourblind", back: "Children notice differences from age 3. Saying 'We don't see colour' teaches them it's shameful to notice or discuss differences. Instead: 'People have different skin colours, like different eye colours. All are beautiful. What matters is how we treat each other.'", emoji: "🌈", tag: "Race Conversations" },
            { front: "Answer Embarrassing Questions", back: "When your child loudly asks about a disability or difference: Don't shush (teaches it's shameful). Answer simply: 'Their legs work differently so they use a chair to help them move around.' Silverman: children's curiosity about difference is healthy — our discomfort is the problem, not their questions.", emoji: "❓", tag: "Hard Questions" },
            { front: "Build Empathy Through Exposure", back: "Diverse books, friendships, media, and experiences teach empathy naturally. If your child's world is homogeneous, actively broaden it: books featuring different backgrounds, cultural events, conversations about inequality: 'Not everyone has what we have. What could we do about that?'", emoji: "🌍", tag: "Building Empathy" },
            { front: "Have the Avoidance Conversation", back: "Which tough conversation have you been avoiding? Using Faber's method: lead with acknowledgment ('This might be confusing...'), name the emotion, invite them to share their thinking. Starting imperfectly is better than not starting at all.", emoji: "💬", tag: "Start the Talk" },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-m20-l3-a3", type: "knowledge_check" as any, title: "Knowledge Check", instruction: "Test what you've learned before moving on.", content: { intro: "Let's check your understanding of talking about race, diversity, and difference.", passMark: 3, questions: [
            { question: "Silverman cautions against 'colourblindness' in parenting because:", options: ["It is scientifically inaccurate", "Children notice differences from age 3 — pretending they don't teaches children it's shameful to acknowledge or discuss them", "It leads to racism", "It avoids important conversations"], correct: 1, explanation: "Children naturally notice physical differences from very early. Pretending not to see colour teaches that these differences are too shameful to mention — the opposite of the open, curious, respectful approach we want children to have." },
            { question: "When your child loudly asks why someone is in a wheelchair, you should:", options: ["Shush them and walk away quickly", "Apologise to the person on your child's behalf", "Answer simply and naturally: 'Their legs work differently — they use a chair to help them move around'", "Tell them they'll understand when they're older"], correct: 2, explanation: "Simple, matter-of-fact answers normalise difference. Shushing teaches that the topic is shameful. A direct, respectful answer models how to talk about disability — and may be followed by modelling friendly interaction if appropriate." },
            { question: "What is the most effective way to build genuine empathy for diversity in your child?", options: ["Giving lectures about fairness and equality", "Exposure — diverse books, friendships, media, and experiences that naturally expand their worldview", "Showing them news about inequality", "Telling them about your own experiences with prejudice"], correct: 1, explanation: "Empathy is built through experience and story, not lecture. Diverse books, friendships, and experiences create natural understanding and connection that translates into genuine respect — not just theoretical agreement with equality." },
            { question: "What is the Faber method for starting a difficult conversation you've been avoiding?", options: ["Start with facts, then move to feelings", "Lead with acknowledgment, name the emotion, then invite them to share", "Have the conversation via text so there's less pressure", "Wait for them to bring it up first"], correct: 1, explanation: "Faber's approach: acknowledge first ('This might feel confusing or hard'), name what you imagine they might be feeling, then invite them to share their thoughts. This sequence ensures the child feels safe before they're expected to engage with a difficult topic." },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-m20-l3-a4", type: "open_response" as any, title: "Reflect", content: { prompt: "What tough conversation have you been avoiding with your child? Using the Faber listening method (acknowledge feelings, name the emotion, invite them to share), write out how you could start that conversation this week.", saveToVault: true }},
        ]
      }
    ]
