```ts
  // ─── MODULE 21: THE DISENGAGED TEEN (Anderson/Winthrop) ────────────────
  {
    id: "kt-m21",
    title: "The Disengaged Teen",
    subtitle: "Reigniting motivation when your teenager has checked out",
    description: "Jenny Anderson and Rebecca Winthrop's research reveals why so many teens disengage — and it's not laziness. These strategies help you understand what's driving the disconnection and rebuild your teenager's sense of purpose and agency.",
    estimatedMinutes: 30,
    sourceBooks: ["The Disengaged Teen — Jenny Anderson & Rebecca Winthrop"],
    sources: ["Adolescent Motivation Research", "Education Psychology"],
    lessons: [
      {
        id: "kt-m21-l1",
        title: "Why Teens Disengage",
        description: "It's not laziness — it's something deeper",
        activities: [
          { id: "kt-m21-l1-a0", type: "reaction_slider" as any, title: "How Are You Feeling?", instruction: "Before we begin, take a moment to reflect.", content: { question: "How would you rate your teenager's current level of engagement with school, family, and life in general?", options: [
            { emoji: "😰", label: "Completely checked out" },
            { emoji: "😕", label: "Mostly disengaged" },
            { emoji: "😐", label: "Somewhat engaged" },
            { emoji: "🙂", label: "Fairly engaged" },
            { emoji: "🌟", label: "Very engaged" },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-m21-l1-a1", type: "info_carousel" as any, title: "Understanding Disengagement", content: { slides: [
            { heading: "The Disengagement Epidemic", body: "Anderson and Winthrop found that teen disengagement is rarely about laziness. The most common drivers:\n• Feeling unseen: 'No one at school actually knows me'\n• Feeling irrelevant: 'Why does any of this matter?'\n• Feeling powerless: 'Nothing I do changes anything'\n• Overwhelm: 'There's too much expected of me and I can't do any of it well'\n• Misalignment: 'What I care about isn't what school values'\n\nDisengagement is a PROTECTIVE response — they withdraw to protect themselves from failure or meaninglessness." },
            { heading: "The Belonging Crisis", body: "Research shows the #1 predictor of teen engagement isn't intelligence, discipline, or resources — it's BELONGING. A teenager who feels they belong (at school, in a family, in a community) will show up and try. A teenager who feels like an outsider will check out.\n\nAsk your teen: 'Where do you feel most like yourself? Where do you feel you belong?' If they can't answer, that's your starting point." },
            { heading: "Performance vs Mastery", body: "Anderson and Winthrop distinguish between performance orientation ('I need to get an A') and mastery orientation ('I want to understand this'). Teens who are performance-oriented burn out faster — every test becomes a judgment of their worth. Teens who are mastery-oriented are more resilient because they're driven by curiosity, not fear.\n\nShift the conversation: from 'What did you get?' to 'What did you learn?'" },
          ]}},
          { id: "kt-m21-l1-a2", type: "flip_card" as any, title: "Why Teens Disengage", instruction: "Flip each card to understand the real drivers of teen disengagement.", content: { cards: [
            { front: "Not Laziness — Something Deeper", back: "Teen disengagement is rarely about laziness. Common drivers: feeling unseen ('no one actually knows me'), feeling irrelevant ('why does any of this matter?'), feeling powerless ('nothing I do changes anything'), overwhelm, or misalignment ('what I care about isn't what school values'). Disengagement is a protective response.", emoji: "🛡️", tag: "Real Cause" },
            { front: "The Belonging Crisis", back: "The number-one predictor of teen engagement isn't intelligence, discipline, or resources — it's BELONGING. A teenager who feels they belong (at school, in family, in community) will show up and try. A teenager who feels like an outsider will check out. Ask: 'Where do you feel most like yourself?'", emoji: "🏠", tag: "Belonging" },
            { front: "Performance vs Mastery", back: "Performance orientation ('I need an A') ties self-worth to grades and leads to burnout. Mastery orientation ('I want to understand this') builds resilience because curiosity — not fear — drives learning. Shift the conversation from 'What did you get?' to 'What did you learn?'", emoji: "📚", tag: "Mindset" },
            { front: "Signs of Disengagement", back: "Watch for: declining grades without clear cause, loss of interest in previously loved activities, spending most time alone, saying 'I don't care' about most things, resisting school or responsibilities, excessive screen use as escape. These are signals, not character flaws.", emoji: "🚦", tag: "Warning Signs" },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-m21-l1-a3", type: "knowledge_check" as any, title: "Knowledge Check", instruction: "Test what you've learned before moving on.", content: { intro: "Let's check your understanding of why teenagers disengage.", passMark: 3, questions: [
            { question: "According to Anderson and Winthrop, what is the most common driver of teen disengagement?", options: ["Laziness and poor character", "Feeling unseen, irrelevant, or powerless — disengagement as a protective response", "Too much free time", "Poor diet and sleep"], correct: 1, explanation: "Anderson and Winthrop's research shows disengagement is almost never about laziness. It's a protective withdrawal response to feeling unseen, irrelevant, overwhelmed, or misaligned with what's being demanded of them." },
            { question: "What is the number-one predictor of teen engagement?", options: ["Academic ability", "School quality", "Belonging — feeling genuinely seen and accepted somewhere", "Parental income"], correct: 2, explanation: "Belonging is the strongest predictor of engagement. A teen who feels they belong — in their family, school, or community — will show up and try. A teen who feels like an outsider, regardless of their capabilities, will disengage to protect themselves." },
            { question: "What does shifting from 'What did you get?' to 'What did you learn?' encourage?", options: ["Lower expectations", "A mastery orientation — learning driven by curiosity rather than grade-based fear", "More relaxed parenting", "Lower academic standards"], correct: 1, explanation: "This shift moves teens from performance orientation (where worth depends on grades) to mastery orientation (where curiosity drives learning). Mastery-oriented teens are more resilient, more intrinsically motivated, and less prone to burnout." },
            { question: "Teen disengagement is best understood as:", options: ["Evidence that your teen is failing", "A deliberate provocation toward parents", "A protective withdrawal response to feeling unseen, irrelevant, or overwhelmed", "Normal teenage behaviour that doesn't need addressing"], correct: 2, explanation: "Disengagement is a protective mechanism — when a teen feels they cannot succeed, belong, or matter, withdrawing feels safer than continuing to try and fail. Understanding this changes how parents respond: from confrontation to curiosity and connection." },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-m21-l1-a4", type: "survey" as any, title: "Check In", content: { question: "What signs of disengagement do you see in your teen?", options: ["Declining grades without apparent cause", "Loss of interest in activities they used to love", "Spending most time alone in their room", "Saying 'I don't care' about most things", "Resisting school or responsibilities", "Excessive screen use as escape"] }},
        ]
      },
      {
        id: "kt-m21-l2",
        title: "Rebuilding Connection & Purpose",
        description: "Practical strategies to re-engage your teenager",
        activities: [
          { id: "kt-m21-l2-a0", type: "reaction_slider" as any, title: "How Are You Feeling?", instruction: "Before we begin, take a moment to reflect.", content: { question: "How confident are you in knowing practical steps to re-engage a disengaged teenager?", options: [
            { emoji: "😰", label: "No idea where to start" },
            { emoji: "😕", label: "Have a few ideas" },
            { emoji: "😐", label: "Somewhat clear" },
            { emoji: "🙂", label: "Fairly confident" },
            { emoji: "💪", label: "Very confident" },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-m21-l2-a1", type: "info_carousel" as any, title: "Re-Engagement", content: { slides: [
            { heading: "The Autonomy Lever", body: "Disengaged teens often feel controlled in every aspect of their life: school dictates their day, parents dictate their evening, social media dictates their social life. Anderson and Winthrop recommend increasing REAL autonomy:\n• Let them choose how they study (not whether)\n• Let them choose activities (don't over-schedule)\n• Give genuine decision-making power in family matters\n• Ask for their opinion — and actually use it\n\nAutonomy doesn't mean permissiveness. It means treating them as capable of making some decisions." },
            { heading: "The Purpose Project", body: "Help your teen connect to something bigger than grades:\n• What injustice bothers them? (environment, poverty, animal welfare)\n• What community could they serve?\n• What skill could they teach someone else?\n• What problem could they solve?\n\nPurpose doesn't have to be grand. A teenager who volunteers at a dog shelter, builds a community garden, or tutors younger kids finds meaning — and motivation follows meaning." },
            { heading: "The 1:1 Investment", body: "Anderson and Winthrop emphasise: disengaged teens are re-engaged by ONE caring adult who sees them. This might be you. It might be a coach, teacher, aunt, or mentor.\n\nWhat this person does: shows genuine interest, remembers details, doesn't judge, holds them to high expectations while showing they believe in them.\n\nSchedule regular 1:1 time with your teen. No agenda. No lectures. Just presence." },
            { heading: "From Passive to Active", body: "Disengaged teens are often passively consuming (scrolling, watching, gaming). The antidote is ACTIVE engagement:\n• Creating something (music, art, code, food)\n• Building something (physical or digital)\n• Competing at something (sport, debate, gaming at a competitive level)\n• Learning something they CHOSE (not school-mandated)\n\nThe shift from consumer to creator is often the turning point." },
          ]}},
          { id: "kt-m21-l2-a2", type: "flip_card" as any, title: "Re-Engagement Strategies", instruction: "Flip each card to discover practical ways to rebuild your teenager's connection and purpose.", content: { cards: [
            { front: "Increase Real Autonomy", back: "Disengaged teens often feel controlled everywhere. Give REAL autonomy: let them choose HOW they study (not whether), choose activities, have genuine decision-making power in family matters, and have their opinions actually used. Autonomy is not permissiveness — it's treating them as capable of some decisions.", emoji: "🔓", tag: "Autonomy" },
            { front: "The Purpose Project", back: "Connect your teen to something bigger than grades: What injustice bothers them? What community could they serve? What skill could they teach someone else? A teenager who volunteers at a shelter, builds a garden, or tutors others finds meaning — and motivation follows meaning.", emoji: "🌱", tag: "Purpose" },
            { front: "The 1:1 Investment", back: "Disengaged teens are re-engaged by ONE caring adult who genuinely sees them. This might be you, or a coach, teacher, aunt, or mentor. What this person does: shows genuine interest, remembers details, doesn't judge, holds them to high expectations while showing belief in them.", emoji: "👤", tag: "One Person" },
            { front: "Passive to Active", back: "Disengaged teens are often passively consuming (scrolling, watching, gaming). The antidote is ACTIVE engagement: creating something (music, art, code, food), building something, competing at something, or learning something they CHOSE. The shift from consumer to creator is often the turning point.", emoji: "🎨", tag: "Active vs Passive" },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-m21-l2-a3", type: "knowledge_check" as any, title: "Knowledge Check", instruction: "Test what you've learned before moving on.", content: { intro: "Let's check your understanding of re-engaging a disengaged teenager.", passMark: 3, questions: [
            { question: "What does giving a teen 'real autonomy' mean?", options: ["Letting them do whatever they want", "Treating them as capable of some decisions — how they study, which activities, genuine input in family matters", "Removing all parental guidance", "Negotiating every rule away"], correct: 1, explanation: "Real autonomy means giving teenagers genuine decision-making power in age-appropriate areas — not unlimited freedom, but real choices that matter. This addresses the 'powerlessness' that often drives disengagement." },
            { question: "What type of purpose most effectively re-engages disengaged teens?", options: ["Career planning for income potential", "Getting better grades for college", "Connecting to something bigger than themselves — serving others, building something, solving a problem they care about", "Winning competitions or awards"], correct: 2, explanation: "Purpose doesn't have to be grand. Volunteering at a shelter, tutoring younger kids, building a garden — these connect teens to meaning outside themselves. Motivation follows meaning, not the other way around." },
            { question: "According to Anderson and Winthrop, what re-engages disengaged teens most powerfully?", options: ["A new school with better programs", "Stricter consequences for not trying", "ONE caring adult who genuinely sees them and believes in them", "More interesting curriculum"], correct: 2, explanation: "The research consistently shows: one trusted adult who genuinely notices a teenager, remembers details, holds expectations, and communicates belief — whether a parent, coach, teacher, or mentor — is the most powerful re-engagement factor." },
            { question: "What is the 'passive to active' shift in teen re-engagement?", options: ["Moving from online to offline activities", "Shifting from consuming (scrolling, watching) to creating and building something they chose", "Moving from school to work experience", "Shifting from passive acceptance to advocacy"], correct: 1, explanation: "The shift from passive consumption (scrolling, gaming, watching) to active creation (making music, building something, coding, cooking, competing) reconnects teens to agency, skill, and the satisfaction of genuine accomplishment." },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-m21-l2-a4", type: "open_response" as any, title: "Purpose Finding", content: { prompt: "What does your teenager actually care about — even if it seems trivial? How could you connect that interest to a sense of purpose or real-world engagement? Write a plan for one experiment this month.", saveToVault: true }},
        ]
      }
    ]
  },
  // ─── MODULE NEW-A: SHAME RESILIENCE (Brené Brown — Daring Greatly) ──────
  {
    id: "kt-m-shame",
    title: "Shame Resilience in Your Family",
    subtitle: "Breaking the shame cycle — for you and your children",
    description: "Brené Brown's research in Daring Greatly reveals that shame is the most powerful, most destructive emotion in family life — and the least talked about. Understanding and interrupting the shame cycle transforms parenting from control to connection.",
    estimatedMinutes: 35,
    sourceBooks: ["Daring Greatly — Brené Brown"],
    sources: ["Shame Resilience Research", "Vulnerability Science"],
    lessons: [
      {
        id: "kt-shame-l1",
        title: "What Shame Actually Is",
        description: "The difference between guilt, shame, and why it matters profoundly",
        activities: [
          { id: "kt-shame-l1-a0", type: "reaction_slider" as any, title: "How Are You Feeling?", instruction: "Before we begin, take a moment to check in.", content: { question: "How often do you think shame (rather than guilt about behaviour) plays a role in your family's emotional life?", options: [
            { emoji: "😰", label: "All the time" },
            { emoji: "😕", label: "Quite often" },
            { emoji: "😐", label: "Sometimes" },
            { emoji: "🙂", label: "Rarely" },
            { emoji: "✅", label: "Almost never" },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-shame-l1-a1", type: "info_carousel" as any, title: "Shame vs Guilt", content: { slides: [
            { heading: "The Critical Distinction", body: "Brown's research makes a distinction that changes everything:\n\nGUILT: 'I did something bad' — the focus is on the BEHAVIOUR. It's motivating: 'I'm going to make this right.'\n\nSHAME: 'I AM bad' — the focus is on the SELF. It's destructive: it makes people want to hide, shut down, or lash out.\n\nGuilty people make amends. Ashamed people become defensive, aggressive, or implode. These require completely different responses." },
            { heading: "How Shame Shows Up in Parenting", body: "We accidentally activate shame in our children constantly:\n• 'You should be ashamed of yourself'\n• 'What were you THINKING?' (said with contempt)\n• 'Why can't you be more like your sister?'\n• Shaming in front of others\n• Withdrawing love as punishment\n• Eye rolls, sighs, disgust responses\n\nEach of these targets WHO THEY ARE, not WHAT THEY DID. Brown's research shows shame does not teach better behaviour — it teaches children to hide who they are." },
            { heading: "The Shame Spiral", body: "Brown identifies a shame spiral that goes:\n1. Trigger (criticism, rejection, failure, comparison)\n2. Internal message ('I am not good enough / I am defective')\n3. Physical response (heat, contraction, wanting to disappear)\n4. Behaviour: fight (aggression), flight (withdraw), freeze (shut down)\n5. Temporary relief then deeper shame ('I reacted badly, which proves I'm broken')\n\nNoticing WHERE IN THIS SPIRAL your child (or you) is, tells you exactly what they need." },
            { heading: "Your Own Shame History", body: "Brown is clear: you cannot give your child what you don't have. If shame was a frequent tool in your own upbringing, it will emerge under stress unless you've worked through it.\n\nCommon parent shame triggers:\n• Your child misbehaves in public\n• School feedback about your child\n• Comparison with 'better' parents\n• Losing your temper\n• Not meeting your own parenting standards\n\nWhen you feel shame as a parent, notice it. Name it. It needs to be witnessed, not acted on." },
          ]}},
          { id: "kt-shame-l1-a2", type: "flip_card" as any, title: "Shame vs Guilt: Key Concepts", instruction: "Flip each card to understand Brown's most important distinction and how shame operates in families.", content: { cards: [
            { front: "Guilt vs Shame", back: "GUILT: 'I did something bad' — focused on BEHAVIOUR. Motivating: 'I'm going to make this right.' SHAME: 'I AM bad' — focused on SELF. Destructive: it makes people hide, shut down, or lash out. Guilty people make amends. Ashamed people become defensive, aggressive, or implode.", emoji: "⚖️", tag: "The Difference" },
            { front: "How We Accidentally Shame Children", back: "Unintentional shaming: 'You should be ashamed of yourself.' 'Why can't you be more like your sister?' Shaming in front of others. Withdrawing love as punishment. Eye rolls, sighs, disgust responses. Each targets WHO THEY ARE, not WHAT THEY DID. Shame doesn't teach better behaviour — it teaches children to hide.", emoji: "⚠️", tag: "Accidental Shaming" },
            { front: "The Shame Spiral", back: "Trigger → Internal message ('I am not enough') → Physical response (heat, wanting to disappear) → Behaviour: fight, flight, or freeze → Temporary relief, then deeper shame ('I reacted badly — which proves I'm broken'). Knowing where in this spiral your child is tells you exactly what they need.", emoji: "🌀", tag: "The Spiral" },
            { front: "Your Own Shame History", back: "You can't give your child what you don't have. Common parent shame triggers: child misbehaves in public, school feedback about your child, losing your temper, comparison to 'better' parents. When you feel shame as a parent, notice it, name it. It needs to be witnessed — not acted on.", emoji: "🪞", tag: "Parent Shame" },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-shame-l1-a3", type: "single_choice" as any, title: "Check Your Understanding", content: { question: "Your 9-year-old cheats on a test. Which response targets guilt (the behaviour) rather than shame (the self)?", options: [
            { label: "'You should be ashamed of yourself — I raised you better than this'", isCorrect: false },
            { label: "'What were you THINKING?!' (with obvious disappointment and contempt)", isCorrect: false },
            { label: "'Cheating isn't okay. What happened — what were you trying to solve? Let's figure out a different way to handle this.'", isCorrect: true },
            { label: "Take away their favourite thing and tell them they've destroyed your trust", isCorrect: false },
          ], explanation: "Addressing the behaviour ('cheating isn't okay') while being curious about what drove it targets the action, not the child. Shame-based responses ('you should be ashamed', contempt) target identity and teach the child to hide, not improve." }},
          { id: "kt-shame-l1-a4", type: "knowledge_check" as any, title: "Knowledge Check", instruction: "Test what you've learned before moving on.", content: { intro: "Let's check your understanding of shame versus guilt.", passMark: 3, questions: [
            { question: "What is the key difference between guilt and shame according to Brown?", options: ["Guilt is worse than shame", "Guilt focuses on behaviour ('I did something bad'); shame focuses on self ('I AM bad')", "They are the same thing with different names", "Shame is only experienced by children"], correct: 1, explanation: "Brown's most important distinction: guilt targets what you DID (motivating — 'I'll make this right') while shame targets who you ARE (destructive — 'I need to hide'). This difference completely changes the parenting response needed." },
            { question: "Which parenting response accidentally activates shame rather than guilt?", options: ["'That behaviour isn't okay — tell me what happened'", "'You made a mistake — how can we make it right?'", "'You should be ashamed of yourself! I raised you better than this!'", "'Hitting hurts — I won't let you do that'"], correct: 2, explanation: "'You should be ashamed' targets identity ('you are someone who should be ashamed'). Shame-based responses teach children to hide who they are rather than change what they do. Behaviour-focused responses teach accountability without attacking personhood." },
            { question: "What typically follows the 'shame spiral'?", options: ["Improved behaviour", "Reflection and remorse", "Fight, flight, or freeze behaviour, then deeper shame when the child reacts badly", "A calm conversation about the incident"], correct: 2, explanation: "The shame spiral leads to defensive or explosive behaviour (fight, flight, freeze), which then triggers more shame: 'I reacted badly — which proves I'm broken.' This self-reinforcing cycle explains why shame leads to escalation rather than improvement." },
            { question: "Brown states that you cannot give your child shame resilience if:", options: ["You don't read books about parenting", "You work too many hours", "You haven't done your own shame work — you can only give what you have", "Your parents were not good parents"], correct: 2, explanation: "Shame resilience in children requires parents who have developed their own capacity to recognise and metabolise shame. If shame triggers in you lead to reactivity you haven't examined, that pattern transmits to your children regardless of your intentions." },
          ] } },
        ]
      },
      {
        id: "kt-shame-l2",
        title: "Building Shame Resilience",
        description: "Brown's four-element framework for families",
        activities: [
          { id: "kt-shame-l2-a0", type: "reaction_slider" as any, title: "How Are You Feeling?", instruction: "Before we begin, take a moment to reflect.", content: { question: "How equipped do you feel to help your child develop shame resilience — the ability to recognise and metabolise shame without being defined by it?", options: [
            { emoji: "😰", label: "Not equipped at all" },
            { emoji: "😕", label: "Quite unsure" },
            { emoji: "😐", label: "Somewhat ready" },
            { emoji: "🙂", label: "Fairly equipped" },
            { emoji: "💪", label: "Very equipped" },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-shame-l2-a1", type: "info_carousel" as any, title: "The Resilience Framework", content: { slides: [
            { heading: "Element 1: Recognise Shame", body: "Help your child name what they're feeling in moments of shame: 'That felt humiliating, didn't it? Like you wanted to disappear?'\n\nChildren who can name shame develop it less. Naming creates distance: 'I'm feeling shame' rather than 'I AM shameful.'\n\nNormalise it: 'Everyone feels this sometimes. Even grown-ups. Even me.' Share a time you felt it. Brown says empathy is the antidote to shame — it cannot survive being spoken out loud and met with kindness." },
            { heading: "Element 2: Reality-Test the Message", body: "Shame sends a message: 'You are defective/not enough/unlovable.' This message is almost never accurate.\n\nHelp children examine it:\n• 'Your brain is telling you that you're stupid because you got a question wrong. Is that actually true?'\n• 'Your shame is saying everyone hates you. What's the actual evidence?'\n• 'You made a bad choice. That's different from being a bad person.'\n\nReality-testing is a skill. It takes practice. Start young." },
            { heading: "Element 3: Reach Out", body: "Shame needs secrecy to survive. Vulnerability kills it.\n\nTeach your child that shame reduces when we talk to a safe person. Brown says: 'Shame cannot survive being spoken out loud to someone who loves you.'\n\nTo be that safe person, they need to know:\n• You won't punish them for being honest\n• You won't change how you feel about them\n• You've felt it too\n• The relationship is bigger than any mistake\n\nEvery time you create safety for honesty, you're building their shame resilience." },
            { heading: "Element 4: Speak Shame", body: "Brown's most powerful tool: learn the language of shame.\n\nInstead of: 'I'm so stupid'\nTry teaching: 'I'm having a shame story — I'm telling myself I'm stupid because I made a mistake. But mistakes don't mean I'm stupid.'\n\nInstead of: (withdrawing, going quiet, hiding)\nTry teaching: 'I feel ashamed right now. I'm going to tell someone I trust.'\n\nThis requires YOU to model it first: 'I messed up at work today and part of me started to feel like a failure. I had to remind myself that one mistake doesn't define me.'" },
          ]}},
          { id: "kt-shame-l2-a2", type: "flip_card" as any, title: "Building Shame Resilience", instruction: "Flip each card to understand Brown's four elements of shame resilience for families.", content: { cards: [
            { front: "Recognise Shame", back: "Help your child name what they're feeling: 'That felt humiliating, didn't it? Like you wanted to disappear?' Children who can name shame develop it less — naming creates distance: 'I'm feeling shame' rather than 'I AM shameful.' Normalise it: 'Everyone feels this sometimes. Even grown-ups. Even me.'", emoji: "🏷️", tag: "Element 1: Recognise" },
            { front: "Reality-Test the Message", back: "Shame sends a message: 'You are defective/not enough/unlovable.' Help children examine it: 'Your brain is telling you you're stupid because you got a question wrong. Is that actually true?' 'You made a bad choice — that's different from being a bad person.' Reality-testing is a skill that takes practice.", emoji: "🔍", tag: "Element 2: Reality-Test" },
            { front: "Reach Out", back: "Shame needs secrecy to survive. Vulnerability kills it. Teach: shame reduces when you talk to a safe person. Brown: 'Shame cannot survive being spoken out loud to someone who loves you.' To be that safe person: don't punish honesty, don't change how you feel about them, the relationship is bigger than any mistake.", emoji: "🤝", tag: "Element 3: Reach Out" },
            { front: "Speak Shame", back: "Teach the language: Instead of 'I'm so stupid,' try: 'I'm having a shame story — I'm telling myself I'm stupid because I made a mistake. Mistakes don't mean I'm stupid.' YOU must model it first: 'I messed up at work and started feeling like a failure. I had to remind myself one mistake doesn't define me.'", emoji: "💬", tag: "Element 4: Speak Shame" },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-shame-l2-a3", type: "knowledge_check" as any, title: "Knowledge Check", instruction: "Test what you've learned before moving on.", content: { intro: "Let's check your understanding of building shame resilience in your family.", passMark: 3, questions: [
            { question: "Why does naming shame help reduce its power?", options: ["It makes the child feel better immediately", "Naming creates distance from the experience — 'I'm feeling shame' is different from 'I AM shameful'", "It teaches children to talk about their feelings", "It tells parents when to intervene"], correct: 1, explanation: "Naming creates psychological distance. 'I'm feeling shame right now' positions shame as a temporary experience rather than a fixed identity. This distance allows the child to observe the emotion rather than be consumed by it." },
            { question: "When a child says 'I'm so stupid after getting a question wrong,' the shame resilience response is:", options: ["'Don't say that — you're not stupid'", "'Everyone makes mistakes'", "'Your brain is telling you you're stupid because you made a mistake — is that actually true? Mistakes don't mean you're stupid'", "'You should have studied harder'"], correct: 2, explanation: "Reality-testing addresses the shame message directly and specifically. It acknowledges what the internal voice is saying, then examines the evidence — 'is that ACTUALLY true?' — building the child's capacity to challenge shame-based thinking." },
            { question: "Brown says 'Shame cannot survive being spoken out loud to someone who loves you.' What does this teach us?", options: ["Children should always talk about their feelings", "To be shame-resilient, children need a safe adult who won't punish honesty or change how they feel about them", "Shame always goes away when you talk about it", "Parents should share everything about their children's shame"], correct: 1, explanation: "Shame thrives in secrecy and silence. The antidote is speaking it aloud to a trusted person — which requires that the child knows the relationship can hold their worst moments without rejection. Every time you create that safety, you build their resilience." },
            { question: "Why must parents model 'speaking shame' before teaching it to their children?", options: ["Children learn by imitation, so parents must demonstrate first", "It makes parents seem more relatable", "Because children will only adopt shame language if they've seen an adult use it authentically", "Parents need practice too"], correct: 0, explanation: "Children learn by watching, not just by being told. A parent who says 'I messed up and started feeling like a failure — I had to remind myself one mistake doesn't define me' demonstrates shame language authentically. This gives children permission and a model to follow." },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-shame-l2-a4", type: "open_response" as any, title: "Your Family Shame Patterns", content: { prompt: "What shame messages did you receive growing up? ('You should be ashamed', comparisons, public embarrassment?) How have these shaped your parenting? What shame-based habit do you most want to change?", saveToVault: true }},
        ]
      },
      {
        id: "kt-shame-l3",
        title: "Vulnerability as a Parenting Practice",
        description: "How choosing courage in front of your children changes everything",
        activities: [
          { id: "kt-shame-l3-a0", type: "reaction_slider" as any, title: "How Are You Feeling?", instruction: "Before we begin, take a moment to reflect.", content: { question: "How often do you choose vulnerability and authenticity with your children — showing them who you really are, including your struggles?", options: [
            { emoji: "😰", label: "Almost never" },
            { emoji: "😕", label: "Rarely" },
            { emoji: "😐", label: "Sometimes" },
            { emoji: "🙂", label: "Often" },
            { emoji: "🌟", label: "Very often" },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-shame-l3-a1", type: "info_carousel" as any, title: "Daring Greatly as a Parent", content: { slides: [
            { heading: "Wholehearted Parenting", body: "Brown's concept of 'wholehearted parenting': showing up with your whole self — imperfections included — rather than trying to model impossible perfection.\n\nWholehearted parents:\n• Acknowledge their mistakes out loud\n• Share age-appropriate struggles\n• Say 'I don't know' rather than projecting false confidence\n• Ask for help rather than pretending to have it together\n• Talk about emotions — including their own\n\nThe irony: admitting fallibility makes you more trustworthy to your children, not less." },
            { heading: "Protecting Kids from Failure: The Backfire", body: "Brown identifies a parenting paradox: the more we try to protect our children from disappointment, failure, and pain, the less capable they become of handling it.\n\n'Never let them fail' teaches: the world is too dangerous for you to handle alone. You need me to make it safe.\n'I believe you can handle this' teaches: you have what it takes. Hard things are survivable.\n\nBeing willing to let your child struggle in supported ways is one of the most loving, courageous things you can do." },
            { heading: "The 'Enough' Conversation", body: "One of the most powerful things you can do for your child: tell them explicitly — not in response to achievement but simply and often — that they are ENOUGH.\n\n'You don't have to earn my love. You already have it.'\n'You being you is what I love — not your grades/performance/behaviour.'\n'You are enough exactly as you are.'\n\nBrown's research shows children who believe they are inherently worthy — separate from what they achieve — are more resilient, more connected, and more capable than those who must prove their worth." },
          ]}},
          { id: "kt-shame-l3-a2", type: "single_choice" as any, title: "Daring Greatly Practice", content: { question: "Your teenage daughter is about to try out for the school play and is terrified of failing. What does 'daring greatly' look like as her parent?", options: [
            { label: "'You'll definitely get it — you're so talented!'", isCorrect: false },
            { label: "'I know this is scary. Trying when you might fail is the bravest thing. I'm proud of you for showing up.'", isCorrect: true },
            { label: "'Just don't bother if you're not confident you'll get in'", isCorrect: false },
            { label: "'I'll talk to the drama teacher to make sure they see how good you are'", isCorrect: false },
          ], explanation: "Brown's 'daring greatly' is about showing up vulnerably, not winning. False reassurance ('you'll definitely get it') sets up shame if they don't. The courageous message is: the act of trying — not the outcome — is what you're celebrating." }},
          { id: "kt-shame-l3-a3", type: "flip_card" as any, title: "Vulnerability as Parenting Practice", instruction: "Flip each card to understand how choosing courage in front of your children changes everything.", content: { cards: [
            { front: "Wholehearted Parenting", back: "Wholehearted parents show up with their whole self — imperfections included — rather than performing impossible perfection. They acknowledge mistakes, share age-appropriate struggles, say 'I don't know', ask for help, and talk about emotions including their own. Admitting fallibility makes you MORE trustworthy, not less.", emoji: "🌕", tag: "Wholehearted" },
            { front: "The Failure Paradox", back: "The more we protect children from disappointment, failure, and pain, the less capable they become of handling it. 'Never let them fail' teaches: the world is too dangerous for you. 'I believe you can handle this' teaches: you have what it takes. Supported struggle is one of the most loving things you can do.", emoji: "🔄", tag: "Letting Them Struggle" },
            { front: "The 'Enough' Conversation", back: "One of the most powerful things you can do: tell your child explicitly — not in response to achievement but simply and often — that they are ENOUGH. 'You don't have to earn my love. You already have it.' 'You being you is what I love.' Brown's research: children who believe they are inherently worthy are more resilient and capable.", emoji: "💎", tag: "You Are Enough" },
            { front: "Celebrating the Try", back: "'Daring greatly' is about showing up vulnerably, not winning. False reassurance ('you'll definitely get the part') sets up shame if they don't succeed. The courageous message: 'I know this is scary. Trying when you might fail is the bravest thing. I'm proud of you for showing up.' The act of trying is what matters.", emoji: "🦁", tag: "Daring Greatly" },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-shame-l3-a4", type: "knowledge_check" as any, title: "Knowledge Check", instruction: "Test what you've learned before moving on.", content: { intro: "Let's check your understanding of vulnerability and wholehearted parenting.", passMark: 3, questions: [
            { question: "What does Brown mean by 'wholehearted parenting'?", options: ["Being a perfect parent who never makes mistakes", "Showing up with your whole self — imperfections included — rather than performing impossible perfection", "Being very emotionally expressive all the time", "Giving your child your complete attention 24/7"], correct: 1, explanation: "Wholehearted parenting means being authentic — acknowledging mistakes, sharing struggles, saying 'I don't know,' and asking for help. The counterintuitive reality: showing vulnerability makes parents MORE trustworthy and relatable, not less." },
            { question: "What is the 'failure paradox' Brown identifies?", options: ["Failure always leads to success eventually", "The more we protect children from failure, the less capable they become of handling it", "Children who fail more often become more successful", "Parents who fail are setting a bad example"], correct: 1, explanation: "Brown identifies this paradox: our instinct to protect children from pain actually reduces their capacity to handle it. Children who experience supported struggle — who are allowed to fail with a caring adult nearby — develop genuine resilience." },
            { question: "When should you tell your child they are 'enough'?", options: ["After they achieve something impressive", "When they're feeling bad about themselves", "Not in response to achievement, but simply and often — regardless of performance", "When they ask for reassurance"], correct: 2, explanation: "Unconditional worth means communicating 'you are enough' as a statement of being, not as a response to doing. Children who receive this unconditionally — not just after achievements — develop inherent self-worth that isn't contingent on performance." },
            { question: "What is the most courageous response when your child is about to try something they might fail at?", options: ["'You'll definitely succeed — I know it!'", "'Maybe try something easier first'", "'I know this is scary. Trying when you might fail is the bravest thing. I'm proud of you for showing up.'", "'Don't bother if you're not confident'"], correct: 2, explanation: "False reassurance ('you'll definitely succeed') sets up shame if they don't. Brown's 'daring greatly' celebrates the act of showing up vulnerably — not the outcome. Praising the courage to try rather than the result builds resilience and shame resistance." },
          ] } },
        ]
      }
    ]

  // ─── MODULE NEW-B: BELONGING vs FITTING IN (Brené Brown — Braving the Wilderness) ──
  {
    id: "kt-m-belonging",
    title: "True Belonging vs Fitting In",
    subtitle: "Teaching your child to belong to themselves first",
    description: "In Braving the Wilderness, Brené Brown makes a distinction that hits hardest for teenagers: true belonging requires you to be yourself. Fitting in requires you to be what the group wants. These two things are opposites — and learning to tell them apart changes everything.",
    estimatedMinutes: 25,
    sourceBooks: ["Braving the Wilderness — Brené Brown"],
    sources: ["Belonging Research", "Identity Development"],
    lessons: [
      {
        id: "kt-belong-l1",
        title: "The Difference That Changes Everything",
        description: "Why the most popular kids are often the loneliest",
        activities: [
          { id: "kt-belong-l1-a0", type: "reaction_slider" as any, title: "How Are You Feeling?", instruction: "Before we begin, take a moment to reflect.", content: { question: "How confident are you that your child has a strong enough sense of self to be themselves even under peer pressure?", options: [
            { emoji: "😰", label: "Very worried" },
            { emoji: "😕", label: "Concerned" },
            { emoji: "😐", label: "Somewhat confident" },
            { emoji: "🙂", label: "Fairly confident" },
            { emoji: "💪", label: "Very confident" },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-belong-l1-a1", type: "info_carousel" as any, title: "Belonging vs Fitting In", content: { slides: [
            { heading: "Brown's Critical Distinction", body: "Brown defines belonging as 'the innate human desire to be part of something larger than us. But it must not require us to change who we are.'\n\nFitting in is the opposite: assessing a group and changing yourself to match what's required.\n\nThe cruel paradox: teenagers who are best at 'fitting in' — who are most chameleon-like and socially strategic — often feel the most profoundly alone. They've never been truly seen, because they never show their true self." },
            { heading: "Belonging Starts With Self", body: "Brown's most counter-intuitive finding: TRUE belonging requires belonging to yourself first.\n\nThis means:\n• Knowing what you actually think, value, and feel (not what you're supposed to think/value/feel)\n• Being willing to stand alone in your own opinion\n• Tolerating the discomfort of not fitting in rather than betraying who you are\n\nThis is rare. It's the work of adolescence. And it's the exact thing that reduces loneliness." },
            { heading: "The Wilderness", body: "Brown uses 'the wilderness' as a metaphor for the experience of true belonging: it feels exposed and dangerous, but it's also where genuine connection is found.\n\nShe identifies people who have 'the wilderness' — who can be in a group without losing themselves, disagree without being disagreeable, and hold their opinion while genuinely staying open to others.\n\nThis is the capacity your child is building during adolescence. It's messy. It's supposed to be." },
          ]}},
          { id: "kt-belong-l1-a2", type: "flip_card" as any, title: "True Belonging vs Fitting In", instruction: "Flip each card to understand Brown's critical distinction and what it means for your child.", content: { cards: [
            { front: "The Core Distinction", back: "BELONGING: Being part of something while being fully yourself — you don't have to change who you are. FITTING IN: Assessing a group and changing yourself to match what's required. These are opposites. The teens who are best at fitting in — the social chameleons — often feel the most profoundly alone because they've never been truly seen.", emoji: "🔑", tag: "The Distinction" },
            { front: "Belonging Starts With Self", back: "True belonging requires belonging to YOURSELF first. This means: knowing what you actually think, value, and feel (not what you're supposed to). Being willing to stand alone in your opinion. Tolerating discomfort of not fitting in rather than betraying yourself. This is the core work of adolescence.", emoji: "🧭", tag: "Belonging to Self" },
            { front: "The Wilderness Metaphor", back: "Brown's 'wilderness' is a metaphor for true belonging — it feels exposed and dangerous, but it's where genuine connection is found. People who 'have the wilderness' can be in a group without losing themselves, disagree without being disagreeable, and hold their own opinion while remaining genuinely open.", emoji: "🌲", tag: "The Wilderness" },
            { front: "The Lonely Crowd", back: "The cruelest paradox: socially successful teenagers — those included in everything — are often among the loneliest. Because they're performing, not connecting. They've never been truly known because they never show their true self. True connection requires authenticity, not performance.", emoji: "👥", tag: "The Paradox" },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-belong-l1-a3", type: "knowledge_check" as any, title: "Knowledge Check", instruction: "Test what you've learned before moving on.", content: { intro: "Let's check your understanding of belonging versus fitting in.", passMark: 3, questions: [
            { question: "According to Brown, what is 'fitting in'?", options: ["The same as belonging", "A healthy form of social adaptation", "Assessing a group and changing yourself to match what's required — the opposite of belonging", "Being included in social groups"], correct: 2, explanation: "Brown makes a critical distinction: fitting in requires you to change yourself to match the group. Belonging requires you to be yourself and be accepted. These are fundamentally different experiences, even though they may look similar from the outside." },
            { question: "Why do socially popular teenagers sometimes feel the loneliest?", options: ["They have too many shallow friendships", "They're performing rather than connecting — having never shown their true self, they've never been truly known", "Popularity is always associated with loneliness", "They don't have time for real friendships"], correct: 1, explanation: "When social success requires constant performance and adaptation, the teenager is always managing impressions rather than making genuine contact. The result: surrounded by people who like the performance, but known by no one." },
            { question: "What does 'belonging to yourself' require?", options: ["Being introverted and self-sufficient", "Knowing your values and being willing to stand alone rather than betray who you are", "Not caring what other people think", "Being popular enough to not need others' approval"], correct: 1, explanation: "Self-belonging means knowing your actual values, thoughts, and feelings — and being willing to tolerate social discomfort rather than abandon them. This is the foundation of all genuine belonging — you cannot connect authentically until you know yourself." },
            { question: "Brown's 'wilderness' metaphor describes:", options: ["The isolation of social rejection", "The feeling of belonging to yourself — exposed and uncomfortable but where genuine connection lives", "The teenage years in general", "The experience of being an outsider at school"], correct: 1, explanation: "The 'wilderness' is Brown's image for the experience of standing in your own truth — uncomfortable, exposed, but authentic. People who can do this (be themselves even when the group expects something different) experience the deepest genuine connection." },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-belong-l1-a4", type: "true_false" as any, title: "Check", content: { statement: "A teenager with a large friend group who is included in everything is unlikely to feel lonely.", isTrue: false, explanation: "Brown's research shows widespread social belonging (fitting in with many groups) and true belonging (being genuinely known and accepted) are entirely different. Many socially successful teenagers report profound loneliness because they're performing, not connecting. True connection comes from authenticity — being known for who you actually are." }},
        ]
      },
      {
        id: "kt-belong-l2",
        title: "Raising Socially Brave Kids",
        description: "Practical strategies for authentic belonging",
        activities: [
          { id: "kt-belong-l2-a0", type: "reaction_slider" as any, title: "How Are You Feeling?", instruction: "Before we begin, take a moment to reflect.", content: { question: "How socially brave would you say your child is — able to be themselves even when the group expects something different?", options: [
            { emoji: "😰", label: "Conforms completely" },
            { emoji: "😕", label: "Often conforms" },
            { emoji: "😐", label: "Sometimes themselves" },
            { emoji: "🙂", label: "Usually themselves" },
            { emoji: "🦁", label: "Very socially brave" },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-belong-l2-a1", type: "info_carousel" as any, title: "Social Courage", content: { slides: [
            { heading: "The Courage to Disagree", body: "Brown calls this 'civility' — the ability to hold your ground in disagreement without needing the other person to be wrong.\n\nHelp your child practise:\n• 'I see it differently'\n• 'I'm not sure I agree'\n• 'That doesn't feel right to me'\n• 'I hear you, and I think...' (not 'but')\n\nDo this at home first. A family dinner table where differing opinions are welcomed without consequences is the training ground for social courage." },
            { heading: "Teaching Values, Not Rules", body: "Rules tell children what to do when you're watching. Values guide them when you're not.\n\nHelp them build their values through questions, not lectures:\n• 'What kind of friend do YOU want to be?'\n• 'What does fairness mean to you?'\n• 'What would you think of yourself if you did that?'\n• 'In 10 years, what will you be glad you stood for?'\n\nChildren who can articulate their values have an anchor when peer pressure hits. They can say 'That's not who I am' rather than needing to justify 'no' with an excuse." },
            { heading: "Model Belonging to Yourself", body: "Brown's challenge to parents: do YOU belong to yourself? Or do you perform for others, avoid conflict at the cost of honesty, and change your behaviour based on the room?\n\nChildren who watch their parents:\n• Hold opinions under social pressure\n• Acknowledge when they're wrong without shame\n• Say 'no' without excessive justification\n• Share genuine feelings (appropriately)\n• Include people on the margins\n\n...learn that it's possible to belong without performing. You are their template." },
            { heading: "People-Pleasing vs Kindness", body: "Help your child see the difference:\n\nKINDNESS: I want to do something good for you.\nPEOPLE-PLEASING: I'm doing this so you'll like me / won't be angry / won't reject me.\n\nKindness is strong and confident. People-pleasing is anxious and exhausting.\n\nSigns of people-pleasing in children: saying yes when they mean no, apologising for things that aren't their fault, changing their opinion when challenged, inability to disappoint anyone.\n\nAddress this early — it tends to intensify and can contribute to significant anxiety and burnout." },
          ]}},
          { id: "kt-belong-l2-a2", type: "flip_card" as any, title: "Raising Socially Brave Kids", instruction: "Flip each card to discover practical strategies for helping your child develop authentic social courage.", content: { cards: [
            { front: "The Courage to Disagree", back: "Brown calls this 'civility' — holding your ground in disagreement without needing the other person to be wrong. Teach phrases: 'I see it differently.' 'I'm not sure I agree.' 'That doesn't feel right to me.' 'I hear you, and I think...' Practise this at the dinner table first.", emoji: "💬", tag: "Disagreeing Well" },
            { front: "Values, Not Rules", back: "Rules tell children what to do when you're watching. Values guide them when you're not. Teach through questions: 'What kind of friend do YOU want to be?' 'What does fairness mean to you?' 'In 10 years, what will you be glad you stood for?' Children with clear values can say 'That's not who I am' when under pressure.", emoji: "⚓", tag: "Values" },
            { front: "People-Pleasing vs Kindness", back: "KINDNESS: 'I want to do something good for you.' PEOPLE-PLEASING: 'I'm doing this so you'll like me / won't be angry / won't reject me.' Kindness is strong and confident. People-pleasing is anxious and exhausting. Signs: saying yes when meaning no, apologising for things that aren't their fault, changing opinions when challenged.", emoji: "⚖️", tag: "People-Pleasing" },
            { front: "You Are the Template", back: "Do YOU belong to yourself? Do you perform for others, avoid conflict at the cost of honesty, change your behaviour based on the room? Children who watch parents hold opinions under pressure, acknowledge when wrong, say 'no' without excessive justification, and include people on the margins — learn it's possible.", emoji: "🪞", tag: "Your Role" },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-belong-l2-a3", type: "knowledge_check" as any, title: "Knowledge Check", instruction: "Test what you've learned before moving on.", content: { intro: "Let's check your understanding of raising socially brave children.", passMark: 3, questions: [
            { question: "What is the difference between kindness and people-pleasing?", options: ["There is no real difference — both come from wanting to help", "Kindness is motivated by genuine care; people-pleasing is motivated by fear of rejection or disapproval", "People-pleasing is more selfless than kindness", "Kindness is external; people-pleasing is internal"], correct: 1, explanation: "Kindness comes from a place of genuine generosity — you WANT to do good for the other person. People-pleasing comes from anxiety — you're doing it to be liked, to avoid disapproval, or to prevent rejection. The action may look the same; the motivation is completely different." },
            { question: "Why are values more powerful than rules for guiding children's behaviour?", options: ["Rules are harder to remember than values", "Values are more flexible than rules", "Rules only work when someone's watching; values guide children when no adult is present", "Values are easier to teach"], correct: 2, explanation: "Rules require external enforcement — someone watching and consequence following. Values are internalised — they guide decision-making even when no adult is present, even when no one will know. 'What kind of person do I want to be?' is a more powerful question than 'What's the rule here?'" },
            { question: "Brown's concept of 'civility' means:", options: ["Being polite at all times", "The ability to hold your ground in disagreement without needing the other person to be wrong — disagreeing while staying connected", "Avoiding conflict to maintain harmony", "Being diplomatic in difficult conversations"], correct: 1, explanation: "Civility, for Brown, is the social courage to maintain your own position while remaining genuinely open to others. You can say 'I see it differently' without aggression or capitulation — holding your view while respecting theirs." },
            { question: "People-pleasing in children is a concern because:", options: ["It makes them too agreeable at school", "It tends to intensify and can contribute to significant anxiety and burnout as they consistently betray their own needs", "It reduces academic ambition", "It makes them bad leaders"], correct: 1, explanation: "People-pleasing creates a pattern of saying yes when meaning no, suppressing real opinions, and apologising for things that aren't their fault. Sustained over time, this erodes identity, creates resentment, and can lead to serious anxiety and emotional exhaustion." },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-belong-l2-a4", type: "open_response" as any, title: "Belonging Audit", content: { prompt: "Does your child 'fit in' or do they 'belong' in their main social group? When do you see them being most authentically themselves? What would help them feel safe showing up as themselves more often?", saveToVault: true }},
        ]
      },
      {
        id: "kt-belong-l3",
        title: "The Loneliness Epidemic",
        description: "Why connection is the most urgent issue for teenagers today",
        activities: [
          { id: "kt-belong-l3-a0", type: "reaction_slider" as any, title: "How Are You Feeling?", instruction: "Before we begin, take a moment to reflect.", content: { question: "How often does your child experience GENUINE connection — being truly known and accepted — rather than just social performance?", options: [
            { emoji: "😰", label: "Almost never" },
            { emoji: "😕", label: "Rarely" },
            { emoji: "😐", label: "Sometimes" },
            { emoji: "🙂", label: "Often" },
            { emoji: "🌟", label: "Frequently" },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-belong-l3-a1", type: "info_carousel" as any, title: "Connected but Lonely", content: { slides: [
            { heading: "The Paradox of the Connected Generation", body: "Today's teenagers are the most socially 'connected' generation in history — and one of the loneliest. Brown and subsequent researchers point to the same culprit: the substitution of performance (social media) for presence (real connection).\n\nDigital communication provides the appearance of belonging without the vulnerability that creates actual belonging. You can have 1000 followers and feel completely unknown.\n\nThe antidote isn't less technology — it's more genuine presence." },
            { heading: "What Real Connection Requires", body: "Brown's definition of connection: 'the energy that exists between people when they feel seen, heard, and valued.'\n\nThis cannot happen:\n• In a group chat\n• Through likes\n• In a performance\n• Through consensus-seeking\n\nIt CAN happen:\n• In one-on-one conversations\n• When you share something real\n• When you disagree and stay close\n• When you're seen at your worst and still wanted\n• In shared experience (sport, cooking, creative projects, adventure)" },
            { heading: "Creating Conditions for Real Connection", body: "Practical actions to help your teenager find genuine belonging:\n\n• Facilitate one-on-one time with friends (not group hangs, which are performance-heavy)\n• Encourage shared-activity friendships (teams, bands, volunteering, creating things)\n• Reduce social media's dominance — physical presence is irreplaceable\n• Create a home where friends want to come, feel comfortable, and are genuinely welcomed\n• Ask your teen: 'Is there anyone at school who feels left out? Could you include them this week?'\n\nThe smallest acts of genuine inclusion are powerful beyond their apparent size." },
          ]}},
          { id: "kt-belong-l3-a2", type: "flip_card" as any, title: "The Loneliness Epidemic & Creating Real Connection", instruction: "Flip each card to understand the loneliness crisis and what creates genuine belonging.", content: { cards: [
            { front: "The Connection Paradox", back: "Today's teenagers are the most socially 'connected' generation in history — and one of the loneliest. Digital communication provides the appearance of belonging without the vulnerability that creates actual belonging. You can have 1000 followers and feel completely unknown.", emoji: "📱", tag: "The Paradox" },
            { front: "What Real Connection Requires", back: "Brown: connection is 'the energy that exists between people when they feel seen, heard, and valued.' This cannot happen in a group chat, through likes, or in a performance. It CAN happen in 1:1 conversations, when you share something real, when you disagree and stay close, when you're seen at your worst and still wanted.", emoji: "❤️", tag: "Real Connection" },
            { front: "Create Conditions for Belonging", back: "Facilitate 1:1 time with friends (not just group hangs, which are performance-heavy). Encourage shared-activity friendships (teams, bands, volunteering). Create a home where friends want to come and feel genuinely welcomed. Ask your teen: 'Is there anyone at school who feels left out? Could you include them?'", emoji: "🏡", tag: "Creating Conditions" },
            { front: "Smallest Acts Count", back: "The smallest acts of genuine inclusion are powerful beyond their apparent size. One teenager who decides to include the left-out person, invite the new kid, or sit with someone eating alone — creates belonging in their world. These acts also build that teenager's sense of who they are.", emoji: "🌱", tag: "Small Acts" },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-belong-l3-a3", type: "knowledge_check" as any, title: "Knowledge Check", instruction: "Test what you've learned before moving on.", content: { intro: "Let's check your understanding of the loneliness epidemic and creating genuine connection.", passMark: 3, questions: [
            { question: "What does Brown identify as the main reason highly connected teenagers can still feel profoundly lonely?", options: ["They have too many friendships to maintain", "Digital connection provides the appearance of belonging without the vulnerability that creates real belonging", "Teenagers are naturally lonely", "Social media platforms are poorly designed"], correct: 1, explanation: "Digital connection allows teenagers to maintain social presence without genuine vulnerability. You can be visible to hundreds of people without being truly known by any of them. Real connection requires being seen, heard, and valued — which requires actual presence and authenticity." },
            { question: "According to Brown, real connection 'cannot happen in a group chat' because:", options: ["Group chats are too distracting", "Technology is unreliable", "Group settings are performance-heavy — true connection requires 1:1 vulnerability, not social performance", "Young people don't communicate well through text"], correct: 2, explanation: "Group interactions — whether digital or physical — activate performance mode. Real connection, as Brown defines it, requires the vulnerability of being genuinely seen and valued — which happens most readily in 1:1 presence, not group performance." },
            { question: "What type of friendships most reliably creates genuine belonging for teenagers?", options: ["Large friend groups with many connections", "Online communities with shared interests", "Shared-activity friendships (teams, bands, volunteering, creating things)", "Friendships with the most popular students"], correct: 2, explanation: "Shared-activity friendships — where teens are building something, competing together, or serving a common cause — create genuine connection through common experience, mutual dependence, and authentic interaction. These conditions create belonging naturally." },
            { question: "Why do 'small acts of genuine inclusion' matter so much?", options: ["They don't — only large gestures count", "They create belonging for the recipient AND build identity and character in the teen who acts", "They make teens popular", "They are required by school codes of conduct"], correct: 1, explanation: "Acts of inclusion matter for both parties. The person included experiences belonging. The teenager who chooses to include builds their own identity — 'I am someone who includes people' — which reinforces their values and character for future social decisions." },
          ] } },
          { id: "kt-belong-l3-a4", type: "open_response" as any, title: "Connection Plan", content: { prompt: "When does your child experience GENUINE connection — not performing, not scrolling, but actually being known? How can you create more of those conditions this month?", saveToVault: true }},
        ]
      }
    ]
  },
  // ─── MODULE 22: ANXIETY DEEP DIVE — SPECIFIC AGES (Goff) ──────────────
  {
    id: "kt-m22",
    title: "Anxiety by Age & Stage",
    subtitle: "What worry looks like at every age — and exactly what to do",
    description: "Sissy Goff's age-specific anxiety strategies help you recognise what's normal worry, what's clinical anxiety, and how to support your child at every developmental stage — from separation anxiety at 2 to existential dread at 16.",

    sourceBooks: ["Raising Worry-Free Girls — Sissy Goff"],
    sources: ["Anxiety Research", "Developmental Psychology"],
    lessons: [
      {
        id: "kt-m22-l1",
        title: "Early Childhood Anxiety (Ages 2–7)",
        description: "Separation fears, monsters, and new situations",
        activities: [
          { id: "kt-m22-l1-a0", type: "reaction_slider" as any, title: "How Are You Feeling?", instruction: "Before we begin, take a moment to reflect.", content: { question: "How would you rate your young child's (ages 2-7) current anxiety or worry level?", options: [
            { emoji: "😰", label: "Very anxious" },
            { emoji: "😕", label: "Quite worried" },
            { emoji: "😐", label: "Some normal fears" },
            { emoji: "🙂", label: "Generally settled" },
            { emoji: "✅", label: "Very secure" },
```

```ts
 */
```

## `src/data/practices.ts`

```ts
// ── Practice Data Model ─────────────────────────────────────

import { somaticScripts } from "./somatic-scripts";

export type PracticeMode = "timed-breath" | "narrated-sequence";
export type PracticeCategory = "breathwork" | "somatic" | "meditation";
export type AudioProvider = "elevenlabs" | "manual-upload";

export interface BreathPhase {
  label: string;
  seconds: number;
  cue?: string;
}

export interface PracticeStep {
  id: string;
  title: string;
  body: string;
  startTimeSec?: number;
  endTimeSec?: number;
}

export interface PracticeAudio {
  enabled: boolean;
  audioUrl?: string;
  durationSec?: number;
  voiceName?: string;
  provider?: AudioProvider;
}

export interface PracticeConfig {
  id: string;
  title: string;
  subtitle?: string;
  category: PracticeCategory;
  mode: PracticeMode;
  durationSec: number;
  audio: PracticeAudio;
  phases?: BreathPhase[];
  rounds?: number;
  steps?: PracticeStep[];
  /** @deprecated Use illustrationUrl instead */
  emoji?: string;
  illustrationUrl?: string;
  benefit?: string;
  // future-ready fields
  locale?: string;
  backgroundAudioUrl?: string;
  ttsScript?: string;
  /** ElevenLabs voice id override (per-script). */
  ttsVoiceId?: string;
  /** Marks this practice as a sleep reading — uses slower, sleep-tuned voice settings. */
  ttsIsSleep?: boolean;
  /** Free-text source/author used to auto-pick a voice when ttsVoiceId is absent. */
  ttsEvidenceSource?: string;
  voiceId?: string;
}

// ── Breathwork Practices ────────────────────────────────────

export const BREATHWORK_PRACTICES: PracticeConfig[] = [
  {
    id: "box-breathing",
    title: "Box Breathing",
    subtitle: "Acute stress and focus",
    category: "breathwork",
    mode: "timed-breath",
    durationSec: 192,
    rounds: 12,
    emoji: "◻",
    benefit: "Equalises all four phases of the breath to create immediate nervous system balance.",
    audio: {
      enabled: true,
      audioUrl: "/audio/box-breathing.mp3",
      durationSec: 192,
      voiceName: "SIGNAL Calm",
      provider: "elevenlabs",
    },
    phases: [
      { label: "Inhale", seconds: 4, cue: "Breathe in" },
      { label: "Hold", seconds: 4, cue: "Hold" },
      { label: "Exhale", seconds: 4, cue: "Breathe out" },
      { label: "Hold", seconds: 4, cue: "Hold" },
    ],
    ttsScript: `Welcome. [pause] Let’s take a moment to settle in. [pause] Find a comfortable position, wherever you are. [long pause]

Today, we’ll practice Box Breathing. [pause] This simple, rhythmic breath helps to gently reset your nervous system, bringing a sense of calm and balance. [long pause]

The pattern is simple: We’ll breathe in for four counts, [pause] hold for four, [pause] breathe out for four, [pause] and hold again for four. [pause] We’ll repeat this square rhythm together.

Let’s begin. [pause]

// ── Somatic Practices ───────────────────────────────────────
// Steps and narrations are sourced from somatic-scripts.ts.
// This array holds the PracticeConfig entries for the player system.


import butterflyHugImg from "@/assets/somatic/butterfly-hug.png";
import grounding54321Img from "@/assets/somatic/grounding-54321.png";
import somaticOrientingImg from "@/assets/somatic/somatic-orienting.png";
import haveningTouchImg from "@/assets/somatic/havening-touch.png";
import neurogenicTremoringImg from "@/assets/somatic/neurogenic-tremoring.png";
import bodyScanImg from "@/assets/somatic/body-scan.png";

const SOMATIC_ILLUSTRATIONS: Record<string, string> = {
  "butterfly-hug": butterflyHugImg,
  "grounding-54321": grounding54321Img,
  "somatic-orienting": somaticOrientingImg,
  "havening-touch": haveningTouchImg,
  "neurogenic-tremoring": neurogenicTremoringImg,
  "body-scan": bodyScanImg,
};

function buildSomaticPractices(): PracticeConfig[] {
  return somaticScripts.map((script) => ({
    id: script.id,
    title: script.title,
    subtitle: script.subtitle,
    category: "somatic" as PracticeCategory,
    mode: "narrated-sequence" as PracticeMode,
    durationSec: script.durationSec,
    illustrationUrl: SOMATIC_ILLUSTRATIONS[script.id],
    benefit: script.description,
    audio: {
      enabled: true,
      audioUrl: `/audio/${script.id}.mp3`,
      durationSec: script.durationSec,
      voiceName: "SIGNAL Calm",
      provider: "elevenlabs" as AudioProvider,
    },
    steps: script.steps,
  }));
}

export const SOMATIC_PRACTICES: PracticeConfig[] = buildSomaticPractices();

// ── All practices combined ──────────────────────────────────

export const ALL_PRACTICES: PracticeConfig[] = [
  ...BREATHWORK_PRACTICES,
  ...SOMATIC_PRACTICES,
];

export function getPracticeById(id: string): PracticeConfig | undefined {
  return ALL_PRACTICES.find((p) => p.id === id);
}

export function formatDuration(seconds: number): string {
  const m = Math.floor(seconds / 60);
  const s = seconds % 60;
  if (s === 0) return `${m} min`;
  return `${m}:${s.toString().padStart(2, "0")}`;
}
```

```ts
export type HabitCategory = "supplements" | "nutrition" | "movement" | "self-care";

export const HABIT_CATEGORIES: { id: HabitCategory; label: string; color: string }[] = [
  { id: "supplements", label: "Supplements", color: "hsl(var(--sage-mist))" },
  { id: "nutrition", label: "Nutrition", color: "hsl(var(--petal-gold))" },
  { id: "movement", label: "Movement", color: "hsl(var(--coral-flame))" },
  { id: "self-care", label: "Self Care", color: "hsl(var(--bloom-blush))" },
];

export const CATEGORY_DOT_CLASSES: Record<string, string> = {
  supplements: "bg-sage-mist",
  nutrition: "bg-petal-gold",
  movement: "bg-coral",
  "self-care": "bg-bloom",
  wellness: "bg-bloom",
  mindset: "bg-bloom",
  custom: "bg-sketch",
};

export type HabitFrequencyType = "daily" | "weekly" | "monthly";

export interface Habit {
  id: string;
  name: string;
  category: HabitCategory | string;
  frequencyType?: HabitFrequencyType;
  duration?: string;
  timing?: string;
  notes?: string;
  createdAt: string;
}

// localStorage helpers
export function getHabits(): Habit[] {
  try {
    const val = localStorage.getItem("mindcast_habits");
    return val ? JSON.parse(val) : [];
  } catch { return []; }
}

export function saveHabits(habits: Habit[]): void {
  localStorage.setItem("mindcast_habits", JSON.stringify(habits));
  window.dispatchEvent(new StorageEvent("storage", { key: "mindcast_habits" }));
}

export function addHabit(habit: Habit): void {
  const habits = getHabits();
  habits.push(habit);
  saveHabits(habits);
}

export function removeHabit(id: string): void {
  const habits = getHabits().filter(h => h.id !== id);
  saveHabits(habits);
}

export function getHabitLog(date: string): Record<string, boolean> {
  const val = localStorage.getItem(`habitLog:${date}`);
  return val ? JSON.parse(val) : {};
}

export function setHabitLog(date: string, log: Record<string, boolean>): void {
  localStorage.setItem(`habitLog:${date}`, JSON.stringify(log));
}

export function toggleHabitForDate(date: string, habitId: string): boolean {
  const log = getHabitLog(date);
  log[habitId] = !log[habitId];
  setHabitLog(date, log);
  return log[habitId];
}

export function getWeekHabitData(weekDays: Date[]): { date: string; log: Record<string, boolean> }[] {
  return weekDays.map(d => {
    const dateStr = d.toISOString().split("T")[0];
    return { date: dateStr, log: getHabitLog(dateStr) };
  });
}
```

```ts
// ── Butterfly Hug ───────────────────────────────────────────

const butterflyHug: SomaticPracticeScript = {
  id: "butterfly-hug",
  title: "Butterfly Hug",
  subtitle: "Bilateral self-soothing",

  description:
    "A gentle bilateral stimulation practice used in trauma therapy to calm the nervous system. The alternating tapping activates both hemispheres of the brain, helping to process emotion and restore a sense of safety.",
  narration: `Find a comfortable seated position. Let your body settle here.

Allow your shoulders to soften. Let your hands rest in your lap for a moment.

Take a slow breath in. And a long, easy breath out.

When you're ready, cross your arms over your chest. Rest your hands gently on your opposite shoulders. Your arms are like wings folded inward.

You can close your eyes. Or soften your gaze downward toward the floor.

Now begin gently tapping. Left. Right. Left. Right. Like butterfly wings. Slow and steady.

There is no rush here. Let each tap be soft and deliberate.

As you continue tapping, let your breath stay slow and natural. You do not need to control it. Simply let it flow.

Notice what arises in your body. Sensations. Images. Feelings. You do not need to understand them. Just notice. Observe without judgement.

If a strong emotion surfaces, slow the tapping down. You are in control. You can pause at any time. You are safe right here.

Continue tapping gently. Left. Right. Left. Right.

Let the rhythm soothe you. Like a gentle rocking. Like the steady beat of your own heart.

If your mind begins to wander, that is okay. Simply return to the feeling of your hands on your shoulders. Return to the rhythm.

Continue for a few more moments. There is no destination. Just presence.

Now, slowly begin to still your hands. Let the tapping come to a natural stop.

Rest both hands over your heart. Feel it beating beneath your palms. Steady. Faithful. Yours.

Take one more slow breath in. And let it go.

You are held. You are here. You are safe.

When you are ready, gently open your eyes.`,

const grounding54321: SomaticPracticeScript = {
  id: "grounding-54321",
  title: "5-4-3-2-1 Grounding",
  subtitle: "Sensory anchoring",
  durationSec: 300,
  description:
    "A sensory-based grounding technique that gently anchors your awareness in the present moment by engaging all five senses. It interrupts anxiety spirals and brings you back to the here and now.",
  narration: `Find a comfortable place to sit or stand. Let your feet connect with the ground beneath you.

Take a slow, deep breath in through your nose. And a long, gentle exhale through your mouth.

Let your shoulders drop. Let your jaw soften. You are arriving here. Right now.

We are going to move through your five senses, one at a time. There is no right way to do this. Just notice.

Begin with sight. Look around you and notice five things you can see. Name them silently to yourself, one by one. A colour. A shape. A shadow. A texture. Something small you might normally overlook.

Take your time.

Now, notice four things you can touch. Feel the fabric beneath your hands. The temperature of the air on your skin. The weight of your body in the chair. The ground beneath your feet. Let each sensation anchor you a little deeper.

Now, listen. Notice three things you can hear. Perhaps a distant sound. Something close. The hum of a room. The rhythm of your own breath. Let the sounds wash over you without needing to name them.

Now, two things you can smell. Perhaps something faint. Something familiar. If nothing is present, bring to mind a scent you love. Freshly cut grass. Warm bread. Rain on pavement.

And finally, one thing you can taste. Perhaps just the inside of your mouth. Perhaps a lingering flavour from your last sip of water or tea. Just notice.

Now, take a slow breath in. And let it go.

Feel the weight of your body. The ground beneath you. The air around you. You are here. You are present. You are safe.

When you are ready, gently open your eyes.`,

const somaticOrienting: SomaticPracticeScript = {
  id: "somatic-orienting",
  title: "Somatic Orienting",
  subtitle: "Vagal safety signalling",
  durationSec: 300,
  description:
    "A polyvagal-informed practice that activates your ventral vagal system by slowly orienting your gaze around your environment. It signals safety to the nervous system and gently brings you out of freeze or shutdown states.",
  narration: `Find a place to sit or stand where you feel relatively comfortable. Let your body land here.

Take a moment to notice the weight of your body. The contact between you and whatever is supporting you right now. Chair. Floor. Ground.

Take a slow breath in. And a long, easy exhale.

Now, like a curious animal scanning a new environment, begin to slowly look around the space you are in.

Let your gaze move gently. Without urgency. Without agenda. Simply notice.

Let your head and neck follow your eyes naturally. There is no need to hold anything still.

Look left. Look right. Look up. Look down.

Move slowly. As if you are discovering this room for the very first time.

Notice anything that catches your eye. A colour. A texture. A source of light. Something beautiful. Something ordinary.

If your gaze lands somewhere that feels pleasant or neutral, rest there for a moment. Let your eyes settle. Notice what happens in your body when you do.

Perhaps a softening. A slight drop in the shoulders. A deeper breath. These are signs of your nervous system recalibrating. You are safe.

Continue looking around at your own pace. There is nothing to achieve here. You are simply orienting. Telling your body where you are. And that you are okay.

Now, let your gaze come to rest somewhere soft. A blank wall. Your hands. The floor.

Feel your feet on the ground. The weight of gravity holding you here.

Take one more slow breath in. And let it go.

You are here. You are oriented. You are safe.

When you are ready, gently return.`,
```
